caption:
Sand on a vibrating plate does not scatter. It draws.

Sprinkle sand on a metal plate and play a tone through it. At most frequencies the sand just jitters messily and nothing happens.

Hit one of the plate's natural resonant frequencies and it snaps into a standing wave. Some regions of the plate oscillate hard. Along certain lines the plate does not move at all: the nodal lines.

Sand bounces away from every moving region and gets trapped on the still ones. Within seconds it has collected along the nodes, and the figure you are looking at is the plate's own vibration map, made visible.

Change the frequency, change the mode, get a completely different figure. Same plate. Same sand.

These are Chladni patterns, and they are why violin makers care about plate tuning.

The higher the frequency, the more complex the figure. Guess why.

caption:
Without Einstein, your GPS would be 10 km wrong by tomorrow.

Your phone finds you by timing signals from satellites 20,000 km up. Light covers 300 metres in a microsecond, so an error of one microsecond is an error of 300 metres on the ground.

Those satellite clocks do not tick at your rate, and two effects pull in opposite directions.

They move at about 14,000 km/h, and special relativity says a moving clock runs slow: roughly 7 microseconds lost per day.

They also sit high in Earth's gravity well, and general relativity says a clock higher up runs fast: roughly 45 microseconds gained per day.

Net result: plus 38 microseconds every single day. Left uncorrected that is about 10 km of drift per day, and the system would be useless within hours.

Relativity is not an exotic correction here. Without it, GPS does not work at all.

Both corrections are built into every receiver in your pocket.

Did you know you were carrying a relativity calculator?

caption:
Your hair is not sticking up. It is drawing the electric field.

Hand on the dome, hair straight out. People call this static "sticking", but it is precisely the opposite: everything here is pushing away from everything else.

A moving belt carries charge up to the metal sphere, where it accumulates. Touch it and that charge spreads over you, because charge on a conductor moves to the surface and gets as far apart as it can.

Every hair now carries the same sign of charge. Like charges repel, so each strand pushes every other strand away. The furthest they can get from one another, while still attached to your head, is straight out along the field lines.

So the shape your hair makes is not random. It is a physical map of the field around a charged conductor.

That is electrostatic repulsion, drawn in keratin.

Have you ever done this one at a science museum?

caption:
A cat with zero angular momentum still turns over. Nothing is broken.

Drop a cat upside down, giving it no spin at all, and it lands on its feet without pushing against anything. That looks like it violates conservation of angular momentum.

It does not, and the reason is elegant.

The cat bends at the waist, splitting itself into two halves that rotate about different axes. It pulls its front legs in, making that half easy to turn, and rotates the front through a large angle. The extended back half counter-rotates through a much smaller angle, because it is far harder to turn. Then it swaps: back legs in, front legs out, and repeats.

Total angular momentum stays exactly zero the entire way down. At no instant is the rule broken.

The cat never gains spin. It changes its own SHAPE, and shape is the one thing conservation laws never fixed.

Astronauts reorient in free fall using exactly this trick.

Try it on a swivel chair with your arms and tell me if it worked.

caption:
Your recorded voice is not wrong. You have never heard yourself properly.

Everyone insists the recording is exactly how you sound. To you it sounds like a stranger. The microphone is not lying: you are simply hearing two different signals.

When you speak, the sound reaches your ears by two separate routes.

One goes out of your mouth, through the air, into your ear canal. That is the version a microphone picks up, and the version every other person has always heard.

The other goes straight through the bones of your skull to your inner ear. Bone carries low frequencies far better than air does.

So your own voice arrives with a layer of bass that nobody else ever receives. A recording only has the air path, so that bass is simply absent.

Your pitch never changed. You lost the low end. It is a shift in timbre, not frequency.

Do not believe it? Plug your ears and talk. That sudden boom is the bone-conducted bass, trapped inside your head.

Try it right now, then tell me what you heard.

caption:
This magnet is not balancing. It is pinned.

Cool certain materials far enough and their electrical resistance drops to exactly zero. That alone is remarkable. But something stranger happens at the same moment.

They expel magnetic field from their interior entirely. Bring a magnet near and the superconductor drives the field back out, and that refusal produces a repulsion strong enough to hold the magnet in midair.

That expulsion is the Meissner effect.

And it does more than push. Field lines that do thread through tiny defects get locked in place, which fixes the magnet at a set height and orientation. You can turn the whole thing upside down and the magnet stays put, hanging underneath.

Ordinary magnetic levitation is famously unstable. This is not levitation balancing on a knife edge. It is quantum mechanics holding something still, in front of you, at a temperature you can reach with liquid nitrogen.

Where would you use frictionless suspension first?

caption:
Why does a camera invent a spin that was never really there?

A film is not motion. It is only a row of still snapshots. Between two snapshots the wheel keeps turning, and the camera sees none of it. If a spoke turns almost a full gap between frames, it lands just short. Every spoke looks the same, so you cannot tell one spoke from the next one.

Your eye joins the nearest spokes, so the wheel seems to crawl backwards. Twenty four snapshots a second cannot honestly follow thirty turns a second. To follow a repeating motion you must sample it more than twice each cycle.

Sample slower than that, and a fast motion disguises itself as a slow one.

So the camera did not record that backward spin. Sampling too slowly created it. That is called aliasing.

A helicopter rotor can look frozen on video, because its turn rate happens to match the camera's snapshot rate. Audio recorders filter out fast vibrations first, because sampling them too slowly would turn them into a false low tone.

Did anyone explain it to you this way at school?

caption:
Why does a pulse flip upside down at a tied end but not a loose one?

Send a bump down a rope and it travels as a moving shape. At a tied end, the rope cannot move up or down. The bump tugs that point upward, and the post tugs back just as hard. The tied point must stay at zero, so the returning bump has to cancel the arriving one.

That equal downward tug launches a fresh bump pointing down. A tied end holds still. A free end swings twice the bump's height. At a free end nothing holds the rope, so the tip flies up.

It overshoots to double the height, then whips the rope back. That sends the bump home still the right way up.

So a pulse flips only where the end is held fast. That flip is called a phase change.

Light bouncing off glass flips the same way, since it meets a medium that slows it down. And a guitar string only rings at notes whose waves fit neatly between its two tied ends.

Guess before you scroll, then check.

caption:
Why does a brighter light not knock tiny charges called electrons out with more energy?

Shine light on clean metal and charges do pop out. That much is expected. Turn the lamp up and more of them pop out. But each one leaves just as slowly. Light does not arrive as a smooth stream. It arrives in separate packets.

One packet of blue light carries far more energy than one packet of red. Each packet hands all its energy to one charge, and no more than that. A brighter lamp simply sends more packets, so more charges are freed.

But a bigger crowd of packets never makes a single packet stronger.

So a brighter light sends more packets, not stronger ones. Each packet is called a photon.

A solar cell works only for colours whose packets carry enough energy, which is why infrared light is wasted. Ultraviolet light burns your skin while bright red light does not, because only its packets carry enough energy per hit.

Who else was taught this wrong?

caption:
In a crash, why does an airbag save you when a wall would kill you?

Either way you are moving at the same speed, and either way you end up stopped. Your body carries a certain amount of motion, and all of it has to be removed. The only thing you can change is how long the removal takes. The force needed is the motion removed divided by the time you take to remove it.

Against a hard wall you stop in about one hundredth of a second. All that motion removed in an instant means a colossal force on your chest. An airbag stretches the same stop out over roughly a tenth of a second.

Ten times longer means about one tenth the force, and your ribs survive it.

So the airbag does not absorb the crash. It spreads it out in time. That trade is called the impulse-momentum theorem.

It is why a car bonnet is built to crumple instead of staying rigid. And why a boxer rolls backwards with a punch instead of meeting it square.

caption:
Why can very pure water stay liquid at minus forty degrees?

Freezing does not begin everywhere at once. It has to start somewhere. That start is a tiny speck of ice, perhaps a hundred atoms across. Building it releases energy inside, but it costs energy at the surface.

A tiny speck is almost all surface, so it costs more than it gains. Below a critical size the speck melts back. Above it, the speck grows. So the first speck must appear by luck, and then survive long enough.

In clean water, with no dust to build on, that luck can take hours. A speck built on dust borrows that surface, so it pays far less to get started.

So pure water is not refusing to freeze. It is waiting for a first speck. That start is called nucleation.

Boiling needs the same start, so smooth clean water can superheat well past a hundred degrees before erupting. A rain cloud holds water below freezing until a dust grain arrives and gives the first ice speck a surface.

What did you think the reason was?

caption:
Why does a crowd of hard spheres freeze with no attraction between them?

These balls only refuse to overlap. They neither pull nor push otherwise. Freezing usually sounds like sticking together, so order ought to be impossible. But disorder is not the only way to have very many arrangements. A crowd settles into whichever layout it has the most ways of making.

In a jumbled pack at high density, each ball is jammed tight by its neighbours. Randomly placed neighbours block each other, while neat rows leave every ball an aisle. Line them up on a neat lattice instead, and every ball gains room to rattle. Above forty nine percent packing, the ordered stack offers more wiggle room.

More rattling room means more arrangements, so the ordered stack actually wins.

So hard spheres crystallise to gain freedom, not to stick. That is called entropy driven ordering.

Marbles shaken in a jar settle into neat layers, because ordered packing leaves each marble more space to move. Oil and water separate for a related reason, since freeing the trapped water gives the mixture more arrangements.

Which part of this surprised you?

caption:
Why do two big particles clump together when nothing is pulling them?

There is no glue between them, and no pull across the gap. But the liquid around them is packed with far smaller spheres. Those small spheres cannot get closer than their own radius to a big one.

So each big particle wears a forbidden shell, fifty nanometres thick. Once the two are nearly touching, the slot between them is too thin for a small sphere. When two big particles touch, their forbidden shells overlap and share space. That overlap hands the small spheres extra room to wander in.

More room means more ways to arrange them, and crowds favour more ways. Meanwhile the small spheres batter the pair from outside, with none left between.

So nothing pulls the particles together. The crowd simply presses them shut. That squeeze is called a depletion force.

Red blood cells stack into neat rolls because large proteins are shut out of the gap between them. And paint makers add polymer coils to make pigment grains cling, using this crowding push instead of glue.

Did anyone explain it to you this way at school?

caption:
Why do tiny charges called electrons push outward even when all heat is gone?

Cool an ordinary gas toward absolute zero and its particles settle to a stop. Its pressure fades away, because that pressure came from moving particles. Electrons refuse this. No two of them may share the same state of motion.

So they fill the slow states first, and latecomers are forced into fast ones. There are only so many slow states, and in a crowd they fill up at once. Even at absolute zero, the top electrons in copper move fantastically fast. Those fast electrons still hammer the walls, so the outward push survives.

Cooling cannot help, because the crowding drives them, rather than the heat.

So electrons stay fast because the rules forbid sharing. That push is called degeneracy pressure.

A white dwarf star stops collapsing on this push alone, holding a sun's mass inside an earth sized ball. The stiffness of metals comes from it too, since squeezing a metal crowds its charges into faster states.

Guess before you scroll, then check.

caption:
Why do you stop sooner by not braking as hard as you can?

Slam the pedal and the wheels stop turning. The car keeps going. A rolling tyre grips the road where it touches, and that grip is strong. A rolling tyre's contact patch is standing still on the road, not sliding across it. But once it locks, the rubber is sliding, and sliding grip is weaker.

Gripping beats sliding, by roughly a third. A locked wheel also cannot steer. You go wherever you were already pointed. A sliding tyre drags backwards along your motion, whichever way you point it. So the car's computer releases and reapplies the brake many times a second.

Each release lets the tyre roll again, keeping it just short of locking.

So braking harder is not braking better. Holding the tyre at the edge of sliding is. That is the difference between static and sliding friction.

A rock climber relies on it. A shoe pressed still against rock holds; the instant it slips, it keeps slipping. And a train driver brakes gently on purpose. Once steel wheels slide on steel rail, there is almost no grip left.

Who else was taught this wrong?

Slam the pedal and the wheels stop turning. The car keeps going. A rolling tyre grips the road where it touches, and that grip is strong. A rolling tyre's contact patch is standing still on the road, not sliding across it. But once it locks, the rubber is sliding, and sliding grip is weaker.

Gripping beats sliding, by roughly a third. A locked wheel also cannot steer. You go wherever you were already pointed. A sliding tyre drags backwards along your motion, whichever way you point it. So the car's computer releases and reapplies the brake many times a second.

Each release lets the tyre roll again, keeping it just short of locking.

So braking harder is not braking better. Holding the tyre at the edge of sliding is. That is the difference between static and sliding friction.

A rock climber relies on it. A shoe pressed still against rock holds; the instant it slips, it keeps slipping. And a train driver brakes gently on purpose. Once steel wheels slide on steel rail, there is almost no grip left.

caption:
Why does a binary pair of dead stars chirp upward before they merge?

Two dense stars circle each other, dragging the shape of space as they go. That stirring carries energy away as ripples travelling at the speed of light. The ripples arrive at the rate the pair circles, so the orbit rate is the pitch. Losing energy means the pair cannot hold its orbit. It falls inward.

A tighter orbit is a faster orbit, so they swing around more often. Halve the separation, and the pair circles nearly three times as fast. Faster circling pours out ripples harder still, which shrinks the orbit faster.

So the loss feeds itself, and the tone climbs until the two finally touch.

So a binary pair sings higher because it is dying. That rising tone is called a chirp.

A satellite in thin air spirals down and speeds up, because losing energy tightens an orbit the same way. LIGO heard this rise in 2015, and the speed of the climb revealed the two masses.

caption:
Why does a plank on frictionless ice slide back as a man walks along it?

Nothing outside pushes the pair sideways, because the ice cannot grip. He pushes the plank backwards, and the plank pushes him forwards. Those two pushes are equal and opposite, so they cancel for the pair.

So the balance point of man and plank cannot shift at all. Say a sixty kilogram man walks along a forty kilogram plank. He steps five metres along it, so the two must share those five. The heavier one counts for more at the balance point, so it has to move less.

Heavier means less shifting, so he moves two metres and the plank three. Together those make five, and the balance point stays exactly put.

So the plank slides back because the balance point holds still. That point is called the centre of mass.

Step off a small boat onto a dock and the boat slides away. Nothing outside pushed the pair. And a rocket moves forward only by hurling fuel backwards, keeping the balance point of both fixed.

What did you think the reason was?

caption:
Why does a straw stop working past ten metres?

Sucking does not pull the drink upward. It only removes the air above it. The air outside presses down on the drink and pushes it up the tube. That outside push is fixed, and it can only hold up so much water.

Air can hold ten metres of water, or seventy six centimetres of mercury. Suck harder and the pressure inside falls toward nothing. Nothing is the floor. Past ten metres the weight of the column simply beats the air's push.

The water stops rising there, and the space above it fills with vapour.

So a straw never lifts anything. The air does, and ten metres is its ceiling. That limit is called the barometric height.

A deep well pump sits near the water, not at the top, because air can push it only ten metres. Mercury barometers stay short because mercury is thirteen times denser, so the same air push holds only seventy six centimetres.

caption:
Why does water pressure depend on depth, and not on how much water there is?

Picture a thin pipe and a wide barrel, both filled to the same height. Press a finger against the bottom of each. The push feels identical. The push at a point is just the weight of the column standing above it.

A taller column means more weight on every square centimetre, so a harder push. One metre down, or ten metres down. Only the height changes the answer. Extra water off to the side sits above its own patch of floor, not yours.

So widening a container adds total force, but it never adds pressure.

So depth sets the push, and width only sets the total. That is called hydrostatic pressure.

A dam is built thick at the bottom because the push there comes from depth, not from the lake's width. Your blood pressure is read at the arm, level with the heart. Raise the arm and the reading drops, just like shallower water.

Did anyone explain it to you this way at school?

caption:
Why can you not simply build a giant of the same shape?

Double a person's height and keep every single proportion the same. Their weight follows volume, so it climbs eight times over. But bone strength follows cross section area, which climbs only four times.

Eight times the load, carried by four times the bone. So the squeeze inside every bone doubles, purely from being bigger. Bone snaps above a fixed squeeze per square centimetre, however big the animal is. Keep scaling and the bones finally crush under the body's own weight.

The only escape is to change shape, growing legs thicker than scaling alone.

So a giant cannot share our shape. Volume outruns area. That is called the square cube law.

An elephant has stubby pillar legs while a gazelle has thin ones, because bone area must grow faster than mass. An ant survives a long fall, because its surface drag grew large compared with its very tiny weight.

Guess before you scroll, then check.

caption:
Why can you not remove gravity everywhere by simply falling?

Step off a tower and, for a moment, you feel no weight at all. Release two small balls beside you and they seem to hang perfectly still. But both balls are falling toward the centre of the Earth, not straight down.

Those two paths lean slightly inward, so the balls drift together as you fall. Ten metres apart, dropped a hundred kilometres, they close by sixteen centimetres. Gravity pulls weaker the further you are from the Earth's centre. A ball above you falls a little slower, and one below falls faster.

So free fall hides the pull, yet it cannot hide how the pull changes.

So falling erases gravity at one point only. The stretch that survives is called a tidal force.

The ocean bulges on both sides of Earth, because the Moon pulls the near water harder than the far water. A moon drifting too close is torn into rings, because that stretch beats its own weak gravity.

Who else was taught this wrong?

caption:
Why does an exploding shell keep flying along its original curve?

The blast looks like the end of the flight, but it is not. The explosion throws every fragment apart with enormous forces. Each push comes with an equal push the other way, inside the shell.

So all those inside pushes add to exactly zero for the whole set. Pushes inside a group only swap motion between the pieces, they never add any. The blast changes the group's average speed by nothing. Gravity still pulls. Only gravity acts from outside, and gravity was already acting before.

So the average position of all the pieces carries on untouched. It sails along the same curve while the fragments spray around it. Catch every piece, average them, and you retrace the old path exactly.

So the shell is gone, but its average point flies on. That point is called the centre of mass.

A firework bursts into a ball of sparks, and that ball's centre keeps falling along the rocket's path. And a high jumper arches so her body clears the bar while her balance point passes underneath.

caption:
Why does simply knowing where a gas particle sits let you extract work?

Picture a sealed box with one gas particle bouncing inside. Knowing nothing, you can pull no work from the box. Not knowing the side, you would get drumming on both faces and the wall would go nowhere. Now you look, and you see the particle in the left half.

You slide a thin wall down the middle, trapping it on the left. The particle drums on that wall, so the wall drifts slowly right. Let it lift a load, and you have turned room heat into work.

One bit of knowing is worth about three zeptojoules at room temperature. To run the trick again, your notebook has to be blank the way it started. But your memory now holds that bit, and memories must be cleared. Clearing that bit dumps at least the heat you gained.

So knowing is never free. The books balance only once you pay to forget. That is called Landauer's principle.

A demon sorting fast and slow particles fails the same way, since its notebook must eventually be wiped. And a computer warms up partly because erasing memory carries a real heat cost you cannot dodge.

What did you think the reason was?

caption:
Why does a wave's speed belong to the rope and not to your hand?

Shake a rope gently, then hard. The bump travels just as fast. Your hand sets the bump's size, and how often you shake. But the travelling depends on how the rope hands motion along itself.

A tight rope yanks each bit back hard, so it responds quickly. A heavy rope is sluggish, so it responds slowly. Heavy here means heavy per metre, not how much the whole rope weighs. Pull the same string four times tighter and waves run twice as fast.

So the speed comes from pull against weight, alone. Shake faster and the waves simply bunch closer together instead. The speed stays put, so the spacing shrinks to match.

So your hand does not set the speed. The rope's pull and its weight do. That is called the wave speed of the medium.

Sound crosses a room at one speed whether you whisper or shout, because the air decides it. And light from a torch and from a distant star arrive equally fast, set by empty space.

Which part of this surprised you?

caption:
Why can a bacterium not swim by flapping back and forth?

At its size, water feels as thick as honey. Stop pushing and it halts within less than the width of an atom. So it moves only while it is changing shape, never after.

Imagine a hinge that opens slowly, then snaps shut. One full open and shut leaves it exactly where it started. Snapping fast gains nothing, because the thick water pushes back harder in exactly the same proportion. Run that motion backwards and it looks the same, just played in reverse.

So whatever it gains opening, it hands back closing, and it goes nowhere. It needs a stroke that differs forwards and backwards in time. So it turns a corkscrew tail, which keeps screwing the same way round.

So a bacterium cannot flap its way along. It must turn a corkscrew that never retraces itself. That rule is called the scallop theorem.

Sperm swim with a wave running down the tail, so the shape never simply retraces itself. And a ship's propeller keeps turning one way, because reversing it would only drag the ship backwards.

Did anyone explain it to you this way at school?

caption:
Why does a fast cricket ball carry a wave nobody can ever detect?

Every moving thing has a wave spacing, called its wavelength. It equals one very tiny number divided by the object's mass times speed. That tiny number is Planck's constant, about ten to the minus thirty four.

A single electron is so light that its wave spacing comes out atom sized. A cricket ball is a hundred billion billion billion times heavier. An electron's wave sits near an atom. The ball's sits far, far below.

So its wave spacing shrinks to about ten to the minus thirty four metres. A wave only shows itself at an obstacle near its own size, and nothing is that small.

So the cricket ball really does have a wave. It is just billions of times finer than anything we can probe. That spacing is called its de Broglie wavelength.

A served tennis ball never spreads or fans out, because its wave is finer than any slit we could cut. And an electron microscope beats a light one, since a slow electron has a wave far finer than visible light.

Guess before you scroll, then check.

caption:
Why does air wreck the parabola instead of just shortening it?

In a vacuum the path is a perfect parabola, the same going up and coming down. Air pushes back on a moving ball, and that push grows with speed squared. Double the speed and the push is four times stronger. Drag always opposes the motion, so it adds to gravity going up and fights it coming down.

So the fast early climb is hit hardest, and the rise flattens quickly. By the top the ball is slow, so it drops almost straight down. No air, two hundred and six metres. Real air, about a hundred and twenty.

So one half of the path is long and low, the other short and steep.

So air does not shrink the parabola. It replaces it. The steep, lopsided real path is called a ballistic trajectory.

A badminton shuttle drops almost vertically after its peak, because drag kills its forward speed within a metre. And a skydiver stops speeding up, because drag grows until it exactly matches her weight.

Who else was taught this wrong?

caption:
Why does a quantum computer not simply try every answer at once?

It really does hold many answers at the same time. But you never read them all. One measurement hands you one answer. Each possible answer carries a wave, with a height and a timing. The taller an answer's wave, the likelier a measurement lands on that answer.

Waves can add up, or cancel, the way ripples do on a pond. Searching a million items takes a million tries. Waves need about a thousand. A quantum program steers those waves so the wrong answers cancel out.

The right answer's waves line up and add, so its height grows. Then one measurement is very likely to hand you that answer.

So the computer gains nothing from holding every answer. It gains by cancelling the wrong ones. That is called interference.

Noise cancelling headphones do this too, adding an opposite wave so unwanted sound dies at your ear. And a soap bubble shows colour because waves off its two surfaces cancel some shades and reinforce others.

Try it tonight and tell me what happened.

caption:
Why is a small soap bubble at higher pressure than a big one?

Connect a small bubble to a big one and the small one shrinks away. It blows itself into the large one, which is the opposite of what you expect. A soap film pulls itself tight, like a stretched sheet of rubber.

That inward pull has to be balanced by extra air pressure inside. On a tightly curved surface the pull aims more steeply inward. A centimetre across, ten pascals extra. A millimetre across, a hundred.

So the smaller the bubble, the harder its film squeezes the air inside. Air always flows from the higher pressure to the lower, so the small one empties.

So a small bubble is not the weaker one. Its tighter curve squeezes harder, so its pressure runs higher. That is called Laplace pressure.

Your lungs coat their smallest air sacs with a soapy film, so tiny sacs do not empty into big ones. And a tiny droplet squeezes itself harder than a big one, which is why fine mists vanish faster.

caption:
Why does a narrower slit spread a laser beam out wider?

Open the gap wider and the bright patch on the wall shrinks. Squeeze the gap thinner and the patch grows, which feels completely backwards. Light is a wave, so every point inside the gap sends out ripples.

A thin gap has no far apart edges, so cancelling starts only at a wide angle.

So the laser is not squeezed by the narrower gap. Pinning light down in space forces it to spread in angle. That is called diffraction.

A telescope must be wide, because a small opening pins the light down and blurs every distant star. And sound spreads out of a doorway the same way, so you hear deep notes around the corner.

caption:
Why does a fast moving charge carry a pancake shaped field?

A charge sitting still has a field spraying out evenly in every direction. Set it moving near light speed and that pattern stops being a sphere. Ride along beside the charge and everything looks normal and perfectly round.

But you are standing in the lab, and lengths along the motion look squashed. So the whole field pattern is flattened in the direction of travel. The same field crowded into a thin disc is packed tighter sideways and thinned out ahead. Sideways the field doubles. Straight ahead it drops to a fifth.

Sideways the field gets stronger, and straight ahead it nearly disappears.

So a moving charge does not drag its field behind it. Motion flattens the pattern into a pancake. That squashing is called Lorentz contraction.

A particle accelerator beam pushes sideways on its own neighbours far harder than a slow beam would. And a fast electron passing an atom lands one sharp sideways kick, which is how it knocks electrons loose.

caption:
Why does doubling your processors rarely double the speed?

Split the job in two and hand half to each chip. That sounds like double. But part of every job refuses to be split at all. Reading the input, choosing a plan, writing the answer: these happen once, in order.

Call that the serial stretch, the part no extra chip can touch. Suppose one tenth of the work is serial and cannot be shared out. Sixteen chips should give sixteen times. They give six point four.

Even with endless chips that tenth remains, so ten times is your ceiling. Shrink the shareable part to nothing and the job still takes that serial tenth of the time.

So extra processors only shrink the shareable part. The stubborn serial stretch sets your ceiling on speed. That is called Amdahl's law.

Ten cooks chop faster, but the oven still bakes for forty minutes, so dinner barely arrives sooner. And adding engineers to a late project helps little, because the design decisions still happen in order.

caption:
Why does averaging a hundred readings only make you ten times better?

Each reading is the true value plus a random wobble, up or down. Averaging helps because those wobbles have no favourite direction and partly cancel. But cancelling is a random walk, not a clean wipe out.

Take a hundred random steps and you drift about ten steps away, not zero. Ups and downs cancel in pairs, but their numbers are never exactly equal. So the leftover error shrinks like the square root of how many readings you took. One reading, one millivolt of noise. A hundred readings, a tenth of that.

Four readings cut the error in half. A hundred divide it by ten.

So a hundred readings do not buy a hundred times the precision. Random wobbles only partly cancel. That is called the root N rule.

Doubling a telescope's exposure time only sharpens the picture by about forty percent, for exactly this reason. And an election poll of four thousand people is only twice as sharp as one of a thousand.

Who else was taught this wrong?

caption:
Why do gas particles fly at five hundred metres a second while smells crawl?

A perfume particle really does move near the speed of sound. But the air is crowded, and it strikes a neighbour almost at once. In room air it flies about seventy nanometres before the next collision.

Every hit sends it off in a fresh random direction. Take a hundred random steps and you finish only ten steps away. Opposite steps mostly cancel, and only the small leftover imbalance carries it along. So progress grows with the square root of the number of steps.

A staggering walk covers far less ground than a straight run. Billions of collisions a second, and the smell still needs minutes to arrive.

So the particles are fast, but smells are slow because the path zigzags. That spreading is called diffusion.

Sugar in still tea spreads painfully slowly, which is why you stir it. Stirring carries it bodily instead. And a drop of ink creeps through still water for hours, though its particles never stop moving.

caption:
Why can three polarising sheets pass light that two of them block?

Cross two of these sheets and the view through them goes completely black. Now slide a third sheet in between, turned halfway. The light comes back. Adding a filter should only remove light, so this looks impossible.

A sheet does not simply block. It keeps the part of the wave lined up with itself. So whatever gets through comes out pointing along that sheet's direction. A wave pointing at right angles to a sheet has no part along it, so nothing passes. Straight into a crossed sheet, nothing. Through the middle one first, a quarter.

The middle sheet sits at forty five degrees and re-aims the light.

So the third sheet does not sneak light past the other two. It re-aims the wave so the last sheet can pass it. That rule is called Malus's law.

Rotating a camera filter changes how much sky glare passes, because only the matching part of each wave gets through. And a quantum measurement behaves the same way, since measuring at a new angle re-aims what you measure next.

What did you think the reason was?

caption:
Why does a star hold steady for billions of years with no control system?

It is a nuclear furnace with no thermostat and nobody watching it. Squeeze the core a little and it grows hotter and denser. Squeezing a gas heats it, and letting it swell back out cools it again. Nuclear burning climbs steeply with temperature, so the fire jumps.

Ten percent hotter, and the core burns about half again as fast. That extra heat raises the pressure, so the core expands against gravity. Expanding cools it, and the burning rate drops straight back down.

It runs the other way too. A cool core shrinks, heats, and burns harder.

So the star holds steady by itself. Heat and gravity keep correcting each other. We call that negative feedback.

A house thermostat does the same, cutting the heater whenever the room drifts above its target. And a steam engine's spinning governor closes the valve as it speeds up, so the speed settles itself.

Which part of this surprised you?

caption:
Why does a nuclear reactor core glow blue under water?

That blue is not heat, and it is not the fuel burning. Light itself travels slower through water, at about three quarters of its empty space speed. The charged pieces flying out of the fuel are barely slowed by the water.

So light in water crawls, while the escaping particle still outruns it. As it races past, it tugs the water's own charges, and they give off light settling back. A charge crosses the water faster than the ripples of light it stirs up. Those ripples pile into a cone behind it, like the shock wave of a jet.

That cone reaches your eye as a sheet of light, strongest at the blue end.

So nothing here beats light in empty space. The reactor simply beats light in water. That glow is called Cherenkov radiation.

A sonic boom is the same pile-up made with sound, when a jet outruns its own spreading waves. Buried ice detectors watch for that faint blue cone, so every neutrino strike announces the direction it came from.

Did anyone explain it to you this way at school?

caption:
Why does one gas need two different numbers for its heat capacity?

Heat a kilogram of water and you quote one number. Gases refuse that. Seal the gas in a rigid steel box and warm it. Nothing moves. Every bit of heat goes into making the gas hotter, and nothing else.

Now put the same gas under a sliding piston that holds the pressure steady. Warm it and the gas expands, lifting that piston against the air above. Warming makes the gas push harder, so it must swell until its push matches the air again. So part of the heat is spent as work, not as temperature.

To get the same rise in temperature you must supply more heat.

So a gas carries two heat numbers because it can push. The gap between them is called the gas constant.

The speed of sound in air depends on the ratio of these two numbers. That ratio puts it near 340 metres per second. And a hot air balloon works at steady pressure. The warmed air expands and shoves the surrounding air aside.

Guess before you scroll, then check.

caption:
Why does a clock on a shelf run faster than one on the floor?

The two clocks are identical. Nothing mechanical is different between them. Gravity does more than pull on things. It also stretches time itself. Light climbing away from a mass arrives with fewer wiggles, and a slower clock is what that means. Deeper in a gravity well, every process runs a little slower.

The floor sits deeper in that well than the shelf, by the shelf's own height. So raise a clock by thirty-three centimetres and it gains a second per billion years. The size is gravity times height, divided by the speed of light squared.

Optical clocks tick a thousand trillion times a second, so even that gap is visible.

So the clock on the shelf gains nothing mechanically. It simply sits where time runs faster. That is called gravitational redshift.

Satellite navigation corrects for this daily, since clocks in orbit gain about thirty-eight millionths of a second. And surveyors can now read height from clock rate alone, because a lower clock always ticks a little slower.

Who else was taught this wrong?

caption:
Why can a tiny system run the second law of thermodynamics backwards for a moment?

The law says disorder grows. Spilt heat never gathers itself back up. But that law is a counting statement, not a command handed down by nature. Air fills a room evenly because far more arrangements look even than look lopsided. Every single arrangement is equally likely, so you see whichever kind has the most.

With five particles, all of them crowding one side happens three times in a hundred. Add particles and that chance collapses. A speck of dust already holds a billion billion. So for anything you can see, the odds of running backwards are hopeless.

But shrink it to one bead jiggling in water and backward steps become measurable.

So the second law is not unbreakable. It is odds so long that bending never shows. That rule is called the fluctuation theorem.

Brownian motion is the same story, where random kicks briefly shove a pollen grain against the crowd. And a tiny machine must fight this, because heat noise can drive its parts backwards as easily as forwards.

caption:
Why does almost every system in physics behave like a spring?

A pendulum, a bond between two atoms, and a bridge share one equation. Anything stable sits at the bottom of some energy valley. At the very bottom the slope is zero, or it would roll away. The steeper the valley under your feet, the harder it pushes you back to the bottom.

So zoom in close and every smooth valley floor looks like the same parabola. A parabola shaped valley pulls back in direct proportion to how far you stray. Swing five degrees and the spring answer is right to a twentieth of a percent.

That is exactly the rule a spring obeys, so the motion comes out identical.

So physics is not secretly full of springs. It is full of valleys, and every valley bottom is a parabola. We call that the harmonic oscillator.

A guitar string, a quartz watch crystal and a swaying bridge all solve the same valley bottom equation. And a carbon dioxide molecule traps heat because its bonds sit in valleys and vibrate like little springs.

What did you think the reason was?

caption:
Why do polarised sunglasses kill glare best at one particular angle?

Glare is sunlight bounced off something flat, like water or a sheet of glass. That bounce is not the light simply turning around at the surface. The arriving light shakes the charges inside the glass, and those shaking charges send it out again. Ordinary light is an even mix of two shake directions, one across the surface and one along it.

And a shaking charge sends out nothing at all along the line it shakes along. At one angle the reflection would sit exactly on that line. Water fifty-three degrees, glass fifty-six. So that half of the light has no way to leave as a reflection.

Only the half shaking sideways bounces off, and it all wobbles one way.

So the glare at that angle is one-way light, which a simple filter wipes out. That is called Brewster's angle.

Photographers turn a polarising filter to see through water, because those surface reflections all share a single wobble direction. And laser tubes use windows tilted to this angle, so one wobble direction passes through with almost no loss.

caption:
Why does heat reach only a sliver of the tiny charges called electrons in a metal?

A metal is a stiff grid of atoms with those charges free to roam. By the old classical rules every one of them should soak up heat. But two of these charges cannot share the same state of motion, so they stack up.

They fill every level from the bottom up to a sharp top edge. Room warmth is a nudge of one fortieth of a volt. That stack is seven volts deep. A charge buried deep has no empty level to enter, so warmth cannot shift it.

Only the ones within a nudge of the top edge have somewhere to go.

So the metal is not being lazy. Only the charges at that top edge can answer. We call it the Fermi surface.

A metal's heat capacity rises straight in step with temperature, because a bigger nudge simply frees a thicker shell. An electric current works the same way, since only charges beside that edge find empty states to move into.

caption:
Why can you hear someone around a corner but never see them?

Sound and light are both waves. Both set out from that person. A wave spreads sideways whenever it squeezes past an edge or a gap. How much it spreads depends on the size of the wave against the gap. Across a wide gap the two edges' ripples fall out of step sideways and cancel each other.

One sound wave can be metres long, about the size of a doorway. One light wave is half a millionth of a metre. Tiny beside that door. So sound, matched to the door, fans out widely into the room beyond.

Light, far smaller than the door, runs straight on and casts a sharp shadow.

So the corner treats them differently only because of size. That spreading is called diffraction.

Deep bass notes reach you outside a club, because long waves bend around the corner and high notes barely do. And a radio signal reaches a valley floor, because its waves are metres long and bend over the ridge.

caption:
Why does a speeding electron throw all its light into one narrow forward beam?

A tiny charge called an electron gives off light whenever its path bends. Sitting almost still, it would spread that light evenly, all around itself. But inside a storage ring it is pushed to within a whisker of light speed.

Now picture running through falling rain. The drops seem to arrive from ahead. In its own frame the light still goes sideways; racing towards us, we see it arrive from ahead. Motion tilts every direction forward. Sideways at rest, a hundredth of a degree at three billion volts. So the whole spread folds forward, into a thin cone wrapped around its motion.

The faster it flies, the tighter that cone. Double the energy and cut the angle in half.

So the electron is not aiming at anything. Its own sideways light is swept forward by its speed. That is called relativistic beaming.

Matter racing near light speed beams its glow forward, so a blazar jet can outshine its whole galaxy. Free electron lasers use this squeeze, wiggling charges near light speed so their light leaves as a pencil beam.

caption:
Why do two careful measurements of the expanding universe disagree?

Space itself stretches, so distant galaxies drift apart. One number sets how fast. The first route reads the oldest light, set free when the universe was young. Feed that baby picture into our best model, then run the model forward. The early light fixes the young universe, and only the model carries that number to today.

The early light says sixty-seven. The nearby stars say seventy-three. The second route climbs a ladder of nearby distances, using pulsing stars and exploding stars. Both teams now quote errors near one percent, so the gap will not shrink away.

Five percent apart, with error bars that do not overlap each other. Nobody yet knows which route is wrong, and that unsolved gap is the whole story.

So one side measures the universe now, and the other predicts it from its youth. That gap is called the Hubble tension.

A missing ingredient in the young universe would change the prediction, so unknown physics could open the gap. Or a hidden systematic error sits in one rung of the ladder. A mis-set ruler skews everything after it.

Which part of this surprised you?

caption:
Why can an insect walk on water but sink straight through alcohol?

The insect is denser than water, so it is not simply floating. Look closely and the surface is dented, like a taut sheet of cling film. Water's own tiny particles grip each other hard, so the surface resists tearing. The pull runs along the surface, so once the surface is dented part of it points upward.

That skin pushes up along every leg, and the total beats the insect's weight. Water pulls seventy two. Alcohol pulls only twenty two. Alcohol's particles grip each other about three times more weakly.

Worse, alcohol soaks the waxy legs and climbs them instead of holding them up.

So the insect is not light enough to float. It rides a taut water skin that alcohol cannot provide. That pull is called surface tension.

A steel paperclip rests on water though steel is eight times denser, because the dented surface holds it. And a drop of soap sinks that paperclip at once, since soap weakens the very pull holding it.

caption:
Why must a quantum computer sit colder than deep space itself?

A qubit keeps its information in two energy states, one low and one high. The step between them is small, matching a microwave ripple of five billion wiggles a second. Heat is random energy shared around, and it grows with temperature.

So that step matches a quarter of a kelvin, while space sits at two point seven. Deep space is therefore more than ten times too warm for this chip. A heat kick bigger than the step can lift the qubit; far smaller kicks almost never can. A stray kick of heat would flip the qubit mid calculation and wipe the answer.

Cool it to ten thousandths of a kelvin and that chance drops below one in a billion.

So the quantum machine is chilled to stop heat whispering to it. That chance is called the Boltzmann factor.

Infrared telescopes are chilled hard too, because their own warm glow would drown the faint sky they watch. And a single photon detector needs the same chill, so random heat cannot fake the click of a real photon.

Go and test it, then report back.

caption:
Why is there still light just outside a surface that reflects everything back?

Aim a beam up at a water surface from below, at a shallow enough slant. It all comes back down. Not one ray gets out into the air. Yet the light does not stop dead at the boundary itself. A wave cannot drop straight to zero at a boundary, so it has to fade away outside.

It leans across and fades out within a small fraction of a hair's width. A wave of green light is five hundred and fifty nanometres. Its reach past the glass is a hundred. That clinging field carries no energy away, so the reflection stays complete. That field only sloshes in and out in place, so nothing ever travels away.

But hold a second glass block inside that reach and light crosses the gap.

So the light stops travelling outside, and still it reaches out a little. That clinging field is called an evanescent wave.

A fingerprint reader works this way, because ridges pressed on the glass steal light from that clinging field. And a quantum particle crosses a barrier the same way, its wave leaking in and reappearing on the far side.

Who else was taught this wrong?

caption:
Why is a fridge cold inside but hot at the back?

A fridge cannot make cold. There is no such thing as cold to make. There is only heat, and heat always drifts from warm things to cool things. So a fridge does not create cold. It carries heat out of the box.

Inside, a liquid is allowed to expand and turn to gas, which makes it very cold. Spreading out and breaking apart costs the liquid energy, and it takes that energy from its own warmth. Colder than the food, so heat flows from the food into it. That gas is then pumped to the coils at the back and squeezed hard, which makes it hot. Squeezing crowds its particles and speeds them up, and faster particles mean a hotter gas.

Hotter than your kitchen, so the heat it collected flows out into the room.

So a fridge is not a cold maker. It is a heat mover, and the warmth at the back is the heat taken from your food. That is called a heat pump.

An air conditioner is the same machine, with the hot coils hanging outside your window. Run one backwards and it heats a house in winter, using less energy than a heater.

Try it tonight and tell me what happened.

caption:
Why does a curved mirror blur the edges of the image it makes?

The middle of the image can be razor sharp. The rim stays soft. A sphere is the easy shape to grind, and it is nearly right. Rays that strike near the middle all cross the axis at one neat point.

But a ray hitting the outer rim is thrown back at a steeper angle. Out at the rim the sphere tilts more sharply than one shared focus would need. It crosses the axis closer to the mirror, missing that first point. So every ring of the mirror has its own focus, spread along the axis.

No screen can catch them all, so the edges smear into a soft halo.

So the mirror is blurred by its own shape. That error is called spherical aberration.

Big telescope mirrors are ground into a parabola instead, because that shape brings every ring to one focus. And a camera lens stacks several glass elements, because one simple curve focuses its rim and its centre differently.

What did you think the reason was?

caption:
Why can a satellite sit over one city only at one exact height?

It is not hovering. It is falling around the Earth like every satellite. To stay above one city, it must go round once in a day. But orbit speed is not free to choose. Gravity sets it.

Close in, gravity pulls hard, so a low satellite laps us in ninety minutes. Far out, gravity is weaker, so one lap takes far longer. Further out the circle is bigger and the needed speed smaller, so the lap takes far longer. There is exactly one radius where that lap takes twenty four hours.

It is forty two thousand kilometres out from the centre of the Earth. It must also circle over the equator, the same way round as the Earth turns.

So the satellite cannot pick its own height. The length of our day picks it. That rule is called Kepler's third law.

Every GPS satellite sits at twenty thousand kilometres, because its orbit has to take exactly half a day. And the Moon needs twenty seven days for one lap, because it circles far out where gravity is weak.

Which part of this surprised you?

caption:
Why does a battery hand over the most power when half the energy is wasted?

Every battery has some resistance inside it, and you cannot switch that off. Hook on a tiny load and a huge current flows, but the load barely resists. So nearly all the heating happens inside the battery, not in the load.

Hook on a very large load and the current falls to almost nothing. Between those extremes there is a peak, and a matched load sits on it. The load takes the most power when its resistance equals the battery's own.

But then the two are equal, so exactly half the energy heats the battery. The same current runs through both, so equal resistances soak up equal shares.

So maximum power and high efficiency are different goals. Matching the two resistances is called impedance matching.

A radio aerial is matched to its cable, because a mismatch reflects the signal back instead of sending it out. And the power grid refuses to match on purpose, because losing half the energy in the generators would be ruinous.

Did anyone explain it to you this way at school?

caption:
How does a pool player stop the cue ball dead on impact?

It strikes, stops instantly, and the other ball leaves with all the speed. The trick only works because both balls weigh exactly the same. In a clean collision, both the motion and the energy must be carried forward. Hard polished balls hardly dent or heat, so almost none of the energy is lost in the hit. By motion we mean weight times speed, added up over both balls.

Equal weights leave only one way to satisfy both at once. If the cue ball kept any speed, the two together would carry more energy than arrived. That one outcome is a complete handover, with nothing left behind. So the moving ball stops dead, and the still one leaves at its speed.

Try it with a heavy ball against a light one and it never happens.

So the pool player does not stop the cue ball by skill alone. It hands over everything because the weights match. That is an elastic collision.

A Newton's cradle shows it endlessly. One ball swings in, one swings out, never two. And a reactor slows neutrons with light atoms, because equal partners take the most energy per hit.

Guess before you scroll, then check.

caption:
Why does opening a switch on a coil make a fat blue spark?

The battery offers only twelve volts. A spark in air needs hundreds. Current running round a coil builds a magnetic field in and around it. That field holds energy, and the coil resists any change to its current.

Open the switch and you ask that current to stop almost instantly. The field's stored energy has to go somewhere, and the only path left is that gap. The faster the current dies, the harder the coil pushes to keep it flowing. Twelve volts go in. Six hundred volts appear across the opening contacts.

So the coil throws up hundreds of volts, and the air itself breaks down.

So the spark is the coil defending its current as the switch opens. That surge is called back EMF.

A spark plug uses this on purpose. Cutting a coil's current makes tens of thousands of volts across the gap. Relays carry a small diode across the coil, giving the dying current a quiet loop to run in instead.

Who else was taught this wrong?

caption:
Why does friction sometimes point the same way you are moving?

You were taught that friction fights motion. Now watch a driving wheel. At the bottom of a rolling tyre, the rubber is not sliding at all. It is planted on the road, still, for one brief instant. The wheel's turn carries that patch backwards exactly as fast as the car carries it forward, so it stands still.

A gripping tyre can give far more force than a skidding one. The engine twists that patch, so it tries to push the road backward. The road pushes forward on the tyre with an equal shove. Grip always pushes back against the way a surface is trying to slip, even before any slipping starts.

So the car is thrown forward by the very force said to hold it back.

So friction does not oppose the car. It opposes sliding between two surfaces. That grip is called static friction.

Your shoe presses the pavement backward, and the ground's grip presses you forward, which is how walking works. A conveyor belt speeds a box up by friction, dragging it forward until the box matches the belt.

Why does friction sometimes point the same way you are moving?

You were taught that friction fights motion. Now watch a driving wheel. At the bottom of a rolling tyre, the rubber is not sliding at all. It is planted on the road, still, for one brief instant. The wheel's turn carries that patch backwards exactly as fast as the car carries it forward, so it stands still.

A gripping tyre can give far more force than a skidding one. The engine twists that patch, so it tries to push the road backward. The road pushes forward on the tyre with an equal shove. Grip always pushes back against the way a surface is trying to slip, even before any slipping starts.

So the car is thrown forward by the very force said to hold it back.

So friction does not oppose the car. It opposes sliding between two surfaces. That grip is called static friction.

Your shoe presses the pavement backward, and the ground's grip presses you forward, which is how walking works. A conveyor belt speeds a box up by friction, dragging it forward until the box matches the belt.

caption:
Why can a singer shatter a wine glass with nothing but their voice?

It is not simply about being loud. A shout will not do it. Flick a wine glass and it rings. That ring is the glass flexing in and out. Every object flexes most easily at one particular rate, its own natural note.

Sing that exact note, and each sound wave arrives just as the glass flexes outward. So every wave gives a tiny push in the direction the glass was already moving. The flexing grows and grows, wave after wave, far beyond a single push. At any other note the pushes arrive out of step and cancel, so nothing ever builds.

Eventually the glass bends further than glass can bend, and it fails.

So it is not force that shatters the glass. It is timing, repeated. That build-up is called resonance.

Soldiers break step on a bridge so their marching cannot build the same way. And every radio works by resonating with one station's rhythm and ignoring all the others arriving at the same time.

What did you think the reason was?

caption:
Why does a magnet fall slowly down a copper pipe that is not magnetic?

Drop a steel bolt through and it clatters straight out. The magnet crawls. Copper is packed with tiny charges called electrons that can drift freely. As the magnet falls, the magnetism through each ring of pipe keeps changing.

A changing magnetism drives those charges around the pipe in circling currents. A bolt drops a metre in half a second. The magnet takes eight. Each circling current is itself a small magnet, and it fights the change. If it helped the fall the magnet would speed up for free, so it must always oppose.

So the pipe above pulls the magnet up, and the pipe below pushes back.

So the copper stays unmagnetised. Its own circling currents resist the falling magnet, and that rule is called Lenz's law.

A train can brake without touching the rail. A magnet sweeping past metal stirs currents that drag it to a stop. An induction hob drives these same circling currents through a steel pan. The pan heats itself, while the glass stays cool.

Check it at home and tell me what you saw.

caption:
Why does everything look blurred underwater until you put goggles on?

Your eye is not harmed, and the pool water is perfectly clear. Most of your eye's focusing is not done by the lens inside it. It happens at the front surface, where air meets the wet cornea.

Light bends there because air and the eye's fluid slow light very differently. But water slows light almost exactly as much as your eye does. So with water in front, that surface has almost nothing left to bend.

Two thirds of your focusing power vanishes, and the image lands behind the retina. The retina catches the light before it comes to a point, so every dot lands as a smear.

So goggles change nothing inside the eye. They put air back in front. That bending strength is called refractive power.

A fish eye carries a nearly spherical lens, because its front surface gets no help from the surrounding water. And a contact lens works by reshaping that same front surface, where the strongest bend in your eye happens.

Did anyone explain it to you this way at school?

caption:
Why is the force a table pushes back with never a number you can look up?

The table does not decide how hard to push. It cannot choose. It is squashed a little by whatever sits on it, like a very stiff spring. It pushes back exactly hard enough to stop the object sinking in.

On flat ground that comes to ninety eight newtons for ten kilograms. Tilt the table and only part of the weight presses into the surface. So the push shrinks, and the rest of the weight drags the object downhill.

In a rising lift the floor must do more, so the push grows.

So the table push is never a stored number. You solve for it from the motion. That force is called the normal force.

The tension in a rope is the same kind of unknown, set by whatever the rope has to hold. And a hinge pushes back with whatever force keeps the beam still, never a value you can look up.

Guess before you scroll, then check.

caption:
Why does a doorknob only shock you in winter?

You build up static charge all year round. Every step across a carpet rubs tiny electric charges off it and onto you. The difference is the air.

Summer air is full of water, and water coats every surface in a thin invisible film. That film conducts, so your charge leaks away as fast as you make it. Winter air is dry. The film is gone.

So the charge has nowhere to go, and it piles up on your skin. Until you reach for metal, and it all leaves at once. Metal carries charge freely, so everything on you rushes across the moment you get close.

So you are not more charged in winter. You are just worse at leaking it away. That slow build and sudden jump is called static discharge.

Chip factories keep their air deliberately humid. Damp air conducts charge away quietly, before it can build into a spark. And a fuel tanker is earthed before filling. Charge that cannot leak away quietly will jump as one spark near petrol vapour.

Who else was taught this wrong?

caption:
Why does blowing across an empty bottle make a clean, deep note?

There is no string, no reed, and nothing solid vibrating at all. The air sitting in the narrow neck behaves like a small plug with weight. The larger body of air below it behaves like a spring.

Your breath knocks that plug downward, squeezing the air beneath it. The squeezed air pushes back, the plug overshoots, and the whole thing bounces. It bounces at one particular rate, and that rate is the note you hear.

Fill the bottle and the spring gets smaller, so the note climbs. A smaller pocket of air stiffens when squeezed, and a stiffer spring bounces faster.

So the bottle is a weight on a spring, made entirely of air. That is called Helmholtz resonance.

It is why an acoustic guitar has a sound hole of exactly that size. And a car with one window cracked open throbs at motorway speed. The cabin of air bounces on exactly the same spring.

caption:
Why does a prism split sunlight into colours when a window pane does not?

Both are glass. Both slow light down and bend it on the way in. Glass bends blue light a little more sharply than it bends red. So inside both pieces, the colours already travel along slightly different paths.

A window has two parallel faces, so the second bend undoes the first. Light meets a parallel second face at the same tilt, so it bends back by the same amount. The colours leave parallel again, shifted sideways by a hair and no more. A prism's faces are tilted against each other, so the second bend adds to the first.

So the colours keep fanning apart, and by the far wall they are separate.

So the prism wins on shape, not on glass. That colour spreading is called dispersion.

A rainbow forms because a raindrop's curved surfaces do not undo the spreading. Blue and red leave the drop at different angles. And a cheap camera lens shows coloured fringes, because its curved glass focuses blue and red at different points.

Go and test it, then report back.

caption:
Why does a bathroom scale read a different weight inside a moving lift?

Your body has not changed. Nothing was added to you or taken away. A scale never measures weight. It measures how hard you press on it. Standing still, you press with your full weight, and it reads that.

Now the lift accelerates upward. The floor has to speed you up too. To speed you upward the floor must push more than gravity pulls, not merely match it. So it pushes harder, and a seventy kilogram person reads eighty four. Accelerating downward, the floor can relax, and the reading drops the same way.

In free fall the floor pushes nothing, so the scale reads zero.

So the lift leaves your mass alone. It changes how hard the floor must push. That is called your apparent weight.

An astronaut floats in orbit while still falling, because the capsule floor pushes on nobody. And a roller coaster drop makes your stomach lift, because the seat stops pressing on you.

Which part of this surprised you?

caption:
Why does the grid carry power at four hundred thousand volts?

It is lethal and it needs enormous towers. There must be a reason. Power is voltage times current. The same power can go either way. The wires themselves waste power, and that waste tracks the current alone.

Double the current and the heat lost climbs four times, not two. More current means both more charge shoved through and a harder shove, so the heat climbs twice over. Four hundred megawatts needs a hundred thousand amps at four kilovolts. Raise the voltage a hundred times and the current falls a hundred times.

So the heat wasted in the wires drops by ten thousand times.

So the grid trades current for volts. A small current means almost no heat, and that waste is called resistive loss.

Phone chargers run thin cables at five volts, so the cable must stay short or the heat wastes your power. Long undersea links push direct current at high voltage for the same reason, keeping the current and the losses down.

Did anyone explain it to you this way at school?

caption:
Why does a hole in a heated metal plate get bigger, not smaller?

The metal swells. It feels obvious that it should squeeze inward and close up. Heat makes every tiny piece of the metal push its neighbours a little further apart. Every gap between them grows by the same fraction, everywhere in the plate.

So the whole plate grows like a photograph being enlarged. Warm the plate by a hundred degrees. The metal and the hole grow alike. In an enlarged photo, every feature grows, including the empty spaces.

The hole is only a gap between pieces of metal, so it is enlarged too.

So a heated hole widens exactly like the metal around it. Everything scales together, and that is called thermal expansion.

A stuck jar lid frees up under hot water, because the lid's opening grows faster than the glass beneath it. Engineers heat a steel ring so its hole widens. They slip it on a shaft, let it cool, and it clamps tight.

Guess before you scroll, then check.

caption:
Why does blowing on hot soup actually cool it down?

You are not blowing cold air onto it. Your breath leaves your mouth at body temperature. The soup cools because it is evaporating. The fastest molecules at the surface escape as vapour. They carry away far more than their share of the energy.

But that vapour hangs just above the surface. Once the air there is full of water, the escaping almost stops. Once the air above is full, as many molecules fall back in as leave. Blowing sweeps that humid layer away. Dry air arrives, and the water starts escaping again at full speed.

So blowing does not cool the soup with cold air. It clears the way so the soup can keep cooling itself. That is called evaporative cooling.

And it is why a fan cools you while a humid day feels unbearable. Air already full of water can accept no more.

Who else was taught this wrong?

caption:
Why does a straight throw miss your friend on a spinning carousel?

You aimed right at her. The ball still curves away sideways. Watch from above, off the ride, and the ball flies dead straight. Nothing pushed it sideways. Nothing had to.

But while the ball travels, the whole floor keeps turning underneath. In half a second the floor has swung about eighteen degrees. Your friend rides that floor, so she is somewhere else on arrival.

From your turning seat, it looks as if a force bent the ball.

So the ball flies straight while the carousel turns out from under it. That invented sideways force is called the Coriolis effect.

Hurricanes spin because air rushing toward low pressure travels for hours while the Earth turns beneath it. And a long-range sniper aims slightly off target, since the ground moves under the bullet during its two-second flight.

caption:
Steel sinks in water. So why does a two hundred thousand tonne ship float?

Drop a steel nail in a bucket and it goes straight to the bottom. The difference is not the metal. It is the shape. Any object in water has to push some water out of the way to make room for itself. That water was already being held up by the same push, so the push equals its weight.

The water pushes back, and that push is exactly the weight of the water shoved aside. A solid nail shoves aside only a nail's worth of water. Far too little to hold it up. A ship's hull is mostly air. It shoves aside a vast volume of water.

Once the water pushed aside weighs as much as the ship, the ship stops sinking.

So floating has much less to do with being light. It is about how much water you push aside. That is called Archimedes' principle.

A submarine uses it deliberately, flooding tanks to sink and blowing them out to rise. And a hot air balloon does the same in air, pushing aside air heavier than itself.

What did you think the reason was?

caption:
Why is one point of a rolling wheel always standing still?

The wheel is racing down the road. Nothing about it looks still. A rolling wheel does two things at once. It moves along and it turns. As long as the tyre does not skid, its rim turns at exactly the speed the car travels. Turning carries the top of the tyre forward, on top of the car's speed.

At sixty, the top of the tyre is doing a hundred and twenty. At the bottom, turning carries the rubber backward just as fast as the car goes forward. Those two motions cancel exactly, so that patch of rubber is briefly at rest.

That is why a tyre grips the road instead of smearing along it.

So a rolling wheel pivots about the patch touching the road. That still point is called the instantaneous axis of rotation.

Photograph a moving bicycle and the top spokes blur away. The rubber near the road is barely moving, so it stays sharp. A tank track lies still where it meets the ground. The top run races forward at twice the tank's speed.

Check it at home and tell me what you saw.

caption:
Why does covering half a lens dim the picture instead of cutting it in half?

Half the glass is blocked. You expect half the scene to vanish. But every part of a lens sees the whole scene. Light from one scene point spreads across the entire lens.

The glass bends all of those rays back to one spot on the sensor. A full lens gathers every ray. Half the lens gathers half of them. So blocking half the glass removes half the rays heading to every point.

Every point of the picture survives, just carrying half the light.

So a lens does not carve the picture into pieces. Each patch of glass builds a full picture, and the opening that sets brightness is called the aperture.

A dust spot on a telescope mirror hides no star. It only removes a small share of the light from every point. Squinting narrows the pupil and darkens the view, yet you still see the whole room, only dimmer and sharper.

caption:
Why does cutting a spring in half make it twice as stiff?

Nothing was added. Half the metal is gone, and yet it fights harder. Think of a spring as a chain of identical coils, one behind another. Pull the two ends, and every single coil feels exactly the same pull. Each coil passes the pull straight to the next, so the same force runs the whole length.

So each coil opens by the same small amount, and those openings add up. Twenty coils give forty millimetres of stretch. Ten coils give twenty. Cut it in half and there are half as many coils to add up.

So the same pull buys half the stretch, which is double the stiffness.

So a short spring is not made of stronger metal. It has fewer coils sharing the stretch. That stiffness is called the spring constant.

Fold a rubber band in two and it pulls back far harder. Each half is shorter, and now two share the load. A long steel cable sags far more than a short one. Extra length means more metal sharing the same pull.

caption:
Why does a hanging spring bounce at the same rate as a flat one?

Gravity drags hard on the hanging mass. Surely that should change the timing. Hang it and the spring stretches until its pull matches the weight exactly. There it sits. Gravity has already been paid for at that new resting point.

Now tug the mass a little further down and let it go. The extra stretch gives an extra pull, and gravity has not grown at all. A spring pulls harder in step with how far it is stretched, wherever it starts from. Flat or hanging, the same mass gives twenty bounces in ten seconds.

So the push back toward rest depends only on how far you moved it. How fast it bounces is set by the push per centimetre and the mass, and hanging changes neither.

So gravity just shifts where the spring rests. Only stiffness and mass set the rhythm, and we call that motion simple harmonic.

A mass bouncing inside a steadily moving lift keeps its rhythm. A constant extra force only shifts the resting point. Pluck a guitar string softly or hard and the note holds steady. The pull grows in step with the stretch.

Who else was taught this wrong?

caption:
Why do oil and water refuse to mix, no matter how hard you shake them?

We usually blame the oil. That turns out to be the wrong suspect. Water molecules are slightly lopsided in charge, so each one clings to its neighbours. Together they form a busy, constantly reshuffling network of grips.

An oil molecule has no charge to offer. It cannot join in. So the water around it must stop reshuffling and form a rigid cage instead. That cage costs the water its freedom, and nature resists losing freedom. There are vastly more jumbled arrangements than tidy ones, so things drift towards the jumbled ones.

By herding all the oil into one blob, the water minimises how much cage it must build. One big blob has far less surface than the same oil split into droplets, so far less cage is needed.

So the oil is not repelled. The water is squeezing it out to keep its own freedom. That is the hydrophobic effect.

Soap works by giving each oil droplet a charged handle. The water will hold it instead of squeezing it out. And every cell membrane in your body forms this way. As water pushes oily molecules together into a sheet two layers thick.

Try it tonight and tell me what happened.

caption:
Why is calm air made of particles racing at five hundred metres per second?

That is faster than a rifle bullet, in a room where nothing stirs. Air is made of tiny particles called molecules, flying in all directions. Temperature is just a measure of how fast they are typically moving.

At room temperature the average speed really is about five hundred metres per second. Huge individual speeds. An average of almost exactly zero. Each one picks its direction at random, and there are countless of them.

For every particle heading left, another heads right just as fast, so the crowd goes nowhere.

So the particles are wildly fast and the air still stays calm. Wind is only the leftover drift, and the rest is called random thermal motion.

A smell crosses a room in minutes, not milliseconds, because each molecule zigzags through billions of collisions on the way. And the pressure holding a balloon open is those particles drumming on the rubber, billions of times a second.

What did you think the reason was?

caption:
Why does a magnet grip your fridge but slide straight off a soda can?

Both are metal. Both conduct electricity. Yet only one holds. Every electron inside a metal behaves like a tiny magnet, with its own north and south. In most materials those tiny magnets point every which way and cancel out.

In iron, something unusual happens. Neighbouring electron magnets line up with each other. Whole regions lock into step, each one a small but real magnet. Bring a magnet close and those regions swing to face it, and the metal pulls back. Each region turns so its north faces the magnet's south, and opposite poles pull together.

In aluminium they will not line up at all. There is nothing to swing.

So it is not about being metal. It is whether the electrons in your fridge door agree to point the same way. That is called ferromagnetism.

Hard drives store your data by flipping such regions one way or the other. And an MRI scanner works by lining up the atoms in your own body.

Check it at home and tell me what you saw.
