caption:
How do noise-cancelling headphones silence a roaring engine by adding sound?

It sounds absurd. More sound should be louder, not quieter. But sound is a wave of pressure, pushing air out and then pulling it back. Send two identical waves together and where both push, the push doubles.

Now flip one of them, so it pulls exactly when the other pushes. They cancel. The air stops moving, and you hear nothing. A microphone on the outside listens to the engine, hundreds of times a second.

The headphone plays that same sound flipped, and the two meet at your ear. The copy must arrive at the very same instant. Is why a steady drone cancels and a sudden bang does not.

So it is not blocking the noise. It is adding its exact opposite. That is called destructive interference.

Aircraft engineers quiet whole cabins this way. Feeding in the opposite of the engine drone so the two cancel at your seat. And an MRI room is kept bearable the same way. The scanner's hammering noise is met by its exact mirror image.

Did anyone explain it to you this way at school?

caption:
What actually pushes a car forward when it speeds up?

Not the engine. The engine only presses parts of the car against each other. A push from inside a system cannot shift the whole system. Every push inside comes with an equal push back, so the pair cancels out. So something outside must shove it, and only the road is touching.

The tyres can give about eight thousand newtons. Hard acceleration needs less. The engine turns the wheels, and the tyre presses backward on the tarmac. The tarmac presses forward on the tyre with exactly the same strength.

That forward press from the road is the one force speeding the car up.

So the engine never pushes the car forward. It only lets the road push it, and we call that grip static friction.

A swimmer pushes water backward, and the water pushes her forward, since nothing inside her body could do it. A rocket has no surface to press on, so it throws its own exhaust backward and gets pushed forward.

Guess before you scroll, then check.

caption:
Earth is spinning at over a thousand kilometres an hour. Why can't you feel it?

Because nothing is pushing you. You are being carried. You only ever feel a change in motion, never motion itself. You feel something only when part of you is pushed, and steady motion pushes nothing. Sit in an airliner at nine hundred kilometres an hour and you can pour a drink without spilling a drop.

The plane, the air and you are all moving together, so nothing presses on you. The Earth is the same, only far steadier. Its spin does bend your path, but the turn is so wide it takes a whole day to come round. The turn is so wide it pulls you sideways only a thousandth as hard as gravity pulls you down.

So you never feel a steady thousand kilometres an hour. You would only feel it change. That idea is called the principle of relativity.

It is why you can walk down the aisle of a speeding train. You and the carriage share one steady motion, so nothing pushes you sideways. And why it took centuries to prove the Earth moves, because every test on its surface moves along with it.

Who else was taught this wrong?

caption:
Why does the bottom of a falling slinky wait three tenths of a second?

Drop anything solid and every part of it starts falling at once. A hanging slinky is stretched, and that stretch pulls the bottom upward. That upward pull exactly balances gravity, so the bottom hangs still.

Let go of the top, and only the top feels the change. The news travels down the coils at about three metres per second. The stretch has to collapse coil by coil before the bottom learns anything.

Until that collapse arrives, the bottom keeps its old balance and stays put.

So the bottom waits about three tenths of a second. It is waiting for a stretch wave to reach it. That delay is called a finite signal speed.

A long train starts moving car by car, because the pull from the engine travels back through the couplings. And an earthquake reaches a distant city minutes late. The ground can only pass the shaking along at its own speed.

caption:
Why does the grid push power at four hundred thousand volts?

That voltage is dangerous and expensive. There must be a reason. Power is voltage times current, so one big number lets the other shrink. The wires themselves waste power by heating up as charge flows through.

That waste depends on the current squared, not on the voltage. More current means both more charge pushed and a harder push, so the heat rises twice over. Raise the voltage twenty times, and the wasted heat drops four hundred times. Twenty times the voltage means a twentieth of the current, and a twentieth squared is four hundred times less heat. So sending the same power at higher voltage means far less current.

Less current means dramatically less heat left behind in the cables.

So the grid trades current for volts to save power. Heat wasted in the wires is called I squared R loss.

A long extension cord gets warm running a heater, because the same current wastes power in every metre. And your phone charger sends five volts only a short way, since a long low-voltage run would waste most energy.

What did you think the reason was?

caption:
Why does a laser beam follow a curving stream of water?

The light is not being dragged along. It is being trapped inside. Light travels a little slower in water than in the air outside it. When a ray hits the surface from inside, it bends away from the wall. Leaving the slower water, the ray tips over towards the surface rather than straight out of it.

Past about forty nine degrees, none of it escapes at all. Bent further and further, the escaping ray would have to skim flat along the surface. Beyond that angle none gets out. Beyond that steep angle the surface stops letting light out. So the whole ray turns back into the water, as if from a mirror.

The stream curves gently, so every bounce stays past that angle.

So the water guides the beam by reflecting it again and again. That trapping is called total internal reflection.

An optical fibre carries internet traffic across oceans by trapping light in glass in exactly the same way. And a cut diamond sparkles for the same reason. Light bounces around inside many times before it finds a way out.

Which part of this surprised you?

caption:
Why does the top of a rolling wheel move twice as fast as its axle?

It is one rigid object, so you expect every part to share one speed. But the bottom of a rolling wheel is momentarily standing still. It grips the road without sliding, so the contact point has zero speed.

Bottom zero, axle one, top two. The speeds climb straight up. The whole wheel is turning about that stationary contact point. The axle sits one radius above it, and the top sits two radii up. Every part swings through the same angle each second, so a point twice as far out covers twice the distance.

Speed grows with distance from the pivot, in a straight line.

So the axle moves at the car's speed and the wheel top doubles it. That pivot is called the instantaneous centre.

A photo of a moving car shows the top spokes blurred and the bottom ones sharp, for exactly this reason. And a tank track races forward on top at double the tank's speed. Its bottom run is planted still on the ground.

Did anyone explain it to you this way at school?

caption:
Why does one thin wire glow while the thick wires beside it stay dark?

They are joined in one line, so the same current passes through all. Same current, and yet only one of them gets hot enough to shine. A thin wire has less room for the charge to move through.

That makes it resist the flow more in every centimetre of its length. Halve the width and you roughly quadruple the resistance. Heating depends on the current squared, times that resistance. Charges forced through a tight wire keep banging into its atoms, and that jostling is heat.

So with the current fixed, the thinnest piece dumps by far the most heat.

So all the wires carry one current. The thin one simply turns more of it into heat. That is called Joule heating.

A fuse protects your house by being the thinnest link, so it melts before the wiring behind the walls does. And a toaster element glows orange for the same reason. It is made deliberately thin and long to resist the current.

Guess before you scroll, then check.

caption:
Why does a brighter lamp not give the knocked-out charges more energy?

Turn a lamp up and everything about it seems to get stronger. Shine light on metal and it knocks tiny charges called electrons loose. Turn the light up, and more of them come out, as expected.

So brighter light delivers more energy in total, but not more per hit. Each packet is called a photon.

Red light never frees charges from zinc, however bright it is, because a single red packet is simply too weak. And sunburn comes from ultraviolet, not from heat, because only those high-energy packets can break the bonds in your skin.

caption:
Why does a magnet take seven seconds to fall through a copper pipe?

Copper is not magnetic. Hold a magnet against it and nothing happens. But drop the magnet inside, and it sinks like a stone in honey. A moving magnet changes the magnetic field seen by the copper around it.

caption:
Why does cutting a spring in half make it twice as stiff?

It has less metal in it now, so you would expect it to be weaker. But stiffness is not about how much metal there is. Pull a spring and every coil stretches by the same small amount. Each coil hands the pull straight on to the next, so every coil feels the full force.

Twenty coils give you twenty of those small stretches, added end to end. Twenty coils stretch twice as far as ten, under the same pull. Cut the spring in half and only ten coils are left to share the load.

Same pull, half the total stretch, so it feels twice as stiff.

So cutting the spring removes stretch, not strength. Stiffness adds up in reverse along a chain, and that is called a series combination. Springs in a line share the stretch, so the more of them there are, the softer the whole thing feels.

A short guitar string sounds higher than a long one, because the shorter length resists being pulled aside more strongly. And a steel beam sags less when you shorten it, since each piece of its length adds its own bending.

What did you think the reason was?

caption:
Why does covering half a lens darken the picture instead of cutting it in half?

Block half a window and you lose half the view. A lens is different. Every point on the lens can see the whole scene in front of it. Light from one point on the object spreads out and hits the entire lens.

Full lens, all the light. Half a lens, half the light, same picture. The lens bends all of that light back to one point on the image. So each image point is rebuilt from rays crossing the whole lens.

Cover half, and every image point still gets rays, just fewer of them.

So the picture stays complete and only grows dimmer. How much light a lens collects is called its aperture.

A camera aperture ring dims the photo as it closes, because narrowing the glass only cuts how much light arrives. And a telescope mirror with a support arm across it still shows the whole sky. It just looks fainter, for the same reason.

Check it at home and tell me what you saw.

caption:
Why doesn't snapping a magnet in half give you a north-only piece?

It feels like breaking a stick. One end north, one end south. But a magnet is not two ends. It is a crowd of tiny magnets. Every atom inside behaves like its own miniature bar, with both poles.

They line up together, so their north ends all point the same way. One bar magnet, two poles. Cut it, and you get four. The poles you feel are just where that line-up begins and ends.

Break the bar and you simply expose a new beginning and a new end.

So each half is a complete magnet again, with both poles. A lone single pole is called a monopole, and none has ever been found.

Cutting a bar magnet ten times gives you a thousand tiny magnets, every one of them still carrying two poles. And iron filings around a broken fridge magnet still form closed loops. The field leaves one pole and returns to the other.

Try it tonight and tell me what happened.

caption:
How can a particle born overhead outlive its own six hundred metre range?

These particles are made fifteen kilometres up, when cosmic rays hit the air. Each one survives about two microseconds before it falls apart. Even at nearly light speed, that buys only six hundred and sixty metres.

And yet detectors at sea level count them in huge numbers. Six hundred and sixty metres allowed. Fifteen thousand travelled. The answer is that time itself runs slower for something moving that fast. Everyone measures light at the same speed. The only way that works out is for a fast clock to run slow.

The particle's own clock ticks once for every thirty of ours. So two microseconds of its life stretches to sixty of ours.

So the particle does not live longer by its own clock. Our clock disagrees with its clock, and that is called time dilation.

GPS satellite clocks must be corrected every day, because their speed and altitude make them tick at a different rate. And particles in an accelerator ring last far longer than they should, giving physicists time to study them properly.

Guess before you scroll, then check.

caption:
Why does opening a simple switch on a coil throw a bright spark?

The battery is only a few volts. The spark needs thousands. A coil stores energy in the magnetic field wrapped around it. That field is held up by the current running through the wire.

A coil fights any change in its current by pushing back with a voltage. As the field collapses it shoves the charges along, trying to keep the current running. The faster the current dies, the bigger that pushback gets. Opening the switch tries to stop the current in a few microseconds.

Such a violent change demands an enormous pushback voltage.

So the switch does not make the spark. The coil makes it, by refusing to stop. That pushback is called back EMF.

A car ignition coil makes twenty thousand volts from twelve, by cutting its current off hundreds of times each second. And a relay needs a diode across its coil. That gives the dying current a gentle path instead of a spark.

Who else was taught this wrong?

caption:
Which wins a downhill race: a ring, a disk, or a sphere?

Weight does not decide it. Size does not decide it either. Each one starts with the same store of height energy. Rolling splits that energy two ways: moving forward, and spinning.

Whatever goes into spinning is not available for speed downhill. The ring spends half its energy spinning. The sphere spends two sevenths. A ring keeps all its mass far from the centre, so it is hardest to spin up. Mass out at the rim has to travel fastest as the wheel turns. It soaks up more of the energy.

A sphere keeps most of its mass close in, so spinning costs it least. Only the shape matters, because mass and radius cancel out of the answer.

So the sphere wins the race, then the disk, then the ring. What decides it is called the shape factor.

Two cans of soup race differently when one is set and one is runny. The liquid inside barely spins at all. And a flywheel stores more energy with its mass out at the rim. That is exactly why the ring loses the race.

caption:
Why does leaving the fridge door open make the kitchen warmer?

A fridge makes cold. Open it, and the cold should spill out. But a fridge does not make cold. It moves heat from one place to another. It pulls heat out of the food and dumps it from the coils at the back.

Moving heat uphill takes work, and the motor burns electricity to do it. Heat never drifts from a cold place to a warm one by itself, so something has to push it. For every hundred joules pulled out, about a hundred and fifty go back in. That electricity ends up as heat too, added to what was moved.

With the door open, the cold air just circles back inside.

So the open fridge is really a heater, and the kitchen slowly warms. Pumping heat while making more of it is called a heat pump.

An air conditioner cools your room only because its hot side hangs outside the window, dumping the heat elsewhere. And a computer warms a small room whatever it calculates, since every watt it draws leaves the box as heat.

Go and test it, then report back.

caption:
Why does a detector still read a signal when the laser is blocked?

Block the beam and the number should drop to nothing. It does not. A detector turns light into a small voltage, and the wires carry it out. But the same wires pick up room lights, mains hum, and warmth from the chip.

Those all arrive as voltage, and voltage carries no label saying where it came from. So the honest move is to block the beam and read what remains. Open reads 1.20 volts. Blocked still reads 0.35 volts.

Subtract, and only 0.85 volts was ever light from the laser.

So the blocked detector is telling the truth about your setup. Part of that signal was never light. That test is called a control measurement.

A kitchen scale is zeroed with the empty bowl first, so the reading counts only what you add. And a drug trial gives some people a placebo, because you must know what improves with no treatment.

Check it at home and tell me what you saw.

caption:
Why can measuring a voltage cut that voltage exactly in half?

A meter is supposed to watch. Instead it joins the circuit. To read a voltage, a meter lets a trickle of current flow through itself. That current has to come from the source, and the source resists giving it.

So the source and the meter share the voltage between them, like two steps. Each takes a share of the volts in proportion to how hard it resists, so two equals split it evenly. A stiff source barely notices. A weak one gives up a lot. A one megaohm meter on a one megaohm source reads only half a volt.

Swap in a ten megaohm meter and the same source reads 0.91 volts.

So the voltage was real until you touched it. The meter drew current and took a share. That is called circuit loading.

A cheap tyre gauge lets out a puff of air, so the pressure it reports is slightly lower. And a cold thermometer cools the drop of water it sits in, reading a temperature it partly created.

Did anyone explain it to you this way at school?

caption:
Why do microwaves stay inside an oven whose door is full of holes?

You can see straight through that mesh. Light gets out easily. An oven's waves repeat every twelve centimetres, and that spacing is called their wavelength. The holes in the door are only about two millimetres across. It is not just that the wave is wider - the metal between the holes is doing the blocking.

So the wave is sixty times wider than the hole it must squeeze through. Metal is full of loose charges, and the wave shoves them until they cancel it out. The metal sheet carries currents that cancel the field, and a hole is simply too narrow. A wave cannot fit sideways inside a hole narrower than itself, so it fades instead of travelling. A little field does poke into each hole, but it dies away fast inside.

By the far side almost nothing is left, so almost nothing escapes.

So the holes are not a gap for these waves. Microwaves are far too wide to fit through. That cut off is called an evanescent wave.

Visible light has waves under a thousandth of a millimetre, so it slips through the same mesh easily. And a radio loses its signal inside a lift, because the metal box blocks waves wider than its gaps.

Go and test it, then report back.

caption:
How can a loop of wire add a fifty hertz hum you never measured?

Your instrument reads a clean signal, plus a steady buzz at mains speed. Mains cables in the wall carry current that reverses fifty times a second. A reversing current wraps a magnetic field around itself, growing and collapsing.

Any closed loop of wire sitting in that field feels a push on its charges. Your signal wire and its return travel apart and back, and the space between them is the loop. The bigger the area your cables enclose, the bigger that unwanted push. Half a square metre picks up about three hundred microvolts of hum.

Twist the pair together and the enclosed area nearly vanishes, so the hum collapses.

So nothing you measured made that buzz. Your own cable loop is a pickup coil. That effect is called electromagnetic induction.

An induction hob heats a pan the same way, driving swirling currents in the metal with a changing field. And a metal detector finds coins by the same push, sensing currents its changing field stirs underground.

caption:
Why does a rolling wheel always have one point standing still?

A car at a hundred kilometres an hour looks entirely in motion. But rolling is two motions added together, forward travel and turning. The turning carries the top of the rim forward, and the bottom backwards.

For a wheel that rolls without slipping, those two speeds are equal. So at the road the backward turn exactly cancels the forward travel. At the top they add instead, so that point moves at double speed.

A long exposure photograph proves it. The rim blurs, the contact patch stays sharp.

So a rolling wheel is never one single speed. The point touching the road is momentarily at rest. That point is called the instantaneous axis of rotation.

A tank track lays its links down at rest on the ground, which is why they do not scuff. And a train wheel grips the rail the same way, because the touching point never slides, it only pivots.

caption:
Why do two light beams circling Earth land 414 nanoseconds apart?

Send one beam east and one west around the very same fibre loop. Both travel at the same speed. Light does not care which way it goes. But while they fly, the ground underneath them turns.

The finish line runs away from the eastward beam, and toward the westward one. So the eastward beam must cover about sixty-two extra metres. A spinning Earth splits them by 414 nanoseconds. A still Earth would not.

Stop the rotation and both arrive together, so the gap measures the spin itself.

So the two beams keep the same speed throughout. The spinning Earth moves the finish line while they fly. That split is called the Sagnac effect.

A laser gyroscope in an aircraft senses turning exactly this way, with no moving parts to wear out. And GPS satellites correct for this split, because ignoring it would shift your position by tens of metres.

Why does measuring too slowly invent a rhythm that was never there?

A camera only sees the world in snapshots, one frame at a time. Between two snapshots anything can happen, and the camera keeps no record of it. So a fast wiggle and a slow wiggle can pass through the same dots.

Count the repeats per second and you have what is called its frequency. A ninety hertz tone, sampled one hundred times a second, lands on those same dots. Each snapshot catches the wave a little further back, so it seems to crawl round ten times a second. So the true ninety becomes a false ten, and nothing can undo it.

The cure is to sample faster than twice the quickest wiggle present. You need at least two snapshots per wiggle, one for its up and one for its down.

So the fake rhythm was never inside the signal. Sampling too slowly built it. That folding down is called aliasing.

A wagon wheel in an old film seems to turn backwards, because the frames land just short of each spoke. And a digital recorder filters out high tones before sampling, so they cannot fold down into the music.

Which part of this surprised you?

caption:
Why does a ten thousand step random walk end only a hundred steps away?

Ten thousand steps sounds like a long way from home. It is not. Each step is a coin flip, forwards or backwards, with no memory of the last. So for every step that carries you out, another is likely to bring you back.

Progress only survives where the flips happen to come out uneven. That leftover imbalance grows, but it grows like the square root of the count. Flip a coin four times and you typically finish two ahead; a hundred times, about ten ahead. Ten thousand steps walked. Only about one hundred steps of distance gained.

To travel twice as far from home, you need four times as many steps.

So the random walker is not stuck. Opposite steps cancel, so distance grows only as the square root. That spreading is called diffusion.

A drop of ink spreads slowly through still water, because each particle staggers randomly instead of travelling straight. And a gambler playing fair coin flips drifts away from even slowly, roughly as the square root of bets.

caption:
How can a whole orbit shrink to a single dot on a strobe map?

A swinging weight traces a busy loop. Watching all of it tells you little. So stop watching continuously. Flash a light once every drive cycle instead. The swing is pushed by a motor with a fixed beat, and we flash once per beat. Each flash records just one thing: where the weight is, and how fast. Position alone does not say what happens next, so we record the speed too.

If the motion repeats exactly once per flash, every flash finds the same place. So five hundred flashes pile five hundred records onto one point. Repeating motion leaves one dot. Chaotic motion scatters five hundred.

Two dots mean the motion takes two cycles to repeat, and a cloud means never.

So the orbit is not lost. Strobing throws away the journey and keeps the repeat. That slice is called a Poincare section.

A car wheel balanced under a strobe looks frozen, because each flash catches it at the very same angle. And a heart monitor stacks beats onto one grid line, so a drifting rhythm shows up immediately.

Guess before you scroll, then check.

caption:
How can pumping at exactly twice the rhythm make a swing grow fastest?

Push a swing once each pass and it builds. That is the obvious way. But a child on a swing pushes nothing. There is nobody there. She crouches and stands, changing how far her weight sits from the pivot.

She stands at the bottom, where she is moving fastest and pulling hardest. That lift does real work, and she crouches at the top, costing almost nothing. She lifts against a big pull at the bottom and lets herself down against a small one. Energy is left behind each time. At the top she is barely moving, so the rope is hardly pulling and crouching costs nothing. The bottom comes round twice in every full swing, so she pumps twice as often.

A three second swing needs pumping at 0.67 times a second.

So the swing grows with no push at all. Changing the length twice each cycle feeds it energy. That is called parametric resonance.

A wine glass of water on a shaking table ripples strongly when the shaking runs at double the wave rhythm. And a skateboarder pumps a ramp by rising and crouching twice each pass, gaining height with no push.

Who else was taught this wrong?

caption:
How can three rotation numbers lose a whole direction?

Three rings, three dials. That should describe any orientation you like. The rings are nested, each one carried by the ring outside it. Normally their three axes point three different ways, covering everything.

Tip the middle ring a full ninety degrees and something quietly breaks. The innermost axis now lies exactly along the outermost one. The middle ring carries the inner one, so tipping it swings the inner axis right round onto the outer one. So three rings can steer only two directions, not three.

Turn either dial and you get the same motion, and one direction is unreachable.

So the object can still turn any way it likes. Only the three rotation numbers fail to describe it. That failure is called gimbal lock.

A map of the globe goes strange at the poles, where every line of longitude meets at one single point. And a flight simulator uses four numbers instead of three, because that extra number removes the blind spot.

caption:
Why does the Martian moon Phobos rise in the west?

Our own Moon rises in the east, like the Sun and the stars. That is because Earth turns faster than the Moon travels around us. Mars turns once in twenty-four hours and thirty-seven minutes.

Phobos circles Mars in only seven hours and thirty-nine minutes. So Phobos goes round three times while Mars turns once. It orbits the same way Mars spins, but it overtakes the ground below. Moving east faster than the ground does, it drifts eastward across the sky. It must come up in the west.

So to someone standing there, it creeps forward, climbing from the western horizon.

So Phobos breaks no rule of the sky. It laps the planet, so its path across the sky is reversed. That is called relative motion.

A fast car on the motorway passes a slower one, and from inside it the slower car drifts backwards. And the space station crosses our sky west to east, because it circles Earth in ninety minutes.

What did you think the reason was?

caption:
Can a sideways cannonball escape Earth as easily as a vertical one?

Straight up feels like the only way out. Sideways feels like falling back. Escaping is a question of energy, not of aim. Gravity's pull weakens with distance, so leaving costs one fixed total amount.

A moving ball carries energy that depends on its speed, and speed alone. Turn the cannon sideways and that energy is exactly the same number. So 11.2 kilometres a second frees it, while 7.9 only keeps it circling.

With no air and a clear path, the sideways shot curves away and never returns.

So sideways and vertical shots need the same speed. Direction sets the route, and energy sets the escape. That threshold is called escape velocity.

A roller coaster car reaches the same top speed from any drop of the same height, whatever the track shape. And a comet falling from deep space arrives at the same speed regardless of which side it approaches.

Which part of this surprised you?

caption:
How can a single pulse make scrambled spins unscramble themselves?

The signal from a sample dies away in milliseconds. It looks destroyed. Each tiny spin turns like a compass needle held in the magnet. The field is never perfectly even, so some spins turn slightly faster than others.

They start together, then fan apart, and their contributions cancel out. Now flip every spin halfway round. The ones ahead are suddenly behind. The flip turns the spins around but not the magnet, so each keeps the very same speed as before. They keep their own speeds, so the fast ones catch up exactly where they started.

At twenty milliseconds the plain signal is 2 percent. The echo is 82.

So the scrambled spins never lost their information. They only spread out, and one flip brings them back. That revival is called a spin echo.

Runners on a track spread out, then all turn around, and they meet again exactly at the start line. And an MRI scanner uses these echoes to tell healthy tissue from damaged, since each recovers at its own rate.

Did anyone explain it to you this way at school?

caption:
Why can a car never slide sideways, yet still park sideways?

Push a parked car from the side and it refuses. The tyres dig in. A rolling wheel can go where it points, forwards or backwards, and nowhere else. So at any instant your car has two choices: roll, and turn the steering.

Sideways is not on that list, at any single instant. But roll forward turning left, then back turning right, and repeat. The two arcs curve opposite ways, so the car comes back beside where it started, not onto it. Each pass shifts you about half a metre toward the kerb.

Four passes and you have moved two metres sideways, using only allowed moves.

So sideways is blocked at every instant, but not over time. A sequence reaches places no single move can. That restriction is called a nonholonomic constraint.

A shopping trolley with fixed rear wheels is shuffled sideways the same way, by wiggling it forwards and back. And a cat in mid air turns around by twisting its body through a loop, using shape changes only.

Guess before you scroll, then check.

caption:
How can weighing the same mug a hundred times keep the wrong answer?

Averaging feels like a cure. More readings, less error. But a measurement can go wrong in two very different ways. Some wobble is random, high one time and low the next.

Average a hundred of those and the wobble shrinks by a factor of ten. Highs and lows cancel as you add them, and the leftover shrinks like the square root of the count. The other kind is a steady offset, like a scale that never read zero. So the scatter falls to 0.2 grams, while a five gram offset stays.

Every reading is shifted the same way, so averaging carries the shift straight through.

So more weighing cannot rescue this. Repetition kills random scatter, but it cannot touch a steady offset. That offset is called systematic error.

A clock that runs three minutes fast is wrong every single time you check it, however often you look. And a poll that only calls landlines misses the same people repeatedly, so a bigger sample stays biased.

caption:
Why can a lone neutron decay when one inside deuterium cannot?

A free neutron lasts about fifteen minutes, then turns into a proton. It can do that because a proton weighs slightly less than a neutron. That leftover mass becomes energy, about zero point seven eight mega electron volts.

Inside deuterium that neutron is glued to a proton, and the glue is strong. Two protons cannot stick to each other, so the decay would have to split the pair apart. Break that glue and the decay must pay more energy than it can give. Two separate protons weigh more than the deuterium nucleus they came from.

So the decay would have to create mass from nothing, and it cannot.

So the neutron inside deuterium is not held safe by a force. It is short of energy by 1.44 mega electron volts. That rule is called energy conservation.

A carbon fourteen nucleus does decay, because its products weigh less and leave 0.16 mega electron volts to spare. And potassium forty in your bones decays only along the paths where the final mass comes out lower.

caption:
Why does a metal still hold huge pressure at absolute zero?

Cool anything far enough and its particles should simply stop moving. But a metal is packed with tiny charges called electrons, and they refuse. No two of them are allowed to sit in the very same state of motion.

So the slowest state fills first, and the next pair is forced to go faster. Fill every level to the top and the average energy stays enormous. That forced motion is still there when the temperature reaches zero. They cannot slow down, because every slower state is already taken by someone else.

And motion pressed inside a box always pushes on the walls.

So the metal is cold, yet its electrons still carry forty gigapascals of pressure. That crowding rule is called the Pauli exclusion principle.

A white dwarf star holds itself up this same way, with crowded charges pushing out against its own gravity. And a neutron star survives on the same crowding rule, with neutrons instead of charges, packed far tighter.

What did you think the reason was?

caption:
How can two big beads attract with nothing pulling between them?

Mix large beads into water that is crowded with far smaller ones. The small ones cannot reach the last sliver of space beside a big bead. So a thin shell around each big bead stays forever out of bounds.

Push two big beads together and their forbidden shells overlap. That overlap hands the small ones extra room, so they gain freedom. Meanwhile the small ones still hammer the outer faces from every side. The small beads never stop jiggling, so they drum on every surface they can reach.

Nothing hammers the narrow gap, so the outside push squeezes them together.

So the two beads attract because the crowd around them gains room. That squeeze is called a depletion force.

Adding thickener to a drink can make cocoa particles clump and settle, because crowding presses them together. And red blood cells stack into neat rolls when large proteins crowd the plasma, the same squeeze.

Which part of this surprised you?

caption:
Why does a 7 tera electron volts proton hitting a wall waste most of its energy?

You might expect all seven trillion volts to go into making new particles. But the target's atoms sit still, while the proton is racing forward. Whatever they make must keep moving forward too, to balance the push.

That forward motion carries energy away, and it cannot be spent on mass. Only the energy seen in the collision's own frame can build anything. Ride along with the wreckage, and whatever energy is left over there is all you can spend. And that shared energy grows only as the square root of the beam energy.

So doubling the beam buys you just forty percent more usable energy.

So the proton carries 7 tera electron volts, yet a fixed wall gives only 115 giga electron volts. Two beams head on give 14 tera electron volts. That is the centre of mass energy.

Two cars crashing head on wreck far more than one car hitting a parked car, for the same reason. And the collider rings two beams against each other instead of a target. Is how it reaches fourteen tera electron volts.

caption:
Why does adding more waves never flatten the ripple at a sharp jump?

A square wave can be built by adding smooth waves of rising pitch. Add ten of them and the shape is close, but the corners ring. Add a thousand and the ringing looks thinner, so you expect it to fade.

It does not. The first spike stays about nine percent above the jump. Each extra wave makes the ripple narrower, but it also makes it steeper. Smooth waves cannot turn a corner instantly, so the sum always swings past before settling. The width shrinks while the height holds, so the spike just crowds the corner.

So the ripple never shrinks in height. It only shrinks in width. That stubborn overshoot is called the Gibbs phenomenon.

caption:
How can an electron outrun light while travelling slower than light speed?

The water glows an eerie blue, and nothing down there is burning. Light in a vacuum is the true speed limit, and nothing beats it. But light slows as it crosses water, held up by the atoms it passes.

In water, light crawls at about seventy five percent of its vacuum speed. A fast charged particle from the fuel can easily exceed that lower speed. As it flies it tugs the atoms, and every tug sends out a ripple.

Those ripples pile into a cone behind it, like a boat's bow wave. Because the particle outruns its own ripples, they can never get ahead and stack into a cone.

So the electron never beats light in vacuum. It only beats the slower light inside water. That blue cone is called Cherenkov radiation.

A jet's sonic boom makes the same cone, because the plane outruns its own sound waves. And detectors buried in polar ice find neutrinos by hunting for this same faint blue cone.

caption:
How can two tiny twists leave a leftover third twist?

Walk three steps east then four north. Swap the order and you land identically. Turns are not like that. Order changes where you end up. The first turn carries the book's own axes with it, so the second turn happens about a moved line. Take the book. Tip it forward, then twist it to the right.

Now start again and do the same two moves in the opposite order. The book ends up facing somewhere else, clearly tilted from the first result. Two twists of 5.7 degrees leave a mismatch of about half a degree. Each twist tilts the other's axis only slightly, so the leftover is a small share of a small angle.

Shrink the twists and the mismatch shrinks faster still, as the angle squared.

So the two twists did nothing wrong. Turning depends on order, so a leftover twist appears. That leftover is called the commutator.

A satellite must apply its steering turns in a fixed order, because swapping them points the dish somewhere else. And a cat dropped upside down rights itself by combining twists in a clever order, with no outside push.

caption:
If friction only opposes motion, what actually pushes a car forward?

The engine turns the wheels, but the engine is bolted inside the car. Pushing on yourself from the inside cannot move you anywhere. So something outside must push, and only the tyres touch the road.

A driven tyre tries to scrape the road backwards where it meets the ground. The road grips back and shoves the car forward, and that grip has a limit. The tyre is not sliding there, so this is the gripping kind of friction. The bottom of a rolling tyre is momentarily still on the road, so it grips instead of sliding.

Push harder than the grip allows and the tyre spins, and you go nowhere.

So the car is pushed forward by the road itself. That gripping push is called static friction.

Walking works the same way, because your shoe pushes the ground backwards and the ground pushes you on. And a rocket has no road to push on, so it throws mass out behind it instead.

What did you think the reason was?

caption:
Why does a triangle force one magnetic bond to be unhappy?

Put a tiny magnet at each corner, each one pointing up or down. Neighbouring magnets prefer to point opposite ways, so each pair wants to disagree. Set the first one up and the second one down. So far, fine.

Now the third must disagree with both, and both cannot be satisfied. Two bonds get their wish. The third is stuck being wrong. A loop with an even number of corners lets up and down alternate all the way round. It does not matter which corner you start from, or which one you flip.

Six different arrangements all tie for lowest energy, so nothing can choose.

So the triangle loses one bond to its own shape, not to weak magnets. That is called geometric frustration.

Water ice has the same problem, leaving leftover disorder that shows up in careful heat measurements. And three friends who each veto a different film hit the same tie, with no happy choice.

Which part of this surprised you?

caption:
Why can a filmed wheel appear to spin backwards?

The wheel is racing forwards. The film insists it is going the other way. Film is not motion. It is a stack of still pictures, twenty-four each second. A spoke looks identical to the spoke beside it, so the eye cannot tell them apart.

Your brain links each frame to the nearest matching spoke, taking the shortest jump. Each frame gives the wheel a twenty-fourth of a second, just too little for a full turn. Spin at twenty-three turns a second and each frame falls just short of a full turn. So the shortest jump points backwards, by one turn every second.

Speed up to exactly twenty-four and the spokes freeze, looking perfectly still.

So the wheel never reversed at all. The camera sampled too slowly, so the backwards motion is an illusion. That mismatch is called aliasing.

A helicopter rotor filmed on a phone can look bent or frozen, because the sensor scans the picture in slices. And a strobe light on a factory line freezes moving parts the same way, by matching flashes to motion.

Did anyone explain it to you this way at school?

caption:
How can a longer ramp get a ball down faster than a straight one?

Take two points, one metre across and one metre down, and roll a bead. The straight ramp is the shortest path, so it should surely be quickest. But speed comes from how far you have already dropped, not how far you travelled. Every metre you fall is turned into speed, no matter which way you came down.

The curved ramp dives steeply at the start, so the bead gains speed early. It travels further, yet it spends most of that distance moving fast. Dropping late is expensive, because you crawl through the whole first stretch.

The winning shape is the curve traced by a point on a rolling wheel.

So the straight ramp wins on length and loses on time. The longer curve is faster. That shape is called the brachistochrone.

A skateboarder drops into a curved ramp rather than a flat slope, gaining speed early for the same reason. And light crossing into glass takes the quickest path rather than the shortest, which is the very same trade.

Guess before you scroll, then check.

caption:
How can a spinning book flip itself over with nothing touching it?

Toss it flat and it spins cleanly. Toss it on its middle edge and it tumbles. Every object has three axes it can spin about: easy, medium, and hard. An axis is hard when the mass sits far from it, and easy when the mass hugs it. Spin about the easiest or the hardest axis and small wobbles just stay small.

Spin about the middle one and a tiny wobble feeds itself and grows. A wobble about the middle axis tips the book so the spin leans further off, which tips it more. For a book, that middle axis sits at 71 percent of the hardest. The wobble grows until the book has turned halfway over, then it reverses.

Nothing pushed it. The total spin never changed, only how the book sat in it.

So the book flips itself because the middle axis is unstable. Spinning there cannot hold steady. That is called the intermediate axis theorem.

A phone tossed spinning about its middle edge tumbles the same way, which is why it lands face down. And a satellite must spin about its widest or narrowest axis, or it slowly tumbles out of aim.

Who else was taught this wrong?

caption:
How can a dropped phone feel weightless while it speeds toward Earth?

Weight is not really something you feel. You feel what pushes back. On a table the table shoves upward, and the phone's sensor reads that. Let go and nothing pushes it any more, so the sensor reads zero.

Gravity has not switched off. Only the reading has changed. Every part of the phone falls at exactly the same rate, together. So no part presses on any other, and nothing inside is squeezed.

Inside a small falling room you could not tell gravity from empty space.

So the phone still accelerates, and it still feels weightless. Free fall cancels gravity locally. That is the equivalence principle.

Astronauts float in the station because they are falling around Earth, not because gravity has gone. And a plane flying a falling arc gives its passengers the same weightless minutes for training.

caption:
Why is a thermometer still thirty-seven percent wrong after one response time?

Drop a cold probe into hot water and the number climbs fast, then crawls. Heat has to flow into the glass and the liquid inside before they match. The bigger the gap in temperature, the faster heat flows in.

So the gap closes quickly at first, then slower as the gap shrinks. Each equal slice of time closes the same fraction of what is left. After one response time, sixty-three percent is done and 37 percent remains.

Wait three response times and only five percent of the gap is left.

So a thermometer never snaps to the truth. It closes a fixed fraction each moment, so the wrong reading fades smoothly. That shape is called an exponential approach.

A hot coffee cools the same way, shedding most of its excess heat early and then lingering warm for ages. And a capacitor charging through a resistor reaches sixty-three percent in one time constant, for exactly this reason.

Go and test it, then report back.

caption:
Why does a pair of black holes chirp upward before they merge?

The detectors heard a rising tone, from a low hum to a quick whoop. Two heavy stars orbiting each other stir ripples in space itself. Those ripples carry energy away, so the pair keeps losing energy. A wider orbit stores more energy, so losing energy leaves the pair no choice but to fall closer.

A losing orbit does not slow down. It shrinks. Closer in, gravity pulls harder, so the pair must whip round faster to hold the orbit. And a smaller orbit means a faster lap, so the tone climbs. Faster orbits radiate even harder, so the loss speeds up as well.

That feedback runs away, and the final laps take a fraction of a second.

So the chirp rises because losing energy makes the orbit tighter and quicker. That runaway is called an inspiral.

A satellite in thin air drops lower and circles faster as it loses energy, in exactly the same way. And Earth's day is slowly lengthening while the Moon drifts outward, the same exchange running backwards.

Which part of this surprised you?

caption:
Why can falling freely not remove gravity everywhere at once?

Step off the board and for a moment nothing seems to pull you. That trick works because everything near you falls at the same rate. But Earth pulls toward its centre, and that centre is one single point.

Two droplets side by side are pulled along slightly converging lines. So they drift together, while a droplet above drifts away from one below. Gravity weakens with distance, so the lower droplet is pulled harder than the one above it. The gaps between them change even though both droplets are in free fall.

That change is what no choice of falling frame can ever hide.

So falling hides gravity at one point, but never across a gap. The stretching that survives is called a tidal force.

Ocean tides exist because the Moon pulls the near water harder than it pulls the far water. And a star falling into a black hole is pulled into a thin stream by this same difference.

caption:
How can spraying oranges with water save them from freezing?

Growers coat the fruit in ice before a frosty night, deliberately. It looks like the worst possible idea, and it works. Water does not merely cool as it turns to ice. It dumps heat.

Cooling a kilogram of water from twenty degrees to zero releases eighty four kilojoules. Freezing that same kilogram releases three hundred and thirty four kilojoules more. All that heat pours out while the temperature sits at zero and stays.

So the fruit under the ice is held at zero, not at minus five. Fruit survives at zero; it is the colder air below that would freeze its cells and burst them.

So the ice keeps the oranges at the freezing point instead of below it. That stored heat is called latent heat.

A drink stays cold while ice is still floating in it, because melting soaks up this same heat. And steam burns worse than boiling water, because it dumps this heat straight into your skin.

caption:
Why is the edge of the observable universe 46 billion light-years away, not 13.8?

Light from the most distant matter has been travelling for 13.8 billion years. But space itself has been stretching the whole time that light travelled. Picture an ant walking along a rubber band that is being pulled.

Every stretch adds distance behind the ant and ahead of it. So that matter now sits about 46 billion light-years away, not 13.8. That matter was only about forty million light-years away when its light set out. Nothing overtook the light. The gap simply grew while the light was flying.

Distance travelled and distance now are two different questions.

So the observable universe is far wider than its age suggests. Space grew beneath the travelling light, and that growth is called expansion.

A runner on a stretching track covers more ground than her stride suggests, because the surface grows beneath her. And distant galaxies look redder as they recede, since the same stretching pulls each light wave longer.

Who else was taught this wrong?

caption:
Why does turning up LIGO's laser both sharpen and shake the measurement?

LIGO measures a mirror's position by bouncing laser light off it. Light arrives in countable packets, so the count wobbles from moment to moment. More power means more packets, and that wobble shrinks against the signal.

But every packet also gives the mirror a small kick as it bounces. More packets mean a rougher, randomly varying shove on a 40-kilogram mirror. The steady part of the push does not matter; only its random unevenness does, and that grows with power. Double the power and counting noise falls, while kicking noise rises.

Somewhere between, the total is least. That is the best a plain laser manages.

So the laser sharpens and blurs at once. The two noises trade against each other, and that floor is called the standard quantum limit.

A photograph in dim light looks grainy for the same reason, because too few light packets reach each pixel. And an electron microscope damages what it views, since the beam that reveals detail also kicks the sample.

caption:
Can an empty box make one atom pass light back and forth?

Put one excited atom between two very good mirrors and wait. The atom drops down and releases one single particle of light. The mirrors trap that light, so it cannot escape and fly away.

The light comes straight back, and the atom absorbs it again. The trapped light keeps returning at exactly the atom's own frequency, so it is absorbed again. This swap repeats, and it works only if swapping beats leaking. So the atom and the empty box are no longer two separate things. The box starts with no light in it at all, and its own emptiness is what sets the swapping rate.

They behave like two pendulums tied by a string, trading energy over and over.

So the empty box is not empty of physics. The atom and the box share one state. Those swaps are called vacuum Rabi oscillations.

A tuning fork beside a matching one hands its vibration over and takes it back, the very same trading. And a superconducting chip swaps energy with a microwave box, which is how quantum computers move information.

caption:
How can a plant with no muscles snap shut in a tenth of a second?

A flytrap's two lobes are held curved outward, under real elastic strain. Water pressure inside the cells slowly bends them toward a tipping point. Touch a trigger hair twice within about twenty seconds and the trap is armed. The second touch sends an electrical signal that tells those cells to dump their water.

Cells on one side release their pressure, and the curved shape turns unstable. Past a certain curve the lobe can no longer hold its bowed shape, and the strain flips it inside out. Loading takes hours. The flip itself takes about 100 milliseconds. The lobes jump from curved outward to curved inward, all in one go.

Stored elastic energy is dumped at once, rather than pushed out slowly.

So the plant never moves quickly. It loads slowly and releases suddenly, and that flip is called snap-buckling.

A slap bracelet flattens the same way, because bending it past a point flips the whole curved strip. And a froghopper's jump uses a stored spring, since muscle alone cannot deliver that power fast enough.

caption:
How can two massless photons make a particle with mass?

A photon has no mass at all, and yet it does carry energy. Mass and energy are two readings of one single quantity. Crash two photons head on and their energy is available in one place.

If that shared energy is enough, it can be spent on making matter. An electron and its antimatter twin cost 1.022 million electron volts together. Charge has to stay at zero, so the light must make a matched pair, never one particle alone. So each photon needs about half a million electron volts, well into the gamma range.

Below that threshold the two photons simply pass through each other.

So mass is not made from nothing. Energy is converted, and massless light pays the bill. That is mass energy equivalence.

A gamma ray near a heavy nucleus makes the same pair, using that nucleus to balance the push. And a particle meeting its antiparticle runs the trade backwards, vanishing into two photons again.

caption:
How can the same quasar flicker twice, 417 days apart?

A quasar is a distant galaxy core blazing as gas falls into a black hole. A heavy galaxy sits between it and us, and its gravity bends light. So the light reaches us by two different routes, and we see two images.

One route is longer, and it also dips deeper into the bent space. Clocks run slower deep in gravity, so light on that route loses extra time as well. So one copy of every flicker arrives 417 days behind the other. Watch one image flare, then wait, and the other image flares later.

That delay measures the geometry, so it even gives the expansion rate.

So one quasar can blink twice over. Its light took two routes of different length, and that is called gravitational lensing.

A supernova behind a galaxy cluster appeared four times, because those bent routes delivered copies at different moments. And the base of a wine glass smears a streetlight into arcs, since uneven glass sends light along different routes.

Who else was taught this wrong?

caption:
Why does freezing need a starting speck before it can begin?

Below zero, ice is the cheaper state, so water should freeze at once. But ice cannot appear everywhere at once. It has to start somewhere small. A tiny ice speck wins energy from its volume and loses it at its surface.

caption:
Why can fifty trapped atoms need a quadrillion numbers to describe them?

Each atom sits in a trap made of light, and can point up or down. Two atoms give four combinations. Three give eight. Each atom doubles the count. Fifty atoms give two multiplied by itself fifty times.

That is about 1.1 quadrillion combinations, from particles you could count by hand. Unlike coins, the atoms can be in all those combinations at once, each with its own share. A quantum state carries one weight for every single one of those combinations. So writing that state down exactly means storing a quadrillion numbers.

Many real states are tidy and compress well, but the hardest ones stay huge.

So fifty atoms are not fifty things to track. The space of their states doubles each time, and that space is called Hilbert space.

A laptop simulating forty such atoms already needs terabytes, because the same doubling outruns memory fast. And chemistry is hard for the same reason, since each extra electron doubles the combinations a molecule holds.

caption:
How can perfect spheres freeze into a crystal with nothing pulling them?

Imagine marbles that only refuse to overlap. Nothing attracts them at all. Shake the tray and you expect a jumbled, disordered pile forever. But pack them tighter and the jumble starts to jam, so nothing moves.

A neat stack leaves every marble a little private room to rattle in. Order buys wiggle room, and once space gets tight, wiggle room wins. A random pile runs out of space first, at about forty nine percent filled.

So the crystal actually has more ways to arrange itself, not fewer. A shaken system settles into whatever arrangement it has the most ways of being in.

So the spheres order themselves to gain freedom, not to lower energy. That is a crystal built by entropy.

Tiny plastic beads in water really do crystallise in the lab, with no glue between them. And stacking oranges in a neat pyramid fits far more into the crate, for the same reason.

Which part of this surprised you?

caption:
Why is a superconductor more than just a wire that lost all its resistance?

Cool some metals far enough and their resistance drops to exactly zero. A wire like that would simply trap whatever magnetic field was already inside. With no resistance, any change in the field stirs currents that cancel the change, so the old field stays. Lead does something stronger. Cool it in a magnet and the field is pushed out.

In lead the field survives only a 39-nanometre skin, and in aluminium less still. Thin currents run in that skin and cancel the field inside exactly. So this is not just easy flow of charge. It is active expulsion.

That expulsion is the sign the metal has genuinely changed state.

So a superconductor is not merely a perfect wire. It throws the magnetic field out, and that is called the Meissner effect.

A cold disc floats above a magnet, because the expelled field pushes back the moment the disc tries to sink. And an MRI magnet runs for years unplugged, since its looping current meets no resistance to slow it.

Did anyone explain it to you this way at school?

caption:
Why can a one nanosecond flash never be a single pure colour?

A pure colour means one steady wave repeating forever, with no beginning. Your flash does begin, and it stops a billionth of a second later. To make a wave switch on and off you must add other waves.

Those extra waves cancel outside the pulse and add up inside it. The shorter the flash, the wider the spread of colours you need. Waves close in pitch take a long time to drift apart and cancel, so a quick cut-off needs distant ones. For a smooth one nanosecond pulse that spread is at least 441 megahertz.

Squeeze the pulse ten times shorter and the spread grows ten times wider.

So the flash is not impure by accident. A short pulse and one pure colour cannot both exist. That trade is called the time bandwidth limit.

A very short laser pulse looks almost white rather than red, because its colours are spread so wide. And a radio station needs a band of channel space, because switching its signal on spreads it out.

Guess before you scroll, then check.

caption:
Why does a narrower slit spread light out more?

Shine a laser through a slit and you get a band of light beyond it. Squeeze the slit narrower and that band gets wider, not thinner. Every point across the slit sends out a wave, and those waves interfere.

The first dark edge sits where waves from the two two halves cancel out. A narrow slit forces a bigger angle before that cancellation can happen. Red light fans out 0.36 degrees through a wide slit, and 1.8 through a narrow one.

So the spread angle is roughly the light's wave size divided by the slit width.

So a narrow slit fans light wider, not tighter. Squeezing a wave sideways makes it fan out, and that is called diffraction.

A small speaker sends bass everywhere but treble in a beam, because low notes have larger waves than the cone. And a telescope blurs faint stars, since its mirror is a wide opening and even that spreads light.

Who else was taught this wrong?

caption:
Why does a star hold steady for billions of years with no control system?

A star is a standoff between gravity pulling in and hot gas pushing out. Suppose the core happens to fuse a little too fast for a moment. The extra heat raises the pressure, so the core expands slightly.

Expanding gas cools, and fusion is fiercely sensitive to temperature. Gas spends energy pushing its surroundings outward, so expanding leaves it cooler. A ten percent cooling cuts the Sun's fusion rate by about a third. So the burn rate falls, the core settles back inward, and the heat returns.

Every wobble is answered by an opposite push. Nobody designed this.

So a star stays steady with no controller at all. A correction that opposes the change is called negative feedback.

Your body holds its temperature this way, because sweating and shivering each push back against the change. And a car's cruise control keeps one speed, since any drop triggers exactly the opposing correction.

caption:
Why does a quantum computer not simply try every answer at once?

It is true that the machine can hold every answer at the same time. But measuring it hands you just one of them, picked at random. A random answer out of a million is worth nothing to you.

Each possibility also carries a weight that can be positive or negative. Like waves, weights meeting out of step cancel, and in step they add. Cancelling the wrong answers cuts a million-item search to about 785 tries.

So the right answer keeps nearly all the weight, and that is what you read. The bigger an answer's weight, the likelier the measurement lands on it.

So a quantum computer does not check everything. It steers wrong answers into cancellation, and that is called interference.

Noise-cancelling headphones kill sound this way, because an inverted wave meets the original and wipes it out. And a two-slit experiment shows dark bands, since paths arriving out of step cancel exactly like these answers.

What did you think the reason was?

caption:
Why does Mars sometimes stop and drift backwards across our sky?

For weeks it slides east against the stars, then reverses, then goes on. Mars never truly reverses. It keeps circling the Sun the one way. Earth is closer in, so it moves faster and finishes a lap sooner. Closer to the Sun the pull is stronger, so an inner planet has to travel faster to stay in orbit.

Earth covers about 30 kilometres each second, and Mars only 24. So roughly every 26 months, Earth catches Mars and sweeps past inside it. During that overtaking, our line of sight to Mars swings the other way. As we pass on the inside, Mars sits off our shoulder and slides back against the far stars.

So the planet appears to slip backwards for a while, then move on.

So Mars only seems to drift backwards. We overtake it on the inside, and that is called retrograde motion.

A car you overtake seems to slide backwards, because your greater speed reverses the way it drifts. And Jupiter does this every year too, since Earth laps it as well and swings our sight line round.

Which part of this surprised you?

caption:
How can one atom swell to about a micrometre across?

An atom's outer charge is not a ball. It is a cloud of likelihood. Push that cloud up to a much higher energy level and it spreads far out. More energy means the nucleus holds that charge less tightly, so it can sit much further out. The cloud's width grows as the level number squared.

caption:
Why does knowing which half a particle is in let you lift a weight?

Put a single particle in a box and slide a partition down the middle. You do not know which side it landed on, so you can do nothing. Guess wrong and the empty side drags the partition back, so on average you gain nothing. Now look. Say it turns out to be on the left.

Knowing which half it occupied is exactly one bit of information. At room temperature that one bit is worth about 2.9 zeptojoules of work.

The books balance later, because erasing that bit costs at least as much.

So knowing something is genuinely worth energy. Information and heat sit in one ledger, and that is called Landauer's principle.

A sorting demon gains nothing overall, because its memory must be cleared and that erasure costs heat. And a hard drive warms as it overwrites data, since erasing each bit dumps at least that much heat.

caption:
Why does making proton beams brighter make each collision harder to read?

caption:
Why does an electric field die out inside a metal in less than one atom's width?

A metal is packed with tiny charges called electrons that roam freely. Drop one extra positive charge into that sea and it does not sit alone. The roaming charges crowd toward it and smother its pull almost at once.

In copper the pull is essentially gone within a tenth of a nanometre. Salty water screens the same way, but its charges are sparse and slow. So its shield is spread over a nanometre, more than ten times wider. Where free charges are plentiful, enough gather within a whisker to cancel the pull entirely.

Density of free charge sets the distance, and metals have a huge supply.

So a metal hides an inside charge within one atom's width. That short shield distance is called the screening length.

A salt solution hides a charged protein the same way. Its free ions crowd in and cut the pull short. And a plasma shields every ion inside it. The same crowding of free charge limits how far each pull reaches.

caption:
How is the Sun turning 4.3 million tonnes of itself into light each second?

Deep in the core, hydrogen nuclei are being forced together into helium. Weigh the four that go in, then weigh the helium that comes out. The helium is about seven tenths of a percent lighter. The Sun fuses about six hundred million tonnes of hydrogen a second, and 0.7 percent of that is 4.3.

That missing sliver leaves as energy, 4.3 million tonnes of it every second. Mass and energy are two readings of the very same quantity. The exchange rate is enormous, so a tiny mass gives a flood of light.

Even so, the Sun has lost only about three parts in ten thousand of its mass.

So the Sun is not burning fuel like a fire. It converts mass into light, and that link is called E equals m c squared.

A nuclear reactor works the same way, since splitting uranium leaves the fragments slightly lighter than the start. And a hydrogen bomb releases that same mass gap, because it fuses light nuclei just as the core does.

What did you think the reason was?

caption:
Why does a tiny ratchet lift no weight in a room at one temperature?

Picture a paddle sitting in gas, linked to a wheel with slanted teeth. A little spring-loaded catch should let that wheel turn one way only. Gas particles batter the paddle, so it should step forward and raise a thread.

But the catch is just as tiny, and the same gas batters it. Whenever the catch bounces up, the wheel can slip backwards just as easily. So forward steps and backward steps come out exactly equal. Stiffen the catch and it stops bouncing, but then it also blocks the forward steps.

The average lift is zero, however patiently you wait for it.

So the ratchet is not broken at all. One temperature offers no direction to work with, and that rule is called the second law.

A cell's walking protein only steps forward because it burns fuel, which supplies the direction heat alone cannot. And a power station needs a cold river, since work only appears between a hot side and a cold one.

Which part of this surprised you?

caption:
When does a lens image fail the paper test?

Hold a card where a lens forms a picture of a bright window. Sometimes a sharp picture lands on the card. Sometimes nothing lands at all. Rays leaving the lens either truly meet at a point, or they spread apart.

If they meet, light is genuinely there, so the paper catches it. A ten-centimetre lens, object at fifteen centimetres, lands a picture thirty centimetres out. If they spread, your eye traces them back to a place with no light.

Move the object to five centimetres and the image sits behind the lens, uncatchable. Held closer than the lens's focal length, the lens cannot bend the rays enough to make them meet.

So the paper test asks a lens one thing. Do the rays truly meet? Rays that meet make what is called a real image.

A cinema projector must form a real image, because a screen can only show light that actually arrives. And a magnifying glass held close casts no picture on a card. Its rays only seem to come from behind.

caption:
Why can three polarisers pass light that two of them block?

A polariser passes only the part of light that shakes along one line. Cross two of them at ninety degrees and no light comes through. Now slide a third sheet in between them, turned to forty-five degrees. A wave shaking along one line still has a slice lying along a tilted line, and that slice passes.

Light suddenly appears, even though you added yet another blocker. The middle sheet does not merely filter. It re-aims whatever passes through. Light leaving it shakes at forty-five degrees, no longer square to the last sheet.

Two crossed sheets pass nothing; add the middle one and 12.5 percent gets through.

So the middle sheet changes the light rather than only blocking it. That projection rule is called Malus's law.

A quantum measurement behaves this way, because measuring along a new axis resets the state instead of just filtering. And 3D cinema glasses use the same projection, since each lens passes only the part aimed along its own line.

Guess before you scroll, then check.

caption:
Why does a helium balloon lurch forward when your car pulls away?

Every loose thing in the cabin slides backward. The balloon does the exact opposite. The air in the cabin has weight too, and it slides backward just the same. So air piles up against the rear window, and the pressure back there goes higher.

The balloon now sits in air that pushes harder from behind than from ahead. Fifty-one millinewtons of air push forward. Only sixteen hold it back. Helium is so light that the balloon's own backward tug is feeble by comparison.

So the air's push wins easily, and the balloon leans toward the windscreen.

So the balloon goes forward because the cabin air goes back. Riding up a pressure slope is called buoyancy.

A bubble in your drink shifts backwards when the car brakes, because the liquid piles up at the front. And hot air rises for exactly this reason, since heavier cool air sinks and shoves the light stuff up.

caption:
How can a dead pinecone open and close with no living cells?

Each scale of the cone is two layers of fibre glued back to back. One layer's fibres run along the scale, and the other's run across it. Both layers take up water from damp air and swell a little.

But each swells mostly across its own fibres, so they grow in different directions. Along the fibres it stretches under one percent, across them about twenty. Two bonded layers changing length by different amounts have no choice but to bend. Glued together, the longer layer must take the outside of a curve, so the pair bows toward the shorter one.

Dry air reverses it, the scale straightens again, and the cone opens.

So a dead pinecone still moves. Two unequal layers bend whenever they wet, and that pairing is called a bilayer actuator.

A wheat awn drills its seed into soil the same way, because daily humidity swings bend it again and again. And a bimetal thermostat curls when heated, since two bonded metals expand by different amounts and force a bend.

caption:
Why must a swimming bacterium use a motion it cannot simply reverse?

To a bacterium, water feels about as thick as honey feels to us. At that size, coasting is hopeless. Stop pushing and you stop instantly. Cut the motor and it glides a tenth of a nanometre, far less than its width.

So the distance you travel depends only on the shape changes you make. Open and close a simple hinge, and the second half undoes the first. So it needs a stroke whose reverse is not just the forward one run backwards.

Its tail turns like a corkscrew, and a corkscrew drives one way as it turns. A corkscrew keeps turning the same way instead of retracing its shapes, so it never undoes itself.

So a bacterium cannot row its way anywhere. It needs a cycle that looks different backwards, and that rule is called the scallop theorem.

A corkscrew always advances as you turn it, because its motion reversed is not the same path undone. And sperm swim with a wave travelling down the tail, since a wave has a direction a flap lacks.

What did you think the reason was?

caption:
Why does a cricket ball carry a wave you could never hope to measure?

Every moving thing carries a wave, and that wave's size is called its wavelength. Its size is one very small constant divided by mass times speed. A cricket ball is a hundred and sixty grams, bowled at forty metres per second.

Do the division and the wave lands at the thirty-fourth decimal place. A proton turns up at the fifteenth decimal place. The ball, the thirty-fourth. So a proton is about ten billion billion times bigger than the ball's own wave.

Waves only show themselves at gaps their own size, and no such gap exists. A wave only bends noticeably around something about as big as the wave itself.

So the cricket ball's wave is real but hopeless to measure. Heavy things hide it, and that is called the de Broglie wavelength.

An electron is so light that its wave spans a whole atom, which is why chemistry needs quantum rules. And a neutron beam maps crystals, because its wave is about as wide as the gaps between atoms.

caption:
Why is a hand generator hardest to crank when its two wires are touching?

With the wires apart the handle spins almost freely. Only friction slows you. Touch the wires together and the handle feels stuck in cold treacle. Turning the coil past the magnet drives a current around the closed loop. Current can only go round a complete loop, so with the wires apart none flows at all.

That current sits inside the same magnet's field, so the field shoves back on the coil. Wires apart, half a watt to turn. Wires touching, about twelve. Shorted, roughly two amps flow and the coil pours out twelve watts of heat.

So your arm has to supply every one of those watts. Nothing arrives free.

So the generator makes no energy of its own. Your work becomes heat, and that shove-back is called Lenz's law.

An electric car brakes on its motor, because pushing current back into the battery makes that same opposing twist. And a gym bike stiffens as you raise its setting, since more current in the coils means more push-back.

caption:
How does gravity keep a comet's whole orbit pinned to one flat sheet?

Space has three directions, yet the comet's path never drifts off a single plane. The Sun's pull always points straight from the comet to the Sun's centre. A pull aimed straight at a point can give no twist about that point.

Twist about the Sun is the one thing that could tilt the comet's turning. The same pull aimed sideways would twist hard. Aimed inward, nothing. So the direction of that turning is locked, and it stays locked for centuries.

The path must stay square to that locked direction, so it stays flat. The turning direction points straight out of the plane the comet sweeps, so fixing it fixes the plane.

So the comet rides no rail. Its orbit is flat because nothing ever twists it, and that is called conservation of angular momentum.

A gyroscope holds its axle pointing one way, because a good mounting gives it almost no twist. And Halley's comet comes back on the same tilted plane each time, since the Sun cannot twist it sideways.

yt_description:
Why is pure water almost a million times worse at carrying current than seawater?

Water itself is a poor path for electricity. The clean stuff barely carries anything. What carries current through a liquid is charged particles called ions, free to drift. Sea salt breaks apart into sodium and chloride ions, billions of them in every drop.

Pure water has almost none. Only one particle in a few hundred million splits apart. Seawater carries current about nine hundred thousand times better. So the bulb in the salt beaker lights, and the pure-water bulb stays dark.

Add one pinch of salt to that beaker and the dark bulb comes straight on.

So water is not really the carrier. The dissolved ions are, and that is called ionic conduction.

Laboratory distilled water hardly carries current at all, because the dissolving step has stripped its ions away. And sweat makes an electric shock worse, since salty water on your skin carries current far better.

caption:
Why does air change the shape of a struck ball's path, not just its range?

Textbooks draw a neat parabola, rising and falling in perfect mirror image. Air shoves back on a moving ball, and that shove grows with the square of speed. So a ball leaving the bat at forty-five metres a second meets a brutal shove early.

Drag strips the forward speed away fast, while gravity keeps pulling down unchanged. So the ball climbs almost normally, then falls on a much steeper line. Without air it would carry 206 metres. The real hit lands near 115.

The peak sits well past halfway, and the descent is short and lopsided. By the top the ball has lost most of its forward speed, so the fall covers much less ground.

So air does more than shrink the range. It rewrites the shape into a lopsided curve, and that is called quadratic drag.

A badminton shuttle shows it hugely, dropping almost straight down once drag has eaten its forward speed. And a skydiver stops speeding up altogether, because that same growing drag rises until it matches their weight.
