caption:
How can a 1.5 volt battery read full, then die the moment you switch on?

A meter draws almost no current. It only reads the battery's resting push. Every cell has resistance inside it, in its paste, its plates and its seals. As a cell ages, that inside resistance climbs, sometimes to several ohms.

With no current flowing, that resistance costs you nothing, so the meter looks perfect. Meter alone reads 1.50 volts. With the bulb on, 0.56. Switch on and current must flow, and it has to pass through the inside too. The same current flows through both, so whichever resistance is larger swallows more of the push.

So most of the push is spent inside the cell, and the bulb starves.

So the battery never had a full 1.5 volts to give under load. That lost push is called the internal resistance drop.

A tired car battery lights the dashboard happily, then barely turns the starter, which demands hundreds of amps. And a phone quits in the cold, because a chilled cell has more resistance inside and sags under load.

What did you think the reason was?

caption:
Why is a ten-thousand-volt lighter spark safer than a shorted 1.5-volt battery?

Voltage is only the push. It does not tell you how much energy is stored. The lighter's crystal makes a huge push, but it holds barely any charge. Energy is charge times push, so almost no charge means almost no energy. So the spark empties in a millionth of a second, worth about a thousandth of a joule.

One spark, a thousandth of a joule. One shorted cell, six hundred. A battery pushes gently, but it can keep pushing for a very long time. A short offers almost no resistance, so even a gentle push drives a big current. Shorted, it drives about seven amps through its own insides and makes heat.

So the cell gets hot enough to burn you, or to split open.

So the spark wins on push and loses badly on energy. What actually hurts you is energy delivered, and that is called joule heating.

A carpet shock reaches thousands of volts, yet it only stings, because the stored energy is tiny. And a car battery reads just twelve volts, but a dropped spanner glows red from the energy it pours out.

Which part of this surprised you?

caption:
How can moving the magnet, or moving the coil, kick one needle the same way?

Push the magnet into a still coil. The needle jumps hard to one side. Now hold the magnet still and slide the coil over it. The needle jumps the same. Only the motion between the two matters, and that motion is identical in both takes.

What the coil actually feels is how much magnetic field threads through its loops. A steady threading pushes nothing; only a changing one drives the charges round the loop. Moving either object changes that threading, at exactly the same rate. Four times faster in, and the voltage comes out four times bigger.

So the voltage follows the rate of change, not which object you chose to move.

So the needle is not reporting the magnet's motion. It reports changing threading, and that is called Faraday's law.

A guitar pickup hears a steel string because the vibrating string keeps changing the threading through a tiny coil. And a transformer never moves at all, because switching its current changes the threading just as motion would.

Did anyone explain it to you this way at school?

caption:
How can particles in a reactor pool outrun light without breaking relativity?

Look down into the water and the whole core glows an eerie blue. That glow comes from tiny charged particles called electrons, flung out by decaying fuel. They cross the water at about ninety-nine percent of light's ultimate speed limit.

But light itself does not travel at that limit once it is inside water. The electron makes 297 million metres a second. Light in water, 226. So the electron really does outrun the light around it, by a clear margin. As it passes, the electron jolts the water's charges, and each jolt sends out a ripple of light.

A glowing shock wave piles up behind it, and that is the blue you see. Because the electron outruns its own ripples, they stack along one cone instead of spreading out.

So nothing beats light in empty space. The reactor glow only beats slowed-down light, and that is called Cherenkov radiation.

A sonic boom has the same shape, made when an aircraft outruns the sound waves it keeps producing. And a boat wake spreads in a sharp V, because the hull moves faster than its own water waves.

Guess before you scroll, then check.

caption:
What would break if a coil pulled your magnet inward instead of pushing back?

Push a magnet into a coil of wire and a current appears in that wire. That current turns the coil into a magnet too, aimed to shove yours back out. Suppose it pulled inward instead. The magnet would dive in all by itself.

Faster motion makes more current, and more current would pull it in harder still. Two joules of heat every second, and nobody pays a thing. So you collect heat in the wire and motion in the magnet, for nothing.

That is a machine making energy from nothing, and none has ever worked.

So the coil has to oppose the magnet. Opposing is the only way the energy books balance, and that is called Lenz's law.

A magnet dropped down a copper pipe drifts down slowly, because the currents it stirs up always push back. And an induction hob heats a pan by that same opposition, turning stirred-up currents into heat in the metal.

Check it at home and tell me what you saw.

caption:
Why can adding more damping make a door close more slowly?

A door closer holds oil in a cylinder, and that oil resists quick movement. Resistance that grows with speed is called damping, and more should mean a calmer close. With too little, the door rushes the last stretch and slams into the frame.

With too much, the oil drags so hard the door creeps the final centimetres. The spring's push is fixed, so heavier drag simply settles the door at a lower steady speed. Just enough damping settles in 2.4 seconds. Three times as much needs 11.7. Between those two failures sits one exact amount, and it is the quickest of all.

So the best quiet close is a knife edge, not simply as much drag as possible.

So extra damping does not buy a faster close. One exact amount wins, and that is called critical damping.

A car shock absorber is tuned near that same point, so the body settles once instead of floating. And a laboratory balance is damped this way too, so its pointer reaches the reading without swinging past.

Try it tonight and tell me what happened.

caption:
Can four blocks lean past a table edge by more than one whole block?

It sounds impossible. Surely the top one tips off past the table edge. A stack tips only when its balance point slides past whatever is holding it up. So the top block can hang out by half its length and still balance.

The pair above the next block balances a quarter of a length out. Each block down must carry the balance point of everything above it, and more weight above means a smaller step. Four blocks reach 1.04 lengths. One block alone reaches only a half. Then a sixth, then an eighth. The steps shrink but they keep adding.

Half plus a quarter plus a sixth plus an eighth is just over one block.

So the blocks never lose their grip on the table. Every balance point still sits over its support, and that is called static equilibrium.

A tower crane carries a heavy counterweight behind its cab, holding the machine's balance point over its base. And a person leaning off a ladder falls at the exact moment their balance point clears the ladder's feet.

What did you think the reason was?

caption:
Why does a small soap bubble hold higher pressure inside than a big one?

Join two bubbles by a tube and the small one shrinks, feeding the big one. A soap film pulls itself tight, like a stretched sheet always trying to shrink. Air pressure inside must push outward hard enough to hold that pull off.

How much extra push you need depends on how sharply the film curves. A tight curve pinches harder, so a small bubble must hold more pressure to survive. The tighter the curve, the more the film's sideways pull aims inward instead of along the surface. A one-centimetre bubble holds 10 pascals extra. A five-centimetre one, just 2.

So air runs from the small bubble into the big one, and the small one dies.

So the smaller bubble always wins on pressure. The extra push follows the curve, and that is called Laplace pressure.

Tiny air sacs in your lungs would empty into bigger ones, so your body coats them with a special film. And a fizzy drink grows its biggest bubbles fastest, because the small ones sit at higher pressure and dissolve.

Check it at home and tell me what you saw.

caption:
Why does a man walking a frictionless plank push it backwards by an exact amount?

Slippery ice underneath means the ground offers the pair no sideways grip. So the balance point of man plus plank cannot shift sideways, whatever he does. His feet shove the plank back. The plank shoves his feet forward. Those two cancel.

The man is sixty kilograms. The plank is thirty, half as much. He walks four metres along it, so the gap between them changes by four metres. The man ends 1.33 metres forward. The plank slides 2.67 metres back. To hold the balance point still, the heavier one must move less, in exact proportion to its mass.

Twice the mass means half the shift, and the two shifts always settle together.

So walking moves the man and the plank opposite ways. Their balance point never moves, and that is called conservation of the centre of mass.

Stepping off a rowing boat kicks it backwards, because your forward push has to be paid for somewhere. And an astronaut who throws a spanner drifts the other way, since nothing outside can hold the pair still.

Did anyone explain it to you this way at school?

caption:
Why does doubling a spring's stiffness speed the bounce by only forty-one percent?

Twice as stiff sounds like twice as many bounces a second. It is not. Stiffness says how hard the spring pulls back for a given amount of stretch. So doubling it doubles the pull, and doubles the acceleration of the same mass.

But distance travelled grows with acceleration times time squared, not times time. The spring still covers the same distance, so only the time is free to change. So doubling the acceleration shortens the trip by the square root of two. Ten newtons per metre gives 0.71 bounces a second. Twenty gives 1.01.

The square root of two is 1.41, so the rate climbs by forty-one percent.

So stiffness does not set the bounce rate directly. The rate follows its square root, and that is called square-root scaling.

A guitar string pulled to four times the tension sounds only twice as high, following the same square root. And a pendulum four times longer swings only twice as slowly, because its rate follows a square root too.

Guess before you scroll, then check.

caption:
Why can a hard sideways push on a moving crate do exactly zero work?

Lean on the side of a sliding crate. Your arms burn and nothing speeds up. Work is not effort. It is force times the distance moved along that force. The crate travels forward. Your push points sideways, square across its travel.

Measured along your push line, the crate covers no distance at all. The same 200 newtons: a thousand joules along, nothing sideways. So the distance in the work sum is zero, which makes the whole product zero.

Only the slice of a force lined up with the motion can change the crate's speed.

So a sideways push can exhaust you and leave the moving crate no faster. Counting only the along-track slice is what we call the dot product.

A satellite circling Earth gains no speed, because gravity pulls square across its motion the whole way round. And a heavy suitcase carried on level ground takes no work, since you lift while it travels horizontally.

Who else was taught this wrong?

caption:
Why does a block leave a smooth dome forty-two degrees before the equator?

Start the block at the very top of a slippery dome and nudge it. While it stays on the surface, it is forced to follow a circle. Going in a circle needs a force pointing inward, and here gravity supplies it. The dome also pushes outward, so the inward force left over is gravity's share minus that push.

But only the part of gravity aimed at the dome's centre counts. As the block slides down it speeds up, so it needs more inward force. The speed grows faster than gravity's share does, so the dome's push must fall to zero. Contact ends where the surface push reaches zero, forty-eight degrees from the top.

At that moment it has dropped exactly one third of the dome's radius.

So the dome cannot hold the block to the equator. A surface can only push, never pull, and that is called a one-sided constraint.

Drive fast over a road hump and the wheels lift clear, because tarmac can only push upward. Sand leaves a turning drum at the angle where the wall stops pushing hard enough to hold it.

caption:
Can moving a marked dot change how much a gliding dumbbell counts as turning?

A two-kilogram dumbbell slides across smooth ice at three metres per second. It never rotates. The painted stripe points the same way the whole trip. Turning is always measured about some chosen point, and you pick that point.

caption:
Why can a snail's pace stop an iron nucleus absorbing a gamma ray?

An iron nucleus absorbs a gamma ray of exactly fourteen point four kilo-electronvolts. Exactly means brutally exact. The accepted band is five billionths of an electronvolt wide. A free atom kicks backward when it emits, stealing two thousandths of an electronvolt.

That theft is hundreds of thousands of band widths, so nothing is absorbed. Lock the atom in a crystal and the whole block takes the kick, so the loss vanishes. The whole crystal is a billion billion times heavier, so the same kick costs it no energy worth counting. Now slide the source at one millimetre per second. The energy shifts forty-eight billionths. A source moving towards you sends its gamma ray out slightly more energetic.

That shift is ten times the whole accepted band, from a crawl.

So the nucleus is an absurdly narrow filter. Motion stretches the gamma ray's energy, and that stretch is called the Doppler shift.

This measured gravity's redshift in a tower, since light falling twenty-two metres shifts enough for that filter to notice. Radar guns use the same shift, reading a car's speed from the tiny frequency change it stamps on the echo.

Which part of this surprised you?

caption:
How can five false discoveries drown out one real discovery?

A lab runs a hundred experiments, and suppose only one effect is real. Each test raises a flag when the odds of a fluke drop below five percent. So among the ninety-nine dead ends, about five will flag anyway.

That is five false alarms standing against one true one. And the one real effect is only caught about eighty percent of the time. So roughly six flags go up, and five of them are wrong.

The five percent was never the chance that a flag is wrong.

So a rare discovery is buried by common mistakes. What matters is how many real effects existed first, and that is called the base rate.

Screening healthy people for a rare disease returns mostly false alarms, because healthy people vastly outnumber sick ones. Genetics labs testing a million genes expect thousands of flukes, so they demand far stricter evidence per test.

caption:
Why does a perfect Carnot engine deliver exactly zero power?

An engine wastes energy whenever heat jumps across a temperature gap. Heat sliding down a gap could have driven an engine on the way, and that chance is thrown away. To waste nothing, the gas must be almost exactly as hot as its heat source. But heat only flows when there is a difference, and a tiny difference flows slowly.

So the perfect engine needs almost forever to finish one stroke. Power is work divided by time, so endless time drives the power to zero. Real engines open that gap on purpose, losing efficiency to gain speed.

Between eight hundred and three hundred kelvin, the best power comes at thirty-nine percent.

So the Carnot limit is a ceiling on efficiency, not a usable engine. Running fast and slightly wasteful is called operating at maximum power.

A car engine could run far more efficiently on gentler cycles, but that gain costs time nobody will spend. Charging a battery slowly wastes less energy, for the same reason: small pushes waste little but take hours.

caption:
How can slipping an insulator into a capacitor let it hold twice the charge?

A capacitor is two metal plates, held close together, wired to a battery. The battery pulls tiny charges called electrons off one plate and piles them on the other. Those piled charges push back, and the battery stops when that push matches its voltage.

Now slide a plastic sheet into the gap. Its own charges shift by a hair. The plates drag its positives one way and its negatives the other, so its push opposes theirs. That shift sets up a weak push of its own, pointing against the plates. So the total push inside the gap drops, and the battery is no longer balanced.

So it pumps more charge on until the push matches its voltage again.

So the insulator stores no charge itself. It weakens the push so more charge fits, and such a material is called a dielectric.

Every phone is packed with such material, because it buys more storage without any extra plate area. Water is an extreme case, and that is why salt dissolves: the pull holding the crystal together is cut eighty-fold.

Who else was taught this wrong?

caption:
If Earth orbits the Sun, why does the Sun swing in a small circle too?

Earth does not orbit the Sun's centre. Both bodies orbit a shared balance point. Gravity tugs on the two of them with exactly the same size of pull. But the Sun is three hundred and thirty thousand times heavier than Earth.

So the same pull shifts it three hundred and thirty thousand times less. Being that much heavier, the Sun sits that many times nearer the balance point than Earth. Their balance point lies 449 kilometres out from the Sun's own centre. That is 449 kilometres of swing, inside a Sun 696,000 kilometres in radius.

So the Sun truly does circle, but its circle hides deep inside itself.

So the Earth and the Sun both circle one shared balance point. That point is called the barycentre.

Jupiter tugs far harder, so the Sun's swing about their balance point actually reaches outside the solar surface. And astronomers find distant planets by watching a star wobble, since an unseen partner swings it around.

caption:
How can a thrown pebble leave asteroid Bennu at twenty centimetres per second?

Bennu is a loose pile of rubble about half a kilometre across. Its whole mass is seventy-three billion kilograms, which sounds enormous. But Earth outweighs it by roughly eighty trillion times. Bennu is also tiny, so you stand far closer to its middle, which wins much of that back.

So the pull at Bennu's surface is about one hundred-thousandth of Earth's. Escaping means outrunning the pull, so a feebler pull needs far less speed. Earth needs eleven kilometres per second to escape. Bennu needs twenty centimetres. That is slower than a gentle stroll, and far slower than any thrown ball.

So a seventy-kilogram astronaut standing there would weigh about half a gram.

So Bennu holds on to nothing tightly. The speed needed to leave follows mass and size, and that is called escape velocity.

Comet sixty-seven P let its lander bounce a kilometre high, because its escape speed is under one metre per second. The Moon keeps no air for the same reason, since hot gas particles outrun its weak escape speed.

What did you think the reason was?

caption:
Why do farmers spray water on crops to stop them freezing?

It looks backwards. Ice on a leaf should be the problem, not the cure. Water does not only cool as it freezes. It also dumps out a large lump of heat. Cooling one kilogram of water by one degree releases about four kilojoules.

Freezing that same kilogram releases three hundred and thirty-four kilojoules. So a freezing film gives out as much heat as cooling that water by eighty degrees. That heat pours into whatever the film is touching, and the bud is right underneath. And while ice and water sit together, the mixture holds steady at zero degrees.

So the bud stays at zero, which is cold but survivable, instead of minus five.

So the farmers are not insulating the crop. Freezing water heats it, and that heat is called latent heat.

Growers flood their groves before a frost, because the freezing surface keeps giving out heat all night. Coasts stay milder than inland, because the seawater must give up that same freezing heat before ice forms.

Which part of this surprised you?

caption:
Why does a spinning coin's wobble speed up as it runs out of energy?

A coin settling on a table rattles faster and faster, then stops dead. Energy is leaking away the whole time, so the sound should surely slow down. But the rattle rate is not set by the energy. It is set by the tilt. A flatter coin runs its contact point round a shorter circle, so each wobble finishes sooner.

As friction drains energy the coin lies flatter, and the tilt angle shrinks. A flatter coin rides lower, so the energy it loses is exactly the tilt it gives up. A ten-degree tilt wobbles eight times a second. A one-degree tilt, twenty-five. The rate climbs as one over the square root of the tilt angle.

So a tilt heading toward zero sends the wobble rate screaming upward.

So the coin gains nothing as it dies. The wobble rate is tied to the shrinking tilt, and that motion is called precession.

A spinning top's lean circles faster as it tips flatter, driven by the same link to the angle. Earth's axis circles once every twenty-six thousand years, a slow version of that same leaning-spin motion.

Did anyone explain it to you this way at school?

caption:
Why can a billion-name list be searched with only thirty yes-or-no questions?

Keep the list in alphabetical order, and ask about the middle name first. Is your name before it, or after it? Either answer kills half the list. A billion becomes five hundred million, then two hundred and fifty million.

Each question two halves what is left, so the pile collapses fast. Ten questions cut the list by a factor of about a thousand. Twenty questions cut it by a million, and thirty by a billion.

So thirty good questions beat a billion one-by-one checks.

So the list is never really searched, it is cut in half. Thirty questions carry thirty yes-or-no bits, and that pattern is called logarithmic scaling.

A dictionary works this way in your hands, since every page you open throws away half the remaining words. Guess-my-number ends in seven guesses for a hundred numbers, because each guess discards half the range.

caption:
Why does a fast air particle travel only seventy nanometres before it hits something?

Air feels like nothing at all. Each particle really does fly at five hundred metres per second. But the air is packed with tiny particles called molecules. In one cubic centimetre there are about twenty-five billion billion of them.

Each one is only a third of a nanometre wide, so most of the space really is empty. Sweep your own width along, and you have swallowed one molecule's worth of space after seventy nanometres. Even so, a particle flies only seventy nanometres between hits. At five hundred metres per second, that gap lasts a tenth of a nanosecond.

So each particle is struck roughly seven billion times every second.

So the air particle is fast, but the traffic is thick. That short free run is called the mean free path.

Pumping a vacuum chamber removes most of the particles, so each survivor flies metres between hits instead of nanometres. High in the atmosphere the air is thin, so a free run stretches to kilometres. Satellites there feel separate hits, not smooth drag.

caption:
How can two crossed fields let through only particles moving at one exact speed?

A beam of charged particles enters the tube at every speed imaginable. An electric field across the tube shoves each particle sideways, equally hard every time. Now cross a magnetic field over it, at right angles to the first. The fields are crossed so that their two pushes point in opposite directions.

A magnetic shove depends on speed. Slow ones barely feel it, fast ones feel plenty. So at one speed the two shoves are equal and opposite, and the particle flies straight. Half again too fast, and the magnetic shove beats the electric one.

Everything else curves into the wall, so a far slit passes only that one speed.

So the fields sort nothing by mass and nothing by charge. They sort by speed alone, and that is called a velocity selector. Both pushes grow with the charge, so charge cancels out and only speed decides.

A mass spectrometer puts one in front, so every particle reaching the detector arrives at the same speed. And a vacuum cleaner cyclone balances air drag against spin, so only the finest dust leaves with the air.

caption:
How can a warm carbon dioxide tank spray snow at minus seventy-eight degrees?

caption:
Why can an insect stand on water but sink straight through alcohol?

A water surface behaves like a taut skin, always pulling itself together. That pull runs at about seventy thousandths of a newton for every metre of contact. The insect's legs are waxy, so water beads away from them and the skin dents. The skin pulls along the leg, and a dented skin aims part of that pull upward.

A dented skin pushes back upward, and that easily beats the insect's tiny weight. Water's skin pulls at 72. Alcohol musters only 22. Alcohol pulls three times weaker, and it also soaks into those waxy legs.

A soaked leg cannot dent the surface, so nothing is left to push up.

So the insect is not simply light enough. Water's skin carries it, and that pull is called surface tension.

A steel needle floats if you lay it down gently, because the dented surface takes its whole weight. And one drop of soap sinks that needle at once, since soap cuts the pull and flattens the skin.

Why is the simple spring model the most useful wrong model in physics?

Take anything with a stable resting place: a pendulum, a marble, a bridge. Its stored energy has a minimum there, like the bottom of a valley. Zoom in close enough on any smooth valley floor and it looks like a parabola.

A parabola means the restoring pull grows in step with how far you moved. The steeper the energy climbs, the harder it pushes you back, so the slope is the force. That is exactly a spring, so one solved answer fits everywhere. The trick only fails when you wander far from the bottom.

For a pendulum swung ten degrees the error is two parts in a thousand.

So the spring model is wrong everywhere and useful almost everywhere. Near a minimum, everything is a spring. That is called the harmonic approximation.

Atoms in a crystal vibrate like springs, which is why heat capacity calculations start from that one solved problem. Quantum fields are treated as springs too, and that is why light arrives in evenly spaced energy steps.

caption:
Why do gas particles escaping a pinhole carry more energy than the gas inside?

The gas has a wide spread of speeds. Some particles crawl, some race. Now poke a tiny hole in the wall. Which ones find it first? A fast particle covers more ground each second, so it meets the hole more often.

The escape rate therefore favours speed, weighting each particle by how quickly it moves. Inside, the average energy is one and a half kT. Escaping, it is two. That is exactly four thirds, and it does not depend on which gas you use.

So the beam coming out is hotter than the box it just left.

So the pinhole does not heat the gas. It simply picks the fast ones, which carry more energy. That is called flux weighting.

A planet loses its lightest and fastest atoms first, which is how thin atmospheres leak away into space. And a queue at a doorway empties fastest for the quickest walkers, for exactly the same reason.

caption:
How can less than one percent of neutrons make a reactor controllable?

Each fission throws out neutrons, and those neutrons go on to cause the next fissions. Most of them appear instantly, within about a ten-thousandth of a second. On those alone, reactor power would double faster than any human could react.

But 0.65 percent arrive late, from fragments that decay seconds afterwards. So operators hold the core just below self-sustaining on the instant neutrons alone. Then the chain can only keep running with help from the late arrivals.

So the clock stretches from a ten-thousandth of a second to a tenth of a second. Power can only step up once per generation, so a slower clock means a slower climb.

So the reactor is controllable because a tiny late fraction sets its pace. That is called delayed neutron control.

A car with slow, heavy steering is easier to drive, because small mistakes take longer to grow. And a bomb works by going above prompt criticality, deliberately skipping the slow neutrons altogether.

Who else was taught this wrong?

caption:
How can adding a middle magnet bring back a beam you just blocked?

A magnet can sort silver atoms into two piles, call them up and down. Take only the up pile, and send it through a second identical magnet. Everything comes out up. The down channel is empty, every single time.

Now put a sideways magnet in between, and keep only its left half. Send that into the up-down magnet, and the down channel carries a quarter of the beam. An atom cannot carry a definite sideways answer and a definite up-down one at the same time. Sorting sideways erases whatever you knew about up and down.

So each atom meets the last magnet with no memory of having been up.

So the middle magnet repaired nothing. It asked a different question, and that clash is called a non-commuting measurement.

Polarising filters show the same trick, since a third filter at forty-five degrees lets blocked light through again. Quantum computers live with this, because measuring one property scrambles the other and destroys the stored answer.

caption:
Why does twice the alpha energy cut a half-life by ten to the twenty-third?

An alpha particle inside a heavy nucleus is trapped behind an electric hill. It does not have nearly enough energy to climb over that hill. So it leaks through instead, as a wave that fades away inside the barrier.

The leak shrinks by a fixed factor for every step it takes through the hill. Doubling the energy makes the hill thinner, so there are far fewer steps. The hill slopes away outwards, so a higher energy meets it nearer the top, where it is narrow. Uranium-238 gives out 4.27 million electron volts. Polonium-212 gives out 8.95.

Uranium lasts four and a half billion years. Polonium lasts a third of a microsecond.

So a small energy change rides on an exponent, turning a doubling into ten to the twenty-third. That is called the Geiger-Nuttall law.

Chemical reaction rates leap with temperature, because an exponent turns a small change into a huge one. And a tunnelling microscope changes tenfold per angstrom, since its leak sits in the very same exponent.

caption:
How can graphene's carriers be massless yet crawl at a three-hundredth of light speed?

In most solids a charge behaves like a particle with a definite mass. Its energy then grows with the square of how fast it moves. In graphene the energy grows straight in proportion instead, exactly like a light beam.

A straight line means one fixed speed, whatever the energy. That is the massless part. On that graph the line's steepness is the speed, and a straight line has only one steepness. But the slope is set by carbon bonds, giving one thousand kilometres a second. Light's slope is set by empty space instead, giving three hundred thousand.

So the shape of the rule copies light, while the size comes from the crystal.

So massless here means one fixed speed, not light speed. The carbon lattice chooses it. That is called the Fermi velocity.

Sound in a solid also has one fixed speed, set by how stiff and heavy that material is. And a ripple on a drum skin travels at a speed the tension of the skin decides.

Which part of this surprised you?

caption:
Why do only four in a thousand of the tiny charges called electrons ever do anything?

A copper wire is packed with these charges, all of them moving fast. But they cannot do as they please. Two may not share the same state. So they stack up in energy levels, from the bottom to a sharp top edge.

In copper that top edge sits at seven electron volts, an enormous energy. Room temperature can only nudge a charge by a fortieth of an electron volt. So only those within a whisker of the top edge can move at all.

Everyone below is locked in, with no empty level nearby to move into.

So a metal is not a hot gas of electrons. Only the thin top layer acts. That is called the Fermi surface.

A metal's heat capacity is tiny compared with a gas, because most of its charges cannot absorb anything. And a packed staircase behaves the same way, since only the people at the very top can step up.

caption:
Why is a pendulum's fixed period wrong by a factor of three point nine?

A pendulum's period is famously the same whether the swing is wide or narrow. That is only true for small swings, and nobody ever says how small. The pull dragging it back is not in step with the angle. Only the share of gravity lying along the arc pulls the bob back, and that is the sine.

It follows the sine of the angle, which falls behind at large angles. A five-degree swing sets the standard. A one-hundred-and-seventy-nine-degree swing takes three point nine times as long. Near the very top the restoring pull almost vanishes, so the bob crawls.

Balance it perfectly upright and the period stretches out without end.

So a pendulum's period is steady only near the bottom. Push it toward the top and time stretches. That boundary is called the separatrix.

A grandfather clock keeps a narrow swing on purpose, because a wider arc would slowly make it run late. Big ship-steadying pendulums must be modelled in full, since their wide swings break the small-angle rule badly.

Guess before you scroll, then check.

caption:
Why does a particle in water make a shock wave of blue light?

Nothing beats light through empty space. But water is not empty space. Light crawls through water at 225 thousand kilometres a second, a quarter slower. A particle from a reactor core can cross that water at 297 thousand kilometres a second.

So the particle outruns its own light, the way a jet outruns its sound. Every point it passes sends out a ripple of light, one after another. The passing charge jolts the water's own charges, and each jolted one sends out light. Those ripples cannot spread out ahead of it, so they stack into a cone.

The cone leans at forty-one degrees and glows blue, because short blue waves stack best. Shorter waves fit more crests into the same cone, so the short blue end piles up strongest.

So no rule is broken. The particle only beats light inside water, never in empty space. That is called Cherenkov radiation.

A supersonic jet drags a cone of sound behind it, because it outruns the noise it makes. And a fast boat leaves a V-shaped wake, since the hull moves quicker than its own water ripples.

Who else was taught this wrong?

caption:
Why would a bacterium-sized scallop flap forever and move exactly zero millimetres?

A real scallop claps its shell and shoots forward, because the water it throws keeps moving. Now shrink that scallop until it is the size of a bacterium. At that size, water feels as thick as honey, and nothing ever coasts.

A big scallop travels a finger's length per clap. A tiny one travels nothing. Stop pushing such a swimmer and it halts within a tenth of a nanometre. With no coasting, flapping faster or slower changes only how long it takes, not how far. So the motion depends only on the shape the swimmer traces, not on speed.

Opening is the exact reverse of closing, so the two moves cancel out.

So the scallop hinge is a reciprocal move, and reciprocal moves cancel at this size. That rule is called the scallop theorem.

Real bacteria escape this trap with a corkscrew tail, a turning shape that never retraces its own path. Sperm cells beat a flexible whip that bends in a travelling wave, so the forward and back strokes differ.

caption:
Why does a coax cable carry its power through the plastic, not the copper?

The copper looks like the obvious route. Current does flow along it, after all. But current in copper is slow. The drift is under a millimetre per second. The signal arrives in nanoseconds, so the energy cannot be riding in the metal.

The copper's real job is to hold an electric and magnetic pattern in the gap. That pattern carries the watts. The copper only steals about four percent per metre. Where an electric and a magnetic field cross, energy streams along at right angles to both. So energy flows through the space between the two conductors, guided by their surfaces.

Cut the cable and the power stops at once, because the guide for that pattern is gone.

So the copper is a track, not a pipe. The power rides the field in the plastic. That is called the Poynting flow.

A transformer moves power across an air gap, with no metal path joining its two coils. And a wireless charger does the same, sending energy through the field rather than through contact.

What did you think the reason was?

caption:
Why would a classical hydrogen atom die in sixteen trillionths of a second?

Picture the old planetary atom. One light charge circling a heavy proton. Circling means constantly changing direction, and changing direction is acceleration. Any accelerating charge radiates light. That is not optional in classical physics.

Radiating costs energy, so the orbit must tighten with every single turn. A closer orbit holds less energy, so losing energy means spiralling in. One orbit lasts a tiny fraction of a picosecond. The whole spiral lasts sixteen. That is roughly a hundred thousand orbits, and then the atom is gone.

But real hydrogen sits stable for billions of years, so the picture must be wrong.

So the classical orbit destroys the atom in picoseconds. Only quantum rules keep matter alive. That is called the stability of matter.

A radio aerial works on exactly this effect, radiating power whenever its charges are shaken back and forth. And a storage ring loses energy on every bend, which is why it must be topped up constantly.

caption:
Why do butterfly scales flash blue when the material itself is brown?

Grind a Morpho wing down to powder and the powder is plain brown. The blue is not in the chemistry. It is in the shape. Each scale carries a stack of ridges, like tiny shelves, spaced 173 nanometres apart.

Light reflects off every shelf, and all those reflections meet again outside. The extra trip down and back between shelves is one blue wave long, so blue returns in step. At that spacing the blue reflections line up in step and reinforce each other. Other colours arrive out of step and cancel, so they simply pass through.

So brown material sends back 450-nanometre blue, purely because of the shelf spacing.

So the butterfly paints with spacing, not with pigment. Change the gap and you change the blue. That is called structural colour.

A soap bubble shows the same shifting colours, because its thin film decides which reflections line up. And a disc fans out a rainbow, since its tracks are spaced close to the size of light waves.

caption:
How can a two-hour day make loose rocks float off an asteroid?

A small asteroid pulls very weakly. It is a rubble pile, not a planet. On a kilometre-wide rock, surface gravity is under a third of a millimetre per second squared. That is roughly thirty thousand times weaker than the gravity you feel on Earth.

Now spin that rock once every two hours. Riding round with the spin needs an inward pull, and the faster the spin the more it needs. The spin throws a surface rock outward harder than the feeble gravity pulls it back. Gravity comes up short, so the loose surface rock is no longer held down.

It drifts away gently, at walking pace or slower, and does not come back.

So the rocks float off because spin beats a feeble gravity. That is called the spin barrier. Rubble asteroids rarely turn faster than 2.2 hours.

A fairground rotor ride holds its riders against the wall, because spin out-pulls gravity there too. And a neutron star has a top spin rate as well, tearing apart if it ever turns fast enough.

Why does averaging a hundred readings only make you ten times better?

They stack like the sides of a triangle. Errors that add at right angles pile up as the square root of how many there are.

So a hundred readings pile up only ten units of error, not a hundred. Divide by all hundred readings and the error has shrunk tenfold. To cut in half your error you need four times as many readings.

To do ten times better again, you need ten thousand of them.

So averaging buys you the square root, never the whole count. That slow shrinking is called the one over root N rule.

Astronomers stack a thousand frames to cut the noise thirty-fold, which is why exposures run all night. Pollsters quadruple the sample to cut the margin of error in half. That is why national polls cost so much.

caption:
Why does an unplugged resistor make half a microvolt all by itself?

Nothing is connected. No battery, no signal, just one kilohm at room temperature. Inside it, the tiny charges called electrons are jostling about with heat. That jostling is random, so at any instant slightly more sit at one end.

A lopsided pile of charge is a voltage, and it flickers constantly. Across a twenty kilohertz band that flicker averages 0.58 microvolts at room temperature. Cool the same resistor to four kelvin and the flicker drops to 0.067 microvolts. The same jostling current pushes a bigger voltage across a bigger resistance.

So the hiss follows temperature, resistance and bandwidth, and follows nothing else.

So the resistor is never truly quiet. Heat alone makes the voltage. That is called Johnson-Nyquist noise.

A radio telescope is chilled hard to cut this hiss, because its own warmth would drown faint signals. And Brownian motion of pollen is the very same jostling, seen as movement instead of voltage.

caption:
Why does a bending beam of tiny charges called electrons fire light into a needle-thin cone?

Move a charge around a slow circle and it radiates almost everywhere. Speed it up and the picture changes, because the charge is now chasing its own light. It is very nearly keeping up. The light it just made is barely ahead.

So the waves pile up in front of it and spread thin behind. At three billion volts the spray narrows from ninety degrees to a hundredth of a degree. Three billion volts puts the electron within a hair of light speed, and that hair sets the angle. That beam of light is thinner than a human hair at ten metres.

So a curved section becomes a searchlight, pointing where the charge heads.

So the narrow cone is pure geometry. A charge almost at light speed cannot spray light backwards. That is called relativistic beaming.

A jet from a black hole looks far brighter when it happens to point at us, for the same reason. And a running sprinter sounds louder ahead than behind, because the sound waves bunch up in front.

Which part of this surprised you?

caption:
Why do microwaves crawl down an empty metal pipe at only three quarters of light speed?

The pipe is hollow. There is nothing inside it to slow a wave down. But the wave cannot go straight. The metal walls will not let it. Metal shorts the electric field out at its surface, so the wave has to bounce instead. So it zigzags, bouncing from wall to wall as it works along the pipe.

Along the zigzag itself the wave still travels at full light speed. Only part of that travel points down the pipe. The rest goes sideways. A half-wave must fit across the pipe, and that is what sets how steeply the zigzag leans. In a standard twenty-three millimetre pipe, a ten gigahertz wave leans over noticeably.

So the pulse advances at 0.755 of light speed, about 226 thousand kilometres a second.

So nothing in the metal pipe slows the wave. The zigzag path simply wastes speed sideways. That is called waveguide dispersion.

A light pulse bouncing along an optical fibre also arrives late, because its zigzag path is longer than the fibre. And a boat tacking into the wind creeps forward slowly, for exactly the same zigzag reason.

caption:
Why does total internal reflection still leave light outside the glass?

Shine a beam inside glass at a steep angle and it bounces fully back. No light escapes, and yet a faint field does poke out past the surface. A wave cannot just stop at a boundary. It has to match smoothly on both sides.

Matching forces a field outside that fades incredibly fast with distance. Past that steep angle no travelling wave fits outside, so the only match left is one that dies away. At the surface it is full strength. A hundred nanometres out, 37 percent. That clinging field carries no energy away, so all the light still returns.

But bring a second glass block within a hundred nanometres and light crosses over.

So total internal reflection leaves a clinging light field that dies within nanometres. That is called an evanescent wave.

Fingerprint scanners work this way, since ridges touching the glass steal light straight from that clinging field. And a quantum particle tunnels through a barrier the same way, its fading tail reaching the far side.

Guess before you scroll, then check.

caption:
Why does silicon stay dark while gallium arsenide glows brightly?

Both are crystals. Both absorb light. Both are used in everyday electronics. Excite either one and you get a loose charge and an empty place to fill. When the two meet again, the stored energy can leave as light. Light carries the energy off easily but almost no momentum, so a mismatch needs a third partner.

But the charge must also match its sideways motion, called momentum, to that empty place. In gallium arsenide the two already match, so light carries the energy away at once. In silicon they do not match, so a crystal vibration has to join in as well.

Needing that third partner slows the light route a million-fold, so heat wins instead.

So silicon is not a poor material. Its mismatch makes light the slow route. That is called an indirect band gap.

Every LED and laser diode uses a matched crystal, because light emission has to beat heat loss. And solar cells prefer silicon, since slow recombination lets the charges survive long enough to be collected.

Who else was taught this wrong?

caption:
How can twisting graphene by 1.1 degrees build a thirteen-nanometre crystal?

Stack two carbon sheets exactly on top of each other and nothing new appears. Now rotate the top sheet by a little over one degree. In some places the atoms line up again. In others they sit badly offset.

That agreement and disagreement repeats, making a large new pattern of its own. A tiny turn slides the sheets apart very slowly, so they take many atoms to line up again. Carbon atoms sit 0.246 nanometres apart. The new pattern repeats every 12.8 nanometres. The pattern is fifty times bigger than the atoms that make it.

So the two sheets behave as if they had a huge new repeating unit.

So twisting adds no atoms. A 1.1 degree turn stretches a tiny spacing into a large one. That is called a moire superlattice.

Two overlapping mesh screens show slow rolling bands, because small offsets only repeat over a long distance. And a strobe makes a fast wheel crawl, since two nearly equal rates beat into one slow rate.

caption:
Why does a charge moving fast squash its electric field into a pancake?

Sitting still, a charge pushes outward evenly, the same in every direction. Now send that same charge past you at ninety percent of light speed. Distances along its direction of travel shrink for a fast-moving object.

Its whole pattern of push gets squashed along the line of motion. The same total push is crowded into a thinner disc, so sideways it grows stronger. Sideways, the push more than doubles. Straight ahead, it nearly vanishes. So the push piles up in a thin disc, side-on to the motion.

A passing charge therefore hits you as a brief sideways slap, not a slow squeeze.

So the pancake is not a new force. It is the same field, flattened by motion. That is called the field of a moving charge.

A particle accelerator beam pushes its neighbours sideways much harder, because every charge in it carries that flattened field. And the magnetic force between two wires is this same flattening, seen from a different point of view.

What did you think the reason was?

caption:
How can an electron feel a magnet it never touches?

Send tiny charges called electrons around both sides of a tightly wound coil. The magnetic field is trapped inside the coil. Outside it is zero. The charges never enter the coil, yet their striped pattern shifts sideways. The stripes appear because the two routes' waves meet again, adding in step or cancelling.

So something outside the coil still carries news of what is locked inside. Field inside the coil is full strength. Field on the path is zero. That something is a potential, whose loop around the coil counts the trapped magnetism. The potential nudges each route's wave along, so the two arrive out of step and the stripes slide.

The two routes collect different amounts of it, so the stripes move.

So the electron feels the magnet through a loop it encircles, not a field it touches. That is called the Aharonov-Bohm effect.

A superconducting ring measures trapped magnetism the same way, through the phase its circling charges collect. And a whirlpool shifts waves passing on either side, even where the water is turning far too slowly to see.

Which part of this surprised you?

caption:
Why does a microscope with no contact still change its current tenfold per angstrom?

A sharp metal tip hovers just above a surface. They never touch. Classically, charge cannot cross that gap. There is a hill of energy in the way. But a charge is also a wave, and a wave does not stop dead at a hill.

It leaks into the hill and dies away fast, halving again and again with distance. Whatever wave survives the gap is what arrives as current, so the current fades just as fast. At five angstroms the current is one nanoamp. At six, it is a tenth. That steepness is the whole trick, since the nearest atom carries almost all the current.

So the machine feels single atoms without ever pressing on them.

So no contact is needed. The leaking wave does the work, and its steep fade gives atomic detail. That is called quantum tunnelling.

Alpha decay escapes a nucleus in the same way, leaking through a barrier it could never climb over. And a flash memory chip stores each bit by pushing charge through a very thin insulating layer.

Did anyone explain it to you this way at school?

Why is a proton so heavy when its three quarks weigh almost nothing?

caption:
Why does a lamp flashing 1001 times a second film as one slow blink?

The camera does not see the lamp. It takes a thousand snapshots each second. Between two snapshots the lamp finishes one whole flash cycle, plus a tiny bit more. The whole cycle is invisible. Only the tiny extra bit survives.

A thousand and one flashes a second, recorded as one slow blink. So the camera reports the leftover: one extra flash per second. A lamp at exactly a thousand would leave no leftover. It would look frozen.

Any two rates a thousand apart hand the camera identical snapshots.

So the camera cannot tell a lamp flashing 1001 times from one. Anything faster than half the snapshot rate comes back disguised. That is called aliasing. Below half the snapshot rate no two rates can leave the same leftover, so nothing is disguised.

Wagon wheels seem to spin backwards in films, because each frame catches the spokes just short of a full turn. And music players take forty four thousand samples a second. Higher tones are filtered out first, or they return as false low ones.

caption:
How can halving the spacing of atomic planes push diffraction spots twice as far out?

Shine X-rays through a crystal and you get a pattern of sharp spots. Each spot comes from one family of parallel planes of atoms inside it. caption:
Why is the second law only overwhelmingly probable, and not an absolute rule?

Entropy rising is not a law of force. It is a statement about counting. There are simply far more messy arrangements of a system than tidy ones. So a system wanders into mess, because mess is where nearly all the states are. The particles keep reshuffling, and every single arrangement is equally likely to turn up.

But nothing forbids a tidy arrangement. It is only very rare. Twenty of the tiny particles called molecules could all sit in one half, once in a million tries. Make it a hundred particles and the odds carry thirty zeros after the decimal point.

Real experiments see this, watching a trapped bead run backwards for a couple of seconds.

So the second law is probable, not forbidden. It wins by staggering margins. That is called the fluctuation theorem.

A shuffled deck does not sort itself, because sorted orders are a vanishing fraction of all orders. And tiny motors inside a cell do run backwards briefly, which biologists measure in the laboratory.

caption:
How can a tiny energy gap make one state sixteen thousand times more common?

Heat is not one speed. Tiny jostling particles called molecules share the energy around. At room temperature the typical jostle is small, about 0.025 electron-volts. Our gap is 0.25. That is ten typical jostles stacked on top of each other.

The chance of paying that price falls away exponentially, not steadily. Every extra jostle of energy must be borrowed at once, and each borrow is as unlikely as the last. Each extra jostle of cost divides the crowd by about 2.7. Ten of those divisions multiply together into a factor of about 16,000.

So a gap you could barely measure decides which state you actually find.

So the energy gap does not add up, it multiplies. That exponential weighting of each state is called the Boltzmann factor.

Reaction rates double for a ten-degree warming, because the same exponential weighting decides how many molecules clear the barrier. And the air thins with height for the same reason. Lifting a molecule costs energy, and that cost is weighted exponentially.

caption:
Why does adding infinitely many waves still leave a nine percent spike?

A square wave jumps straight up. Smooth waves have to imitate that jump. Stack a few smooth waves and you get a wobbly copy of the square. Add more waves and the wobble shrinks everywhere, except right at the jump. Smooth waves cannot turn instantly, so they always swing past a sudden edge.

The jump is one unit tall. The best fit overshoots to one point zero nine. Adding terms does not shorten that spike. It only makes it narrower. The overshoot comes from chopping the sum off sharply, and every chop is equally sharp. Squeezed into a thinner sliver, the spike slides closer to the jump forever.

So every fixed point you pick does settle down to the right value.

So the spike never dies. It only thins, because the sum settles point by point. That overshoot is called the Gibbs phenomenon.

Sharpen a photo too hard and bright halos appear beside every edge, the same overshoot from cutting off fine detail. And a digital filter can ring just before a drum hit. A sharp cut in the kept ripples does the same thing.

caption:
How can a beaker of water boil and freeze at the same moment?

Put a beaker of water in a chamber and pump the air out. Boiling is not fixed to 100 degrees. It happens when the pressure above falls low enough. A bubble can only form when the vapour inside it can shove the air above out of the way. At 611 pascals, a hundred and sixty times below normal air, room-cold water boils.

Normal air presses at 101325 pascals. The chamber holds only 611. The fastest particles called molecules escape first, so what stays behind is colder. That escape carries heat away, and the water chills itself within seconds.

It reaches zero degrees while bubbles are still rising, and ice forms.

So the water boils and freezes together. At 611 pascals solid, liquid and vapour all balance. That is called the triple point.

A pressure cooker does the reverse. Higher pressure inside lifts the boiling point to about 120 degrees, so food cooks faster. And on Mars the air is very thin, so liquid water on the surface would boil away almost at once.

Who else was taught this wrong?

caption:
Why can a rubber band wrapped twice never slip down to one wrap?

Loop a band twice around a pole. Now stretch and slide it however you like. Every move is smooth, and the band never leaves the pole. Count how many times it circles the pole. That count is a whole number.

A smooth change would have to pass through one and a half wraps. The band is a closed loop, so it has to come back to its own start. Only whole turns do. But half a wrap around a pole is not a thing. The count can only jump. Stretching moves the wrap count by zero. Cutting moves it by one.

A jump needs a cut, or a slide straight across the pole. Neither is allowed.

So the rubber band keeps its two wraps, because a whole number cannot drift. That locked count is called a winding number.

A tangled phone cord keeps its twists until you free an end. The twist count also jumps only in steps. And a whirlpool in liquid helium spins with a whole number of turns, so it cannot quietly fade away.

caption:
Why can a neutron never bounce lower than 13.7 micrometres above a mirror?

Drop very slow neutrons onto a polished floor and they bounce again and again. Gravity pulls each one down. The floor throws it back up. A quantum particle is also a spread-out wave, and that wave must fit the gap.

Squeeze it into a thinner gap and the wave has to bend more sharply. Sharper bending costs energy, so squeezing down costs more than it saves. Sitting lower saves gravity's energy, but bending sharply costs more than that saving. The lowest allowed bounce reaches 13.7 micrometres. The next one reaches 24.

So the cheapest compromise sits at one definite height, and nothing lower survives.

So gravity and a floor give the neutron a lowest bounce of 13.7 micrometres. That is called a bound quantum state.

An electron in an atom cannot fall into the nucleus, for exactly the same squeezing cost. And a guitar string has a lowest note, because the longest wave that fits sets the floor.

What did you think the reason was?

caption:
Why can a superconducting ring trap magnetism only in fixed chunks?

Cool a ring of metal until it carries current with no resistance at all. Inside it, charges pair up and share one single wave around the whole ring. Go once around the ring and that wave must return to the same value.

So it can only fit a whole number of cycles into the loop. One step of trapped magnetism is 2.07 femtowebers. Two steps are 4.14. Magnetism through the loop winds the wave on as it goes round, so the field is part of the count. Magnetism threading the ring shifts that wave, so it too is locked to steps.

Nothing between the steps can survive, so the trapped amount jumps.

So the ring traps magnetism only in equal steps, because one wave must close on itself. That is called flux quantisation.

A SQUID sensor counts those steps, so it can measure fields a billion times weaker than the Earth's. And an electron in an atom obeys the same closing rule, which is why its energies come in fixed levels.

Which part of this surprised you?

caption:
How can the top of a falling chimney beat a dropped brick downward?

A dropped brick speeds up at g, about ten metres per second squared. The chimney cannot do that. Its base is hinged to the ground. So it must swing as one rigid piece, turning about that hinge.

Gravity pulls at the middle, yet the far tip must ride the same turn. In one rigid turn, a point twice as far from the hinge must move twice as fast. Work out the turn and the tip accelerates at 1.5 g, half again as fast. The lower half pays for it. That part accelerates slower than free fall.

So the chimney is not falling faster. It is turning, and the tip sits far out.

So the chimney top outruns free fall because the hinge turns falling into turning. That is called rigid-body rotation.

Tall chimneys famously snap in mid air, because the top demands more acceleration than gravity alone can deliver. And a ruler hinged at one end falls away from a coin at its tip. The tip outraces free fall.

caption:
Why does checking spin sideways erase half your spin-up atoms?

Send silver atoms through a magnet and the beam splits in two, up and down. Keep the up beam. Send it through the same magnet again and nothing is lost. Now turn the second magnet sideways. That beam splits left and right, fifty fifty.

Take the left beam and send it back through an upright magnet. Once it reads left the atom is left, and left is an even mix of up and down. Before the sideways check, 100 percent read up. Afterwards, only 50 percent do. Half of it now reads down, though every atom read up a moment earlier.

Asking sideways does not read the up-down answer. It overwrites it.

So checking sideways rewrites the up-down answer, and half your atoms flip. Such questions are called incompatible measurements.

A polaroid filter turned forty five degrees passes half the light. It asks a different question, so it resets the answer. And position and speed clash the same way, since pinning one down scrambles what you knew about the other.

caption:
Why can turbulence in a pipe die out after thousands of pipe widths?

Push water down a long pipe and smooth flow can break into a churning patch. Textbooks say that above a certain speed, turbulence is simply the new state. But watch one patch for long enough and it can vanish, all at once.

The patch is not a settled state. It is a long-lived visitor. A patch holds together only by chance, and one unlucky wobble drops it back to smooth flow. Patches die out below Reynolds number 2040. The old textbook line said 2300. Its chance of dying in the next second stays roughly constant, like a radioactive atom.

Faster flow lets a patch split in two before it dies, so turbulence spreads.

So turbulence in a pipe lasts only while splitting beats dying. That balance point is called the critical Reynolds number.

Radioactive atoms behave the same way, with a fixed chance of decay each second and no ageing. And a forest fire survives only while new patches catch alight faster than old ones burn out.

Who else was taught this wrong?

caption:
Why does a clear fluid turn milky near its critical point?

Seal carbon dioxide in a strong tube and warm it toward 31 degrees. Liquid and gas grow more alike, and the surface between them fades away. Near that point the fluid keeps flickering between dense patches and thin ones. Near that point switching between dense and thin costs almost no energy, so the patches swell.

Those patches grow. Far away they span a nanometre; close in, hundreds. Far from the point a patch spans 1 nanometre. Near it, 500. Light waves are about five hundred nanometres long, so the patches now match them. Blobs far smaller than a light wave barely scatter at all, which is why the fluid looked clear.

Patches that size bounce light every way, so the tube looks like milk.

So the clear fluid turns milky when its patches grow as big as light waves. That is called critical opalescence.

Clouds look white for the same reason. Their droplets are near the size of light waves, so they bounce every colour. And a magnet near its Curie temperature grows matching patches too, which makes it sluggish and easy to disturb.

caption:
Does an astronaut freeze at a black hole's edge, or just fade away?

From far away, her clock appears to tick slower as she falls. Her image seems to hang at the edge, dimming but never quite gone. On her own watch nothing strange happens. She crosses in a fraction of a millisecond.

The light stretches and thins until your detector receives nothing further.

So the astronaut does not freeze. Her signals just stretch away within milliseconds. That stretching is called gravitational redshift.

A fire engine siren drops in pitch as it drives away. Each sound wave is stretched on its way to you. And GPS satellites tick faster than ground clocks, so their signals must be corrected every single day.

caption:
Why do tiny particles called molecules fly at 500 metres a second, yet smells crawl?

Open a perfume bottle across the room and it takes minutes to reach you. At 500 metres a second, a straight flight would need a hundredth of a second. But air is crowded. Each particle hits another after about 70 nanometres.

That is seven billion collisions a second, each one flinging it a new way. A straight flight crosses a five metre room in 0.01 seconds. Staggering takes 625000. Pure staggering would take a week; real rooms are quicker only because the air itself moves. The path becomes a random stagger, forward and back and sideways.

A stagger covers ground like the square root of time, so long trips crawl. Each random step half undoes the last, so distance grows only as the square root of the steps.

So the molecules really do fly fast. They simply get nowhere, because the path staggers. That spreading is called diffusion.

Ink in still water takes hours to spread, though every part of it is always moving quickly. And a stirred cup mixes in seconds, because bulk flow carries the particles instead of letting them stagger.

caption:
Why does the straightest flight path look bent on every flat map?

A flight from London to Tokyo swings far north over the Arctic. On the map that looks like a detour. In the air it is the shortest way. Straight should mean something a pilot can feel: never turning left or right. Any other path would have to keep curving to one side, and curving always adds length.

Follow that rule on a globe and your path traces a great circle. The route that looks curved is 9590 kilometres. The map-straight one is 11285. A flat map cannot hold a round Earth without stretching something badly.

Mercator stretches the far north, so northern shortcuts get drawn as long curves.

So the flight path is straight on the Earth, and the map is what bends. Such a shortest path is called a geodesic.

Light near the Sun bends on our sky, yet it travels straight through spacetime that mass has reshaped. And a tight string pulled over a globe always lands on a great circle, which is the same shortest path.

Guess before you scroll, then check.

caption:
Why must erasing one bit dump heat into the room?

A memory bit is a ball sitting in one of two wells, left or right. Reading it is free in principle. Erasing means forcing it left, whatever it was. Two possible starting places become one. The number of options has cut in half.

Physics cannot destroy options, so the lost choice must reappear as disorder outside. The underlying motions run backwards just as well, so nothing can truly be forgotten. It leaves as heat, at least the temperature times a fixed tiny constant. Erasing one bit costs 2.87 zeptojoules at room temperature, 0.74 in liquid nitrogen.

That is about a hundredth of the energy in one photon of green light.

So erasing the bit is the step that must dump heat, not the computing itself. That floor is called the Landauer limit.

Your laptop wastes far more than this floor, yet every reset it performs still owes the same minimum. And a reversible computer dodges the charge by never erasing, keeping every step undoable instead.

Who else was taught this wrong?

caption:
How can a sheet one atom thick block 2.3 percent of the light?

Graphene is a single layer of carbon atoms in a honeycomb. Hold it up and you can see it. A one-atom film is visible. Its charge carriers, called electrons, move near one special point as if massless. Massless electrons carry no scale of their own, so nothing about the material is left to set the number.

That makes its light absorption depend only on fundamental constants. The answer is pi times the fine-structure constant, which comes to 2.3 percent. That constant is simply how strongly light grips an electric charge, and it equals one over 137. No thickness, no density, no purity enters. Only pi over 137.

Stack two sheets and you block 4.6 percent. Stack three and you block 6.9.

So a single atom of carbon stops 2.3 percent of the light, and we call that universal optical absorption.

Counting graphene layers under a microscope works this way, because each added sheet darkens the image by one fixed step. And the fine-structure constant also sets how strongly every atom grips light, since it measures the electric charge itself.

caption:
Why does oxygen glow green in the aurora but stay dark in your room?

The green light comes from single oxygen atoms, not from the pairs you breathe. A particle from the Sun knocks one of those atoms into an excited state. Its jump back down breaks the usual rules, so the atom dawdles for 0.7 seconds.

Nearly a second is an eternity for an atom, which usually glows within nanoseconds. Any collision during that wait steals the energy away silently, with no light. A knock carries the energy off as motion, and motion is heat, not light. In your room the atom is struck about 14 million times in that wait.

A hundred kilometres up it gets about six hits, so many of them glow.

So oxygen in your room is not too cold, it is too crowded. Losing the energy to collisions is called quenching.

Glow-in-the-dark paint survives the opposite way, because its slow atoms are locked inside a solid, away from collisions. And a fluorescent tube works only at low pressure, since crowded atoms would give up their energy as heat.

What did you think the reason was?

caption:
If a muon holds no electron inside, why does one appear when it dies?

A muon is a heavier cousin of the electron, about 207 times its mass. Wait 2.2 microseconds and only thirty-seven of every hundred muons remain. The tempting story says a tiny electron sat inside, waiting to get out.

But picture each particle as a ripple in its own field instead. A field already fills all space, so making a particle means shaking it, not unpacking it. The weak force links those fields, so one ripple can stir the others. The muon ripple dies away, and ripples rise in the electron and neutrino fields.

Charge and energy carry across the handover, yet no contents ever spill out.

So the muon does not open up. Its field hands the energy to the electron field, and that is called a decay.

A neutron left alone turns into a proton within fifteen minutes, by exactly the same field handover. And sunlight exists because the same weak force turns protons into neutrons deep inside the Sun's core.

Which part of this surprised you?

caption:
Why does a molecule that tries a trillion times a second still wait ten seconds?

Picture a bead in a valley, with a hill between it and the next valley. Heat rattles it about a trillion times a second. Each rattle is one try. But a try only escapes if that rattle happens to be unusually large.

The hill costs thirty typical thermal kicks. Most kicks are one kick tall. Each extra kick of energy must be borrowed all at once, and each borrow is as unlikely as the last. The odds of that fall as e to the minus thirty, about one in ten trillion. So a trillion tries a second give roughly one escape every ten seconds.

Raise the hill by three more kicks and the wait grows twentyfold.

So the molecule is not slow, it is unlucky. That exponential wait above a barrier is called Kramers escape.

A protein folds in milliseconds yet holds its shape for hours, because the same exponential barrier governs both. And magnetic grains in a hard drive hold your data for years. Flipping one must clear a tall energy barrier.

Did anyone explain it to you this way at school?

caption:
Why can glass be solid while its atoms still sit like a liquid?

Look inside window glass with X-rays. The atoms sit in no repeating pattern. A crystal solidifies by snapping its atoms onto a grid. Glass never does. Cool it fast enough and the atoms never get the time they need to find the grid. Instead, cooling makes the melt thicker, and the thickening runs away with itself.

Near the glass point the thickness has climbed by twelve powers of ten. So each atom now needs about one hundred seconds to slip past its neighbours. Your experiment lasts seconds, so on your clock nothing moves. It looks solid.

Cool it more slowly and that arrest happens a little lower in temperature.

So glass is not frozen by order, it is frozen by slowness. We call that arrest the glass transition.

Cold honey barely moves while warm honey pours freely, because the same runaway thickening stalls its flow. And pitch in a famous experiment drips once a decade. It is a glass, flowing on its own slow clock.

Go and test it, then report back.

caption:
How does a twenty-site grid of atoms become a trillion-state problem?

The Hubbard model keeps two rules. An atom can hop, or pay to double up. Each site has exactly four options: empty, one up, one down, or both. Two sites give sixteen combinations. Three sites give sixty-four.

Twenty sites give four to the twentieth power, about 1.1 trillion states. Adding one site does not add options. It multiplies them by four. A quantum state is not one arrangement but a weight on every arrangement at the same time. A real crystal holds around ten to the twenty-third sites, so the list never closes.

So solving it exactly means storing a trillion numbers, for a tiny patch.

So the twenty-site patch is small, yet its list of states is exponential. That is called the many-body problem.

Chemists hit the same wall simulating molecules, because every added electron multiplies the list of possible arrangements. And quantum computers are wanted mostly for this reason, since their own state space grows at the same exponential rate.

Who else was taught this wrong?

caption:
How can laser beams cool atoms when every photon kick pushes them?

One beam alone would just blow the atoms downstream. That part is true. So use two beams instead, pointing straight at one another. Tune both a little red, below the colour the atom likes to absorb.

An atom moving toward a beam sees that light shifted up, into the colour it absorbs. So it absorbs more from the beam it is running into, and less from behind. Each absorption knocks a sodium atom back by 3 centimetres per second. The atom spits each photon back out in a random direction, so those kicks cancel over time.

The kicks always oppose the motion, so the atoms feel thick syrup.

So the laser does not push the atoms, it drags them. That velocity-dependent friction is called optical molasses.

Atomic clocks drop cold atoms through a cavity, because slow atoms stay long enough to be measured precisely. And air slows a cyclist the same way, since the faster you move the harder the oncoming air hits you.

caption:
Why does a sharper microscope eventually turn its target into a black hole?

To see fine detail you must light it with a wave shorter than the detail. Shorter waves carry more energy, so sharper always means harder hitting. Energy also gravitates. Pack enough of it into one spot and it collapses. The more energy you cram into one spot, the wider the horizon it throws around itself.

So two lengths race each other as you keep zooming in. The detail you want shrinks, while the hole your probe makes grows. At about ten to the minus thirty-five metres the hole outgrows the target.

Past that point, looking closer only hides more behind a horizon.

So the microscope defeats itself. The smallest length you could ever resolve is called the Planck length.

Particle accelerators need more energy for finer detail, because the same trade between wavelength and energy applies. And quantum gravity is expected exactly at this scale, since that is where measuring and bending space stop separating.

What did you think the reason was?

caption:
How can 300 qubits hold an unimaginable list but return only 300 bits?

Writing the state of 300 qubits takes two to the three hundredth numbers. That is a 91-digit count, more than the atoms in the visible universe. Those numbers are real. They interfere, and they steer what happens next.

But reading the register is a measurement, and each qubit answers one or zero. So 300 qubits in, 300 bits out. Ninety-one digits collapse to three. Mapping those odds would take more runs than there are atoms in the universe. Run it again and you get another 300 bits, drawn from the same odds.

So the vast list is real but not deliverable. It only shapes the odds.

So the qubits compute with a huge list, yet deliver 300 bits. That ceiling is called the Holevo bound.

Quantum algorithms must funnel the answer into a few bits, because only that much can ever be read out. And a quantum channel cannot beat one bit per qubit when sending messages, since the same bound caps the transfer.

Which part of this surprised you?

caption:
How can starlight push harder than gravity on the heaviest stars?

Light carries a push. Every photon leaving a star shoves whatever it meets. Gravity pulls each gram of the outer layers inward with a fixed weight. Both weaken with distance in exactly the same way, so their contest is fixed.

Weight grows in step with the star's mass, simply and slowly. But light output grows far faster. A hundred Suns of mass shines like a million. A heavier star is squeezed hotter inside, and heat makes light climb far faster than weight does. So climbing in mass lets the outward push win long before the pull catches up.

At that crossing the surface is no longer held. It is blown off.

So starlight sets its own ceiling on how heavy a star can stay. That ceiling is called the Eddington limit.

Quasars brighten only to this limit, because gas falling in is blown away again once the light wins. And a solar sail flies on the same push, since sunlight carries momentum and hands it to the sail.

Did anyone explain it to you this way at school?

caption:
How can two black holes lose three Suns of mass and still grow bigger?

In 2015 LIGO watched two black holes merge, of 36 and 29 Suns. The one left behind weighed 62 Suns, so three Suns went missing. Those three Suns left as gravitational waves, a ripple in space itself.

Now measure the horizons instead of the masses. Count area, not mass. A black hole's horizon area grows with the square of its mass. The two before covered 233,000 square kilometres. The one after covers 367,000.

Squares add unfairly. One 62-Sun horizon beats a 36 and a 29 together.

So the two black holes shed mass, yet the total horizon area only rose. That rule is called the area theorem.

Entropy never falls in a closed system, because a horizon's area is literally a black hole's entropy. And a merger can never be run backwards, since splitting one horizon into two would shrink the total area.

Guess before you scroll, then check.
