caption:
Why does a pulse flip upside down at a fixed end but not a free one?

Send a hump along the rope and watch it arrive at the wall. At the wall the rope cannot move. That end is held still. The hump still pulls the wall upward as it arrives, and pulls hard.

By Newton's third law the wall pulls back down with an equal force. That downward pull launches a new hump inverted, turned by 180 degrees. Now free the end, letting it slide on a smooth pole. caption:
How can a laser paint a fake star ninety kilometres above the ground?

Telescopes need a bright point to measure how the air is smearing starlight. Real stars are rarely where you need one, so astronomers make their own. Meteors burn up high above us and leave behind a thin layer of sodium.

That layer sits about 90 kilometres up, far above every cloud. Sodium absorbs one very particular orange colour, 589 nanometres, and little else. The atom throws that light back out in every direction, so a little of it returns to us. So a laser tuned to that colour is absorbed and then spat straight back out.

The returning glow is a point of light exactly where you aimed it.

So the laser does not reach a star, it lights one. That trick is called a sodium guide star.

Street lamps glow that same orange from sodium, because an atom emits only the colours it can absorb. And eye clinics photograph your retina with adaptive optics, since the same trick measures and cancels the blurring.

caption:
What made one cloud-chamber track look like an electron with the wrong charge?

In 1932 Carl Anderson photographed cosmic rays crossing a strong magnetic field. A magnet bends a moving charge, and the bend direction gives its sign. How tight the bend is gives the momentum, that is, how hard it is to stop.

It curved the wrong way for an electron, but was too light for a proton. Anderson set a lead plate across the chamber to find which way it travelled. A particle can only lose energy in the plate, so the tighter curve must be the side it left on. It lost energy crossing the plate, falling from 63 to 23 million electron-volts.

So it moved upward, it was positive, and it was as light as an electron.

So the track was no mistake. It was antimatter, the electron's positive twin, and that is called the positron.

PET scanners image your brain using positrons from a tracer, because each one meets an electron and vanishes into light. And every charged particle in a modern detector is identified the same way. Its path curves inside a magnet.

caption:
Why does the Hubble constant come out with two values that disagree?

One route starts nearby. Measure a star's true brightness, then work out its distance. Compare that distance with how fast the galaxy recedes, and you get the rate. That ladder gives 73 kilometres per second for every megaparsec of distance.

The other route starts at the oldest light, released 380,000 years after the Big Bang. The early route does not measure today's rate. It assumes what the universe held in between. Its ripple pattern fixes the early universe, which is then run forward in time. That route predicts 67.4, and the two error bars do not overlap.

The gap is about five standard deviations, far too big for bad luck.

So the Hubble constant may be telling us our simple model is incomplete. That clash is called the Hubble tension.

Neutron star mergers offer a third route, because their gravitational waves give a distance without any brightness ladder. And any two methods that disagree beyond their error bars point the same way. Something is missing, or something is wrong.

Which part of this surprised you?

caption:
How can an uncharged neutron find hidden magnets inside a crystal?

A neutron carries no electric charge, so electric fields hardly notice it. But it still spins, and a spinning neutron behaves like a tiny bar magnet. Inside the crystal, the atoms also act like tiny magnets, lined up in a pattern.

So each neutron feels those atomic magnets and bounces off them at set angles. Only at certain angles do the bounces off every layer arrive in step and add up. The magnetic bounce is almost as strong as the ordinary nuclear one. Having no charge also lets the neutron reach deep inside, not just the surface.

So the neutron reads hidden magnetism because it has spin without charge. Those extra bright angles are called magnetic Bragg peaks.

Neutron beams image water inside a running fuel cell, because hydrogen scatters neutrons strongly while metal barely does. And an MRI scanner works on the same idea, reading the faint magnetism of hydrogen nuclei to map a body.

caption:
Why does a nineteen kilohertz tone sampled twenty thousand times become a fake low note?

Recording does not capture sound continuously. It takes quick snapshots, twenty thousand each second. Between two snapshots, a fast wave can complete almost a whole extra wobble. The recorder cannot know that. It only sees where the wave sat at each snapshot.

So the stored dots trace a much slower wobble that fits them equally well. Each snapshot catches the wave a little further along, and that slippage comes full circle once a second. Nineteen thousand wobbles against twenty thousand snapshots leaves one slow wobble per second. To pin a wave down you need more than two snapshots per wobble.

So the fake note is a beat between the nineteen kilohertz tone and the snapshot rate. That impostor is called aliasing.

A spoked wheel on film can look frozen or backward, because the camera samples it far too slowly. And a strobe light freezes a spinning fan in the same way, by flashing once per turn.

Guess before you scroll, then check.

caption:
Can two fading black-hole notes agree on one mass and spin?

After two black holes merge, the new one wobbles and rings like a struck bell. That ringing leaks away as gravity waves, dying out in a few milliseconds. The pitch of the ring depends only on the hole's mass and its spin.

Double the mass and the note drops by half. Nothing else shifts it. A bell rings at several pitches at once, and so does a black hole. Each pitch, read alone, gives a mass and spin. They must match. If the two disagreed, the thing that rang would not be the black hole our theory describes.

So two notes from one black hole ringdown must point to the same mass. That test is called black-hole spectroscopy.

Tapping a wine glass tells you its size and thickness, because every ringing pitch comes from the same object. And geologists read a planet's interior from earthquake ringing, since one inside structure must explain every measured tone.

caption:
Why must a pulsar clock run fifteen years to hear nanohertz gravity waves?

A pulsar is a dead star sweeping a radio beam past us, like a lighthouse. Its flashes arrive so regularly that we predict them years ahead, to the nanosecond. A passing gravity wave stretches and squeezes the space the radio beam crosses.

So the flash arrives a little early, then a little late, across the wave's cycle. To see a whole cycle you must watch at least as long as the cycle. Less than a full swing looks exactly like the pulsar slowly drifting on its own. And one nanohertz wave takes about thirty years to complete a single swing.

So the pulsar array is a detector whose size is its years of patient watching. That limit is called the observing baseline.

You cannot measure a tide from a ten-tiny visit, because one rise and fall takes twelve hours. And astronomers find slow exoplanets only after watching a star for longer than that planet's whole year.

caption:
Why does one centimetre of height change a clock at all?

A clock is really a counter. It counts swings of something that swings steadily. In gravity, the rate of those swings depends on where the clock sits. It is not the clock that changes. Time itself runs slower where gravity pulls harder. Lower down, deeper in the pull, every swing takes a hair longer. Every clock, of every design, shifts by the same amount, so it is time itself that differs.

Raise the clock one centimetre and the rate shifts by a part in a billion billion. That is small, but the best clocks measure it, so they can read height. Point two such clocks at each other and the faster one is higher.

So one centimetre of height shows up as a change in ticking rate. Surveying that way is called chronometric levelling.

A barometer also measures height, because air pressure falls steadily as you climb away from the ground. And sea level is set by gravity rather than distance from the centre, so clocks can map it.

What did you think the reason was?

caption:
Why must a gamma source creep at a tenth of a millimetre per second?

A nucleus swallows gamma rays only at one extremely exact energy. Normally the nucleus recoils as it emits, like a gun kicking, and the energy shifts. Lock that nucleus into a crystal and the whole crystal takes the kick instead.

Because the crystal is huge, almost no energy is lost, and the line stays razor sharp. To tune across that line you need one part in three million million. Moving the source slightly shifts the gamma energy, and a tenth of a millimetre per second is plenty. Moving shifts the energy by your speed divided by the speed of light, and a crawl is already a trillionth.

So a gamma line this sharp turns a snail's pace into a full energy scan. That recoil-free trick is called the Mossbauer effect.

A police radar reads your speed the same way, turning motion into a measurable shift in returned waves. And astronomers weigh stars using that same shift, since a star's motion slides its light in colour.

Which part of this surprised you?

caption:
Why do higher-energy particles give a cleaner percentage but a bigger error?

A detector measures energy by letting a particle smash into dense material. The particle shatters into a shower of thousands of smaller particles. The detector counts those pieces, and the count tells you the original energy.

Counting is noisy. Count a hundred things and you are off by about ten. Each piece turns up by chance on its own, and such independent counts wobble by about their square root. Ten out of a hundred is ten percent. A hundred out of ten thousand is one percent. So the absolute wobble does grow, but it grows slower than the energy itself.

So higher energy showers give a worse absolute error and a far better percentage. That square-root rule is called counting statistics.

A poll of ten thousand people is far tighter than one of a hundred, because random errors grow slowly. And a long camera exposure looks smoother for the same reason, since more collected light steadies each pixel.

caption:
Why does a wave's speed belong to the rope and not to your hand?

Flick the rope gently and a small hump runs away down it. Flick it hard and you get a taller hump, arriving at the same moment. The rope carries a wave by pulling its neighbours sideways, bit by bit. A bigger hump pulls harder but also has more rope to shift, and the two exactly cancel.

How fast that pull spreads depends on the tension and on the rope's heaviness. Loosen the rope to a quarter of the pull, and the speed two halves. Your hand only sets how big the humps are, and how often they come.

So a stronger flick carries more energy, but it still arrives on time.

So the speed is written into the rope, not into your hand. We call that the wave speed of the medium.

Sound crosses a room at 343 metres per second whether you whisper or shout, because the air sets the speed. And a guitar is tuned by tightening the string, since only the string's pull and its weight set the speed.

caption:
Why does a quantum computer need a fridge colder than deep space?

A qubit is two energy levels, and the gap between them is tiny. That gap sits near 5 gigahertz, in the microwave range. In energy that is 20 microelectron-volts, twenty millionths of an electron-volt.

Heat is energy too, and it shakes everything with about kT per wiggle. Set those equal and the gap matches a temperature of 0.24 kelvin. Deep space sits at 2700 millikelvin. The fridge runs near 10. Each extra multiple of the thermal kick makes a flip exponentially less likely, not just a little rarer.

At 10 millikelvin the gap is 24 times the thermal shake, so the qubit stays put.

So the fridge is not about speed. It stops heat from flipping the qubit, and we call that thermal excitation.

Infrared telescopes are cooled hard for the same reason, because their own warmth would outshine the faint sky. And a superconductor works only below its own energy gap, since heat above that pulls the paired charges apart.

caption:
Why is big G the worst measured constant in physics?

Gravity feels strong because the whole Earth pulls you. Between small objects it is feeble. Two one-kilogram balls ten centimetres apart pull with seven billionths of a newton. You cannot shield gravity, so every nearby wall and person tugs on the experiment.

Careful laboratories still disagree by far more than their own stated errors. The scatter between the best results runs into hundreds of parts per million. Repeating a measurement averages away noise, but never a bias that leans the same way every time. So the problem is not the theory. It is hidden bias inside each careful setup.

So big G stays the worst measured constant because gravity is weak and impossible to screen. That leftover bias is called a systematic error.

Weighing a neutrino is hard for the same reason, since the signal sits far below every background. And the electron's magnetism is measured beautifully instead, because that force is enormously stronger than gravity.

caption:
How does silent sound hold beads in midair every four millimetres?

Two facing speakers send ultrasound up and down, pitches far too high to hear. The two sound waves pass through each other and add up along the gap. In some places they cancel, so the air there barely moves at all.

Those quiet spots repeat every half a wave, about four point three millimetres. Loud sound pushes on anything inside it, and the push aims toward the quiet spots. The loud regions on either side push harder than the quiet gap, so the bead is squeezed into it. So a light bead slides into a quiet spot and stays trapped there.

So sound parks the beads at its own quiet spots. Those fixed quiet spots are called pressure nodes.

A guitar string holds still points along its length for the same reason, where two travelling waves cancel. And a microwave oven burns hot spots into food because its waves also cancel and add in fixed places.

Two facing speakers send ultrasound up and down, pitches far too high to hear. The two sound waves pass through each other and add up along the gap. In some places they cancel, so the air there barely moves at all.

caption:
How does a bacterium climb a smell it cannot sense across itself?

A bacterium is two micrometres long, and the smell barely differs from head to tail. Random jostling of the chemical swamps that difference, so a nose-to-tail comparison is useless. But it can swim. In four seconds it covers about eighty micrometres.

Swimming turns a hopeless difference in space into a large difference in time. So it remembers the smell a few seconds ago and compares it with now. Improving? Keep swimming straight. Getting worse? Tumble and pick a new direction.

So the bacterium never measures across itself. It compares now with seconds ago. That biased wandering is called chemotaxis.

A blindfolded person finds a warm radiator by walking and noticing whether the air is getting warmer. And a heat-seeking missile steers the same way, comparing readings over time rather than across its narrow body.

Which part of this surprised you?

caption:
Why must a telescope mirror chase the air every millisecond?

Starlight sets out as a flat sheet and travels that way for thousands of years. The last few kilometres of air are warm and cold in moving patches. Each patch slows the light slightly differently, so the flat sheet arrives crumpled. A lens can only build a bright point where every part of the wave arrives in step.

A crumpled sheet cannot focus to a single point, so the star smears into a blob. Fix those crumples and an eight-metre telescope sharpens by more than tenfold. A thin mirror bends to cancel the crumples, and wind reshuffles them within milliseconds.

So the mirror must redraw the air's crumples a thousand times a second. That chasing system is called adaptive optics.

Noise-cancelling headphones work the same way, measuring incoming sound and producing its exact opposite in real time. And a camera's stabiliser shifts its lens to cancel your shaking, correcting faster than the shake itself.

caption:
How does an eight-micrometre blood cell squeeze through a three-micrometre tube?

It does not shrink. Its contents and its skin both stay exactly the same size. A red cell is a flattened disc, dented on both faces like a soft cushion. That shape gives it far more skin than a ball of the same volume would need.

Roughly a third more skin than it strictly needs to wrap its contents. Squeezing the same volume down a narrow tube makes a long thin shape, which needs more skin. Stretching a cell skin is brutally hard, but folding slack skin costs almost nothing. So it folds into a bullet shape, slides through, and springs back afterwards.

So the cell is never squashed smaller. Its spare skin lets it squeeze and recover. That springy skin is called the spectrin network.

An empty plastic bag passes through a narrow slot easily, because folding slack material takes far less force. And a soap bubble resists stretching the same way, which is why bubbles round up instead of thinning unevenly.

caption:
Why is diffusion instant across a cell but hopeless across a centimetre?

A dissolved particle is knocked about by water, taking a random step each instant. Random steps do not add up like walking. Half of them go backward. Progress grows only as the square root of the steps taken, so twice as far needs four times as many. So doubling the distance does not double the time. It quadruples it.

One micrometre takes about a millisecond. Ten thousand times farther takes a day. A centimetre is ten thousand micrometres, so the time grows a hundred million times. That is why a cell needs no pumps and your body needs a heart.

So diffusion wins inside a tiny cell and loses across a centimetre. That squared-distance rule is called random-walk scaling.

Lungs branch into hundreds of millions of sacs so oxygen only ever diffuses a fraction of a millimetre. And stirring your coffee matters because sugar alone would need days to spread across the whole cup.

Check it at home and tell me what you saw.

caption:
Why does maximum power transfer throw away exactly half the energy?

Take a twelve volt source with two ohms of resistance inside it. Try load after load and watch how much power actually reaches the load. The peak arrives when the load matches the source, at two ohms. Raise the load and the current falls faster than the share rises, so power drops either side of the match.

Three amps flow. Eighteen watts land in the load, eighteen heat the source. Raise the load to eight ohms and the power falls to eleven and a half watts. But now only three watts are wasted inside, so efficiency climbs to eighty percent.

So peak power and high efficiency sit at different loads, and you must choose.

So maximum power is not maximum efficiency. Equal resistances split the energy in two, and that condition is called impedance matching.

A radio aerial is matched to its cable, because there the tiny signal power matters more than the waste. And a power grid deliberately avoids matching, since losing half the nation's electricity would be ruinous.

caption:
Why is a black hole's shadow bigger than the hole itself?

The hole has a surface of no return, the place where light can no longer escape. Gravity near that surface bends passing light, pulling in rays that were heading safely by. A ray aimed a little wide is curved inward and swallowed anyway.

So the region that eats light is far wider than the surface itself. Only rays passing well outside survive, and they outline a bigger dark circle. The bending also magnifies the hole, like a lens spreading its image outward. Rays that just miss are bent round toward us, so the edge we see comes from further out.

So the shadow is a magnified outline of every ray the black hole captures. That bending is called gravitational lensing.

A distant galaxy can appear as a ring around a nearer cluster, because mass bends its light around. And the Sun shifts star positions during an eclipse, since its gravity bends the starlight grazing past.

What did you think the reason was?

caption:
Can a moving camera make a head-on collision simple to solve?

Two balls on a track. Two kilograms at six metres per second, one kilogram at rest. From the ground you need two conservation laws and a page of algebra. Now walk alongside at four metres per second, the weighted average speed of the pair.

In that camera the heavy ball moves at two, the light one at four. In that camera the two balls are moving toward each other, not both one way. Seen from there, the total motion of the pair cancels exactly. Energy is kept as well, so the only option left is to reverse both speeds. Zero total motion fixes the ratio of their speeds and equal energy fixes the sizes, so only directions can change.

Reverse them, step back onto the ground, and read off two and eight.

So the collision never became simpler. Your viewpoint did. That moving frame is called the centre of mass frame.

A tennis serve is easier to judge from the ball's own rest frame, where the racket simply reverses it. And particle physicists always work in the centre of mass frame, because there the total motion is zero.

Which part of this surprised you?

caption:
Why does one tennis ball bounce high off steel and dead off foam?

Drop it a metre onto a steel plate. It comes back fifty six centimetres. Drop the same ball on thick foam and it barely clears four. A bounce stores energy in squash, then hands some of it back.

Both sides squash, so the ball and the surface each take part. Steel returns almost all of that stored energy. Foam keeps nearly all of it. Steel springs straight back to its own shape, so almost none of the squash is left behind as heat. The foam cells crush and rub, turning the stored energy into warmth.

So the bounce is a property of the pair, not of the ball alone.

So the ball carries no fixed bounce of its own. The pair of surfaces decides, and that number is called the coefficient of restitution.

A cricket pitch plays fast or slow because ball and soil return different fractions of the energy. And crumple zones are built to give nothing back, since a bouncy car would double the change in motion.

Did anyone explain it to you this way at school?

caption:
Why would a one farad air capacitor need a whole city of metal plate?

A capacitor is two plates facing each other, holding opposite charge. One farad means one coulomb of charge stored for every volt applied. The store grows with plate area, and shrinks as the gap widens. A closer opposite plate pulls harder on the charge, so the same voltage holds far more of it.

With a one millimetre air gap, one farad needs a hundred and thirteen square kilometres. That is slightly more ground than the whole city of Paris covers. So the only way out is to make that gap absurdly small.

A supercapacitor uses rough carbon and a gap a millionth of a millimetre wide.

So a farad is an enormous unit. Area buys you very little, while closing the gap buys everything, which is why we call these supercapacitors.

A touchscreen reads your finger as a tiny capacitor, because your skin changes the gap and the store. And a thundercloud holds charge the same way, its huge area making up for a huge gap.

Guess before you scroll, then check.

caption:
Why don't two torches paint Young's stripes on the wall?

Two slits lit by one lamp give clean bright and dark bands. One lamp splits the same burst into both slits, so whatever it does, it does to both. Two separate torches of the same colour give a smooth patch and nothing more. Bands appear only when two waves hold a steady phase between them.

A hot filament emits in tiny bursts, each starting at a random moment. That steadiness lasts about a micrometre for a torch, and twenty centimetres for a laser. So the bands from one burst are erased by the next, billions of times a second.

Your eye adds up all those shifting patterns and sees an even glow.

So the two torches are not too weak. They keep no shared clock, and that steadiness is called coherence.

A hologram needs a laser, because only a steady phase can record the pattern in the light. And radio telescopes across continents combine their signals only when locked to one atomic clock.

Who else was taught this wrong?

caption:
Why does a two thousand times microscope mostly make a bigger blur?

Turn the magnification up and the image grows, but no new detail appears. A lens cannot turn a point of light back into a point. Light is a wave, so it spreads at the rim and lands as a small disc.

That disc is set by the light's wavelength and how wide the lens gathers. Green light stops at about two hundred nanometres. A flu virus is half that. Two things closer than that arrive as one blob, whatever the eyepiece does.

So extra magnification only stretches that blob, larger but never clearer.

So the microscope is being honest. Light itself sets the limit near two hundred nanometres, and anything beyond is called empty magnification.

A telescope is built wide for the same reason, because a bigger opening shrinks that spreading disc. And phone cameras stop gaining sharpness past a few megapixels, because the tiny lens already blurs each point.

caption:
Why do the tiny charges called electrons crawl, while the lamp lights instantly?

Flip a switch and a lamp ten metres away lights with no delay at all. Yet in an ordinary three amp wire, each charge drifts a seventh of a millimetre per second. A wire holds so many charges that even a crawl adds up to three amps. That is slower than a garden snail. Hours to reach the lamp.

A snail does thirteen millimetres a second. The drift does about one seventh. But the lamp does not wait for any particular charge to arrive. Closing the switch sets up an electric push all along the wire.

That push spreads at nearly the speed of light, so everything starts together.

So the electrons really do crawl. The signal does not, and the two speeds are called drift velocity and signal speed.

A water pipe already full delivers flow the instant you open the tap, though each drop moves slowly. And a traffic jam clears from the front, so news of the green light outruns every car.

Go and test it, then report back.

caption:
Why does everything look blurred when you open your eyes underwater?

Open your eyes in a pool and the world smears, even with perfect vision. Most of your focusing is not done by the lens inside the eye. Two thirds of it happens at the curved front window, the cornea.

That window bends light because air and wet tissue slow light very differently. In air the cornea gives forty eight dioptres. Under water it gives five. Water slows light almost as much as tissue does, so the bending nearly disappears. With that much power gone, the picture now forms far behind the retina instead of on it.

Goggles put a layer of air back in front, and the power returns at once.

So your eye is not blurred by the water itself. It lost the air it was focusing against, and that gap is called the index difference.

A fish solves it with a round, far stronger lens, since its own cornea can barely bend light. And a glass rod looks weaker in water for the same reason, because the contrast at its surface shrinks.

Check it at home and tell me what you saw.

caption:
How can a bulging pocket of air underwater spread light instead of focusing it?

Trap air under a curved sheet in a tank and send a wide beam through. The same bulging shape cut in glass pulls the beam into a focus. Made of air, that identical shape pushes the beam apart instead.

Bending depends on which side slows light more, not on the shape alone. Glass in water converges at seven and a half dioptres. Air diverges at thirteen. A wave always turns toward whichever part of it is held back. Glass is slower than water, so the middle of the beam lags and curls inward.

Air is faster than water, so the middle races ahead and the beam curls outward.

So the bulging pocket never changed shape. It changed which side is slower, and what counts is called the relative refractive index.

An air bubble inside glass looks dark at its rim, because it throws light away from your eye. And a diver's mask acts as a lens too, since its flat air gap magnifies everything by a third.

Did anyone explain it to you this way at school?

caption:
Why does the best heat sensor sit where superconductivity is failing?

caption:
What does a rocket push against in empty space?

People say it pushes on the air. But in orbit there is no air. A rocket needs nothing outside itself. It carries everything it is going to throw. Burning fuel makes hot gas, and the engine hurls that gas backward, very fast.

A skateboarder throwing bricks forward rolls backward, because the thrown mass carries away the push she gains. And a squid darts ahead by jetting water behind it, gaining exactly the push that water carries off.

caption:
Why does a clock on a shelf run faster than one on the floor?

Nothing is wrong with either clock. Both are excellent, and they still disagree. Time itself runs at different rates at different heights in gravity. Climbing out of gravity costs a wave energy, and a wave with less energy ticks more slowly. Deeper in the pull means lower down, and lower down means slower ticking.

Lift a clock one metre and its ticks speed up by a tiny fraction. Over a year, a clock one metre higher gains about three nanoseconds. Optical clocks now count ticks so finely that thirty centimetres is enough to see.

So the shelf clock really does run faster than the floor one. That height effect is called gravitational redshift.

GPS satellites tick faster than ground clocks, so their signals are corrected daily or navigation drifts badly. And light climbing out of a star loses energy in the same way, arriving slightly redder than it left.

caption:
How can a steady magnetic field bend an electron without speeding it up?

A thin electron beam curves into a perfect circle inside a magnetic field. At ten million metres a second in a hundredth of a tesla, that circle is six millimetres across. Magnetism only ever pushes a moving charge across its path, while an electric field pushes along it. The magnetic push always acts sideways, at right angles to the motion.

A sideways push changes direction. It cannot add speed along the path. Crossing five millimetres it gains nothing. A thousand volts per metre would give five electron volts. So the speed stays fixed while the heading keeps on turning.

Energy still moves around, but it comes from whatever holds the field steady.

So the magnetic field steers without speeding anything up. A force at right angles does no work, and that rule is called the work energy theorem.

A cyclotron speeds particles with an electric field, and uses its magnet only to bend them round. And the aurora glows because Earth's field curls charges toward the poles without changing their speed.

What did you think the reason was?

caption:
Why can the darkest point in a shadow be bright?

Block a narrow beam with a small round disc and look behind it. Dead centre in the shadow sits a small bright dot. Light spreads from the rim of the disc as fresh little waves. Any edge a wave passes sets it spreading sideways, so the rim becomes a fresh source.

Every point on that rim lies the same distance from the centre line. So all those waves arrive in step, and build back to full brightness. Arriving in step, they reinforce each other rather than cancelling out.

Poisson predicted this to mock the wave theory. Arago then went and saw it.

So the shadow centre is bright because every path there is equal in length. Waves adding in step like that are called constructive interference.

A hologram works the same way, because light arriving in step from many points rebuilds a whole image. And noise cancelling headphones use the opposite case, adding a wave exactly out of step to kill the sound.

Which part of this surprised you?

caption:
Why does a charged particle in a magnetic field trace a spiral, not a circle?

A magnet pushes it sideways. That push can never speed the particle up. Split its motion in two. Part runs along the field lines, part across them. One part crosses the field lines. The larger part runs beside them.

The magnetic push only bites on the part going across the field. A charge sliding straight along a field line never cuts across it, so it feels no push. So that part is bent around into a steady circle, over and over. The part running along the field feels no such push.

So it keeps coasting forward at the same speed the whole time.

So the charged particle circles across the field and coasts along it. That wound path is called a helix.

The aurora glows where these spirals guide charged particles down along Earth's field lines into the air. A magnetic bottle traps hot gas the same way, because the spiral tightens where the field grows stronger.

caption:
How does a spinning copper disk make steady direct current in a fixed magnet?

The magnet never moves. Only the disk turns between its poles. Copper is packed with tiny charges called electrons, and they turn with the disk. A charge moving across a magnetic field is pushed sideways, at a right angle.

The needle sits on one side and stays there. It never swings back. Every part of the disk always moves the same way through the field, so the push never flips.

So the copper disk hands you one steady direction, never an alternating one. That is called a homopolar generator.

A railgun runs on the same push, using a huge current and field to fling a metal slug. And a loudspeaker is this run backwards, because a current in a field makes the cone move.

caption:
How does Earth's feeble magnetism make three quarters of a volt across a jet?

A jet's wing is solid metal, full of tiny charges called electrons. The whole wing flies through Earth's weak magnetic field at speed. A charge moving across a magnetic field gets pushed sideways. Sideways here means at right angles to both the flight path and the field, which runs along the wings.

So those charges drift toward one wingtip and crowd together there. The far tip is left short of them, so a real voltage appears. The crowded tip soon pushes back hard enough to stop more charge arriving, and that standoff is the voltage. Fifty microtesla, two hundred fifty metres a second, sixty metres of wing.

Multiply those three and you get three quarters of a volt, tip to tip.

So the jet's own motion across Earth's magnetic field makes the voltage. That is called motional emf.

A power station works the same way, sweeping copper coils through a magnetic field to push charge along. And a tethered satellite makes volts by dragging a long wire through Earth's field in orbit.

Who else was taught this wrong?

caption:
How can a hammer blow reach you through a steel rail fifteen times faster than through the air?

Press an ear to the rail and you hear the blow twice. Sound is a squeeze handed along, each bit of material shoving the next. How fast it travels depends on stiffness, and on how heavy the material is. A stiffer bit springs back onto its neighbour sooner, while a heavier bit is slower to start moving.

Steel passes that squeeze along at five thousand metres a second. Steel resists squeezing about a million times harder than air does. It is also six thousand times denser, which drags the speed back down.

Stiffness wins that contest, so the squeeze runs fifteen times faster than in air.

So the steel is not louder. It is stiffer. Speed comes from stiffness divided by density, and that is called the speed of sound in a medium.

An ultrasound scan reads the body the same way, because stiffer tissue passes the pulse along faster. And earthquake waves race through the stiff deep mantle far faster than through loose surface soil.

caption:
Why does a resistor placed after a bulb dim it by exactly the same amount?

Wire a bulb and a six ohm resistor in a loop with a twelve volt battery. Now swap the two parts, so the resistor sits after the bulb instead. The bulb glows exactly as brightly in both arrangements.

Many students expect the first part in line to use the voltage up first. Six watts in the bulb before the swap. Six watts after it. But a loop offers one path, so the same current passes through every part. Charge is never used up, so whatever flows into a part must flow straight out of it.

Voltage is shared out by resistance, never by position around the loop.

So the resistor dims the bulb the same wherever it sits. Current is equal everywhere in the loop, and that rule is called current continuity.

A fuse protects a circuit from either end, because the same current runs through every part of it. And a water loop behaves the same way, since one narrow pipe slows the whole flow wherever you fit it.

What did you think the reason was?

caption:
How does a metal detector find gold that a magnet will not pick up?

Gold is not magnetic. Hold a magnet against a gold ring and nothing happens. But the detector's head is not a plain magnet. Its field switches on and off. A changing magnetic field pushes charge around inside any metal nearby. A steady field stirs nothing, which is why the plain magnet from before did nothing at all.

Gold carries current beautifully, so those swirls run strong. So little loops of current begin to swirl inside the gold itself. Every current makes a magnetic field of its own, and these are no exception.

So the gold answers back with a faint field, and the coil hears it. The gold's changing field pushes charge in the coil as well, and that tiny voltage is the beep.

So the metal detector never pulls on the gold. It listens for the currents it stirred. Those are called eddy currents.

An induction hob heats a steel pan by driving these same swirling currents straight into its base. And a coin sorter inside a vending machine reads each metal by how strongly it answers back.

Check it at home and tell me what you saw.

caption:
Why does a hoop lose a downhill race to a ball of the same mass?

Same mass, same ramp, same height. Release them together and the ball wins. Both start with the same store of energy, set only by the height. At the bottom that store has split two ways: sliding along, and spinning.

Spin is expensive when mass sits far from the centre. Mass at the rim has to travel far faster than mass near the middle, so it costs more energy. A hoop keeps all its mass at the rim, as far out as it can be. So the hoop locks half its energy into spin. The ball, under a third. Rolling ties the spin to the speed, so neither body can skip the spinning share.

So less is left over for going forward, and the hoop arrives late.

So the hoop loses the downhill race on shape, not on mass. That reluctance to spin is called rotational inertia.

A flywheel stores energy by putting its mass far out, exactly where the hoop wastes it. And a tightrope walker carries a long pole because its far-out mass makes tipping wonderfully slow.

caption:
Why does an alpha particle leak out of a nucleus it could never climb over?

Inside uranium, two protons and two neutrons cling together as one small lump. Around the nucleus stands a steep electric barrier, pushing that lump back in. The barrier stands near twenty-eight. The lump carries barely four.

caption:
Why does a spool roll toward you at fifty degrees but away at seventy?

A spool of thread, with the thread coming off underneath its inner axle. Pull almost horizontally and the spool rolls toward your hand. Pull steeply and the very same spool rolls away from you.

A rolling spool turns about the point where its rim touches the floor. The point touching the floor is momentarily still, so the whole spool swings about it. The pull reverses when the cosine of its angle equals the radius ratio. That angle is exactly where the line of pull runs through the contact point itself. An axle half the outer radius gives sixty degrees. A quarter gives seventy six.

Below that angle the line of pull passes ahead of the contact point, so it drives forward. A pull that misses the pivot on one side twists the spool that way, like a spanner.

So the spool does not care how hard you pull. The angle decides, through the pivot where it touches, and that pivot is called the instantaneous centre.

A yo-yo climbs or falls by the same rule, because the string leaves it at a chosen radius. And a wheel at a kerb lifts or jams depending on where your push line passes the corner.

caption:
Why does a spherical mirror blur the edges of its own image?

Shine a row of parallel beams at a curved mirror and watch where they cross. Beams near the middle meet neatly at one point, half the radius away. Beams from the rim cross a few millimetres earlier than that.

A sphere turns its outer rays a little too steeply, purely because of its shape. Out at the rim a sphere tilts more steeply than a single focus needs, so it over-bends those rays. On a two metre mirror that smears the focus into a millimetre wide blur. A parabola curves slightly flatter at the rim, by exactly the right amount.

caption:
Why does a prism split sunlight while a flat glass slab does not?

Send white light through a window pane and it comes out white. Both are the same glass, and both bend light at every face. Glass slows blue light slightly more than red, so it bends blue harder. Light bends at a surface because it changes speed there, so the slower colour bends more.

Through a sixty degree prism, red and blue leave nearly a degree apart. In a slab the two faces are parallel, so the second bend undoes the first. At a parallel face the light leaves at the same angle it entered, so the bend reverses. The colours leave shifted sideways by a hair, but travelling the same way.

A prism's faces are tilted, so the second bend adds to the first instead.

So the prism does not create colour. Its wedge shape refuses to undo the split, and that spreading is called dispersion.

A rainbow forms the same way, because a raindrop bends blue light more than red on the way through. And a diamond flashes colour for the same reason, since none of its cut faces sit parallel.

caption:
Why is the normal force never a number you can look up?

Stand on a bathroom scale. It reads six hundred and eighty six newtons. Ride a lift upward and it jumps to eight hundred and twenty six. To speed you upward the floor must push harder than your weight, and the scale reads the extra. Your mass has not changed. The push from the floor has.

The floor is never told what to push. It only refuses to let you sink. Standing still, six hundred and eighty six newtons. Rising briskly, eight hundred and twenty six. So the push grows or shrinks by exactly as much as the motion demands.

On a thirty degree slope it falls to five hundred and ninety four.

So the normal force is never handed to you. You solve for it, from the motion the surface allows. Pushes like that are called constraint forces.

A rollercoaster seat pushes hardest at the bottom of a loop, because the track must also curve your path. And a book on a table gets a gentler push if you lift some of its weight with a finger.

Which part of this surprised you?

caption:
Why does pure water barely carry current while tap water carries it easily?

Dip a meter into tap water and current flows without any trouble. Dip the same meter into ultrapure water and the reading almost dies. Current needs charged particles that are free to move between the plates.

Water itself splits only very rarely into charged pieces called ions. A centimetre cube of pure water measures eighteen million ohms. Tap water, two thousand. Tap water carries dissolved salts, which break apart and supply billions more carriers.

So the current was never really the water. It was the passengers riding in it.

So pure water is a poor carrier and tap water is a good one. The dissolved pieces doing the work are called ions.

A car battery works because sulphuric acid splits into charged pieces that ferry charge across the plates. And seawater carries current about a million times better than pure water, thanks to its salt.

caption:
How can one single step have two completely different lists of components?

Walk three metres east, then four metres north. You finish five metres away. Your list is three and four. The step itself is one arrow. Now turn the grid, so its first axis points straight along your walk.

On the old grid the sideways part is three. On the new one, five. On the turned grid the whole five metres lies on the first axis and nothing is left over. Same walk. Same start, same finish, same five metres of ground covered. The numbers changed because the rulers changed, not because you moved differently.

So components belong to the grid you chose, and the arrow belongs to the world.

So one single step has many lists and one true length. That independence is called coordinate invariance.

A map bearing changes when you switch from grid north to true north, but the road does not. And physics laws are written as arrows so they hold in every frame, whichever axes you pick.

Guess before you scroll, then check.

caption:
Why does a clear glass rod vanish when you lower it into oil?

In air the rod is perfectly clear, yet you still see it plainly. You see it because every surface throws a little light back at you. A surface reflects when the speed of light jumps as it crosses over.

Air to glass is a big jump, so about four percent bounces straight back. Match the oil to the glass and that falls to a hundredth of a percent. Light also bends at a surface only when the speed changes, so matched oil stops the bending too. Now the speed barely changes at the surface, so almost nothing bounces.

With no reflection and almost no bending, there is little left to see.

So the glass did not turn invisible. The oil erased the contrast at its surface, and that trick is called index matching.

Immersion microscope lenses put oil between glass and slide, so hardly any light is lost at the gap. And wet paper turns see-through, because water fills the air gaps that bounced the light around.

Who else was taught this wrong?

caption:
Why does a spinning bucket's water curve into a bowl instead of staying flat?

No one stirred it. After a while the water turns as one solid block. Water settles until its surface sits square to whichever way down is. Any slope left over would let the water slide, so it stops only when the surface is square to down. Standing still, down is simply gravity.

Spinning, each parcel also needs a push toward the centre to keep turning. Gravity pulls with ten. At the rim, the turning needs nearly sixteen. Add those two together, and the effective down tilts outward near the wall. Riding with the water, that needed inward push feels exactly like an extra outward tug.

So the surface tilts to match, rising about eight centimetres at the rim.

So the spinning water is still level, in its own sense. Down has tilted, so the surface follows. That shape is called a paraboloid.

A motorcycle leans into a turn so the rider's effective down runs straight through the bike. And a spinning dish of liquid sets into a perfect curve. Telescope makers use exactly that as a mirror.

Try it tonight and tell me what happened.

caption:
Why are you radiating nearly nine hundred watts and not freezing solid?

Nine hundred watts would empty a day of food in under an hour. Your skin sits at about thirty four degrees, so it glows in infrared. Add that glow over your whole skin and it comes to 889 watts.

But the walls around you are warm too, at twenty two degrees. They glow back at you, and your skin soaks that glow up. Anything that glows strongly also soaks up strongly, so your skin drinks the room's glow in. You send out 889 watts. The room sends back 757.

So what actually leaves you is the difference, about a hundred and thirty watts.

So the watts you radiate are not the watts you lose. Radiating is a two-way trade, so only the net counts. That is called radiative exchange.

A cold window chills you from a metre away, because it sends back far less glow than a warm wall. And frost forms on grass on a clear night above freezing, since the open sky returns almost nothing.

Go and test it, then report back.

caption:
Why must a laser hold more atoms excited than resting?

Light passing an excited atom can shake its energy loose as a twin photon. Now two identical photons travel on together, and the beam has grown. But light passing a resting atom is simply swallowed instead.

Warmth alone excites about one in a hundred. A laser needs most of them. So the beam grows only if excited atoms outnumber the resting ones. Heat always leaves more atoms low than high, whatever the temperature. Heat hands out big kicks only rarely, so climbing always stays less likely than sitting low.

So no hot box will ever lase. You must pump the atoms yourself.

So a laser must be pumped out of balance on purpose. That upside-down state is called population inversion.

A fibre amplifier boosts internet light the same way, pumping erbium atoms up before the signal arrives. And a maser did it first with ammonia, sorting excited molecules out of the beam by hand.

Which part of this surprised you?

caption:
Why does warming pure silicon make it carry current better, not worse?

Warm a copper wire and its resistance climbs. Everyone expects that. In copper the charges are already free. Heat only shakes the lattice. So the shaking gets in their way, and the wire resists a little more.

Pure silicon is different. Nearly all its charges are locked into bonds. Warm both by twenty degrees. Copper stiffens slightly. Silicon collapses. Heat tears a few charges loose, and the count roughly doubles every nine degrees. More free charges means more carriers sharing the work, so the resistance falls.

So silicon gains carriers far faster than the jostling can slow them.

So warming silicon creates the very charges it lacked. That falling resistance is called a negative temperature coefficient.

A thermistor measures your fever this way, because its resistance drops sharply with every degree of warmth. And a glass rod conducts once white hot, which once shocked chemists into rethinking insulators.

Did anyone explain it to you this way at school?

caption:
How can plain sunlight push a spacecraft when there is no wind in space?

Space is empty. Nothing blows against the sail, and nothing touches it. But light arrives as tiny packets of energy called photons. A photon weighs nothing, yet it still carries a punch, called momentum.

When a photon bounces off a mirror, it leaves going the other way. So the sail must have turned it around, and the sail gets shoved forward. Whatever you push, pushes back on you just as hard, so turning the photon shoves the sail. A mirror sail collects twice the shove a black sail would get.

One photon is nothing. A square kilometre catches them by the trillion.

So sunlight presses on the sail with about nine newtons per square kilometre. That is called radiation pressure.

A comet's tail streams away from the Sun because this same pressure blows its fine dust outward. And laser tweezers hold one living cell perfectly still, using nothing but the push of light.

Guess before you scroll, then check.

caption:
Why does a thirty degree pendulum still count as a small-angle problem?

A pendulum swings because gravity keeps pulling it back toward the bottom. The strength of that pull follows the sine of the angle, not the angle. Sine is a curve. The angle is a straight line. They are different things.

But near zero they hug each other closely, so physicists swap one for the other. At ten degrees the swap is half a percent out. At thirty, under five. Five percent is smaller than the error in your stopwatch and your string.

So the simple formula still predicts the swing you can actually measure. Making that swap is the only reason the usual pendulum period formula exists at all.

So thirty degrees is small enough, because small means small error, not small angle. That swap is called the small-angle approximation.

A grandfather clock keeps good time because its period barely changes over the small arc it swings. And a guitar string obeys the same trick, since its sideways pull is nearly straight-line for small bends.

Who else was taught this wrong?

caption:
Why does a fifty thousand volt X-ray tube stop at one hard edge?

Inside, charges are hurled at a metal target at enormous speed. Fifty thousand volts gives each one exactly fifty thousand electron volts. Slamming into the target, a charge brakes hard and throws off light. A charge slammed to a stop cannot lose that energy quietly, so it throws it out as light.

Usually it brakes in stages, so the light comes out at every energy. But sometimes one charge dumps everything it has into a single packet. That packet is the tube's hard limit. Double the volts and the limit two halves. The more energy a packet carries, the shorter its wave, so the biggest packet is the shortest one.

So no X-ray can carry more, because there was never more to give.

So those fifty thousand volts set one shortest wavelength, near 0.025 nanometres. That edge is called the Duane-Hunt limit.

A photocell shows the mirror image, where dim blue light frees charges but bright red will not. And a dental X-ray runs at lower volts on purpose, keeping the hardest rays out of you.

Send this to whoever argues about it.

caption:
Why does torque point out of the page when the door swings sideways?

Push a door handle. The door sweeps around, and nothing moves outward. So an arrow pointing at your face looks absurd. Nothing goes that way. But a turn has no single direction. Every point moves a different way.

One thing about the turn does hold still: the line it spins around. We want an arrow so two turns can be added the way two pushes are. Push far from the hinge and the turn is strong. Close in, weak. That line is the hinge, and it runs straight out of the page.

So we label the turn with an arrow along that line, and your right hand fixes the sense.

So the torque arrow is not where anything goes. It names the axis, and that is called an axial vector.

A spinning top stays upright because its axis arrow resists being tipped by gravity's steady twist. And a bicycle wheel held by one hand fights you sideways, since the arrow must swing first.

caption:
Why does a jet-black silicon wafer look clear to an infrared camera?

To your eye it is a solid dark slab. No light gets through it. Light arrives in packets called photons, each carrying a fixed amount of energy. Silicon absorbs a photon only if it can shake a charge free.

Red light carries more than the price. Deep infrared carries less. So red photons are swallowed, and the wafer looks black to you. An infrared photon cannot pay that price, so nothing absorbs it. A photon cannot pay in parts: it either buys a freed charge outright or is not taken at all.

So it sails straight through the silicon and out the other side.

So the wafer is black and clear at once. That fixed minimum price is called the band gap.

Night-vision windows are cut from germanium, which stays clear far deeper into the infrared than glass. And a television remote shines bright infrared light that a phone camera sees but your eye cannot.

Which part of this surprised you?

Why does dye speed up in a squeezed channel instead of bunching up there?

caption:
Why can a gamma ray make matter only above 1.022 million electron volts?

A gamma ray is pure light, the most energetic packet there is. Pass one close to a heavy nucleus and it can vanish entirely. The nucleus is needed to take up the recoil, since light cannot simply stop by itself. In its place appear an electron and its opposite twin, a positron. Charge can never be created, so a minus can only appear if a plus appears with it.

One electron's mass costs 0.511. You must buy two of them. Mass is only energy in a locked-up form, so making it costs energy. So the bill is 1.022 million electron volts, and not a fraction less.

Below that, the gamma ray cannot afford the pair and simply passes on.

So the gamma ray buys matter at one fixed price. That swap is called pair production.

A PET scanner watches the reverse, where a positron meets an electron and both become gamma rays. And the early universe made particles freely, because everything then carried far more than this threshold.

caption:
Why can one spot on a bat hit hard with zero sting in your hands?

Hit near the handle and your palms sting. Hit near the tip, they sting the other way. A blow does two separate things to the bat at once. It shoves the whole bat backward, handle and all.

And it spins the bat about its own middle, driving the handle forward. A struck bat always spins about its own balance point, whatever your hands are doing. Those two effects cancel at one place, two thirds down a uniform stick. Hit inside that place and the shove wins, so the handle kicks back.

Hit beyond it and the spin wins, so the handle kicks the other way.

So one spot leaves your hands perfectly still, because the two effects cancel there. That is called the centre of percussion.

A tennis racket has the same spot, and hitting off it sends the shock straight into your elbow. And a hammer is balanced so its head lands there, keeping the handle quiet in your grip.

caption:
What is a radio's tuning knob really moving when you slide past a station?

Every station arrives at the antenna at once, all mixed together. Inside sits a coil and a pair of plates that swap energy back and forth. That swapping has one favourite rhythm: a number of wobbles a second, called its frequency.

At that rhythm the answer towers. A little off, and it collapses. A station in step adds a little each cycle, while one out of step keeps cancelling itself. So the matching station comes through loud while its neighbours stay faint. The knob turns those plates, which shifts the circuit's favourite rhythm. Closer plates hold more charge, so the energy takes longer to swing across and the rhythm slows.

So you slide that narrow peak along until it sits on one station.

So the knob slides the circuit's own rhythm onto the station you want. That sharp peak is called resonance.

A wine glass shatters when a singer holds exactly its own rhythm, feeding it energy every cycle. And a playground swing climbs higher only when you push in time with its natural rhythm.

caption:
Why doesn't a dam feel the water's push halfway down?

Water pressure is not the same everywhere. It grows with depth. Deeper water carries the weight of all the water above it, so it presses harder. At the surface it is nothing. Ten metres down it is strongest. The push does not act at five metres. It acts nearer six point seven.

So the load on the wall is a triangle, thin at the top and thick at the base. The wide bottom of that triangle carries most of the force. Balance the turning effect and the single push sits two thirds of the way down. The deep half pushes much harder, so the single equal push must sit well below the middle.

That is why every big dam is built thick near the ground.

So the water does not press evenly on the dam. Pressure rises with depth, so the push sits low. That is called the centre of pressure.

A submarine hatch needs its strongest fittings at the bottom, because pressure there is greater than at the top. And a grain silo wall is thickest near the ground, because the grain presses harder the deeper you go.

caption:
Why can a hot metal sheet look cold to a thermal camera?

A thermometer says it is hot. The camera paints it cool blue. A thermal camera does not sense heat. It counts the glow a surface sends out. Every warm thing glows in infrared, invisible light just beyond red.

But surfaces differ in how well they give that glow off. Black paint gives off nearly all it can. Polished metal gives almost none. A shiny surface throws light back instead of making its own, and the camera assumes it does not. Black tape sends out ninety five percent of the maximum. Bare aluminium sends three.

So the camera sees a faint glow and calls the shiny metal cold.

So the metal really is hot. It is just a poor emitter, so the thermal camera under-reads it. That property is called emissivity.

A vacuum flask has a silvered inner wall, because a shiny surface radiates very little heat away. And a radiator is painted rather than polished, since paint gives off far more warmth than bare metal does.

Guess before you scroll, then check.

caption:
Why can't a perfect green-light microscope ever see atoms?

Grind the glass better, polish it longer, and the answer does not improve. The limit is not the lens. It is the light you are using. Green light has a crest-to-crest length of about 550 nanometres.

Two points closer than roughly half that length send back waves that overlap. Each point arrives as a blur about that wide, so two blurs that overlap read as one. The best oil lens stops near 196 nanometres. Atoms sit 0.3 nanometres apart. That is a gap of six hundred times, so no amount of polishing closes it.

To see atoms you need a probe with a far shorter crest-to-crest length.

So a microscope is limited by the light it uses, not by its glass. That floor is called the diffraction limit.

Electron microscopes do see atoms, because electron waves are thousands of times shorter than green light waves. And a radio telescope must be gigantic for the same reason, since its waves are metres long instead of nanometres.

Who else was taught this wrong?

caption:
How can one amp outmuscle Earth's magnetic field from four millimetres away?

Earth's field steers every compass on the planet. It sounds unbeatable. But that field is weak, only about fifty millionths of a tesla. A current makes its own rings of magnetism around the wire.

That field falls with distance, halving each time you double the gap. Very close to the wire, then, it can be enormous. One millimetre from a one-amp wire gives two hundred microtesla, four times Earth's.

At four millimetres the two are equal, and the needle sits halfway. A needle points along the total of all fields at once, so two equal fields split the difference.

So one amp beats a planet by getting close. The magnetic field grows steeply as you approach the wire. That is called the Biot-Savart law.

An electromagnet lifts scrap cars, because many turns of wire stack their fields in the same place. And a compass beside a live wire twitches, which is exactly how Orsted found magnetism from current.

Why does weightless air add nearly three kilograms to a scuba tank?

Air feels like nothing. A room full of it seems to weigh zero. But air is made of tiny particles called molecules, and each one has mass. At room pressure they sit far apart, so a litre of air weighs about a gram.

caption:
How can a 120-volt outlet secretly reach 170 volts?

The label says 120. The screen shows peaks going far higher. Mains voltage is not steady. It swings smoothly up and down, sixty times a second. Most of the time it sits below its peak, and twice a cycle it is zero.

So calling the peak the voltage would overstate what the outlet can do. Instead we quote the steady voltage that would heat a wire just as much. Heating grows with the square of the voltage, so the big moments count far more than the small. That heating-equal value is 120. The true peak is 170.

The peak is larger by the square root of two, about 1.41 times.

So the outlet really does reach 170 volts. The 120 is a heating average, not a maximum. That is called the RMS voltage.

The plastic in a plug must survive the peak, not the average, or it breaks down twice a cycle. And a loudspeaker rated in watts is judged the same way, since heating depends on the squared average.

Which part of this surprised you?

caption:
What closes the magnetic rings in the gap between two charging capacitor plates?

A current makes rings of magnetism around itself. That much is old and solid. A charging capacitor has current in the wires, but the gap holds only air. Slide your imagined surface into that gap and the current vanishes. The rule counts whatever crosses any surface stretched across the ring, and the answer must not depend on which.

Yet a small probe still finds the very same rings in there. In the gap something else changes: the electric field grows as charge piles up. A changing electric field makes magnetism exactly as a current would.

Four microtesla around the wire. Four microtesla in the gap, at the same radius.

So the magnetic rings never break. The changing field in the gap carries the story across. That is called displacement current.

A radio wave crosses empty space, because a changing electric field makes magnetism and that makes electricity again. And a touchscreen senses your finger through glass, since your approach changes the field and that change registers.

caption:
How can a magnet bend an electron violently and still give it zero energy?

The beam curves hard. Something is clearly pushing on it. A magnet pushes a moving charge sideways, never forwards. The push is always square to the way the charge is heading.

Energy changes only when a push has some part along the motion. A purely sideways push has none of that part at all. So the speed never changes, only the direction. As the electron turns, the push turns with it, so it never once points along the motion.

A hundred electron-volts going in. A hundred electron-volts coming out.

So the magnet steers the electron without feeding it any energy. Sideways pushes do no work. That is called the work-energy theorem.

A cyclotron uses magnets only to bend the beam round, and separate electric fields to speed it up. And a satellite in a circular orbit keeps a constant speed, because gravity there pulls square to its motion.

yt_description:
How can a magnet bend an electron violently and still give it zero energy?

The beam curves hard. Something is clearly pushing on it. A magnet pushes a moving charge sideways, never forwards. The push is always square to the way the charge is heading.

Energy changes only when a push has some part along the motion. A purely sideways push has none of that part at all. So the speed never changes, only the direction. As the electron turns, the push turns with it, so it never once points along the motion.

A hundred electron-volts going in. A hundred electron-volts coming out.

So the magnet steers the electron without feeding it any energy. Sideways pushes do no work. That is called the work-energy theorem.

A cyclotron uses magnets only to bend the beam round, and separate electric fields to speed it up. And a satellite in a circular orbit keeps a constant speed, because gravity there pulls square to its motion.

caption:
How can a five-volt coil make a two hundred volt spike when you switch it off?

There is no battery bigger than five volts anywhere in the circuit. A coil stores energy in the magnetic field its own current builds. That field can only shrink if the current through the coil falls.

A coil fights any change in its current, pushing to keep it going. A falling current shrinks the coil's field, and a shrinking field drives charge to keep the current going. Open a switch and you demand that the current stop within microseconds. The faster you force that change, the harder the coil pushes back.

Half an amp killed in twenty five microseconds, through ten millihenry, gives two hundred volts.

So the coil is not making energy from nothing. It spends stored energy very fast, so the voltage soars. That spike is called back EMF.

A spark plug gets tens of kilovolts from a twelve-volt battery, by collapsing a coil's field very quickly. And a relay needs a diode across it, because the spike would otherwise destroy the transistor switching it.

caption:
How can air make a scale under-read by 1.2 grams per litre?

Put a sealed one litre flask on a balance. Now pump the room away. The reading climbs, and nothing at all was added to the flask. Anything sitting in air shoves air aside, and that air pushes back upward. Air presses harder on the bottom of the flask than the top, and that difference is the lift.

That upward push equals the weight of the air the object displaced. A litre of sea-level air at twenty degrees weighs about 1.2 grams. So a one litre object always weighs 1.2 grams light in ordinary room air.

Go up a mountain, where a litre of air weighs 0.9 grams, and the error shrinks.

So the scale is honest and the air is cheating. That upward push from a surrounding fluid is called buoyancy.

A helium balloon rises because the air it shoves aside weighs more than the balloon and its gas together. And national mass standards are corrected for air before anyone trusts them, since a kilogram block displaces real air too.

What did you think the reason was?

caption:
Why do two pendulums on one string keep trading their swing back and forth?

Nobody touches them. The string between them is the only link. Start them swinging together and they stay together, at one steady rate. Start them swinging opposite and they also hold that pattern, but a little faster. Swinging opposite, the string pulls each bob back as well as gravity, so they hurry.

Those two patterns run at slightly different rates. Any other start is simply those two patterns added together. One swinging and one still is simply the two patterns half each, and both then run on. Because their rates differ, the two patterns slide slowly out of step.

So one pendulum falls still while the other swings hard, every twenty seconds.

So the pendulums never push each other directly. Two steady patterns drift apart and swap the motion. Those patterns are called normal modes.

A guitar string feeds the wooden body, because the two share the same patterns and trade energy. And two clocks on one shelf slowly pull into step, since the shelf lets each one feel the other.

Which part of this surprised you?

caption:
Why does a bathroom scale in a lift lie about your weight?

You did not gain mass between floors. Nothing about you changed. A scale never measures mass. It measures how hard you push on it. Standing still, you push with your weight, and the numbers match.

When the lift starts upward, you must accelerate upward too. The only thing that can push you up is the scale beneath you. Gravity still pulls just as hard, so the scale must push harder than your weight to lift you. So it pushes harder, and it reports that larger push.

Seventy kilograms standing still becomes eighty four while the lift picks up speed.

So the scale is honest about force and wrong about weight. It reports your apparent weight, which is what we call it.

A roller coaster presses you into the seat at the bottom of a dip, for exactly the same reason. And astronauts float weightless in orbit, because their capsule falls with them and never presses back.

Did anyone explain it to you this way at school?

caption:
Why can wet sand stand up, but flooded sand slumps flat?

Dry sand slumps too. Only damp sand holds a shape. Between two grains, a little water forms a tiny bridge. A water surface pulls itself tight, like a stretched skin.

That curved bridge pulls the two grains together. That tight skin is trying to shrink, so it drags the two grains it touches toward each other. Each bridge squeezes with about three thousand pascals. Flood it and that falls to nothing. Add too much water and the bridges merge into one pool.

With no curved surfaces left, nothing holds the grains, so it slumps.

So wet sand holds because tiny bridges pull the grains together. Flooded sand has no bridges left, so it slumps. That pull is called capillary suction.

A wet paintbrush keeps a fine point, because water bridges hold the bristles together until it dries. And a damp cloth clings to a table, since the thin water layer pulls the two surfaces together.

Go and test it, then report back.

caption:
Why isn't an atom half excited when the heat around it matches its energy gap?

It sounds fair. Give it exactly the energy it needs, and split the atoms evenly. Heat does not deliver a fixed amount. It jostles, and the kicks vary wildly. The chance of a big kick falls off sharply as the kick gets bigger.

Climbing the gap costs one full unit of that jostling energy. That costs a factor of about one third in chance. Each extra unit of climbing cuts the chance by the same factor, and one unit costs about three. So out of a hundred atoms, twenty seven sit up and seventy three sit down.

Even a fair-sounding match leaves most of them in the lower state.

So the atom is not a coin toss. Climbing costs energy, so climbing stays unlikely. That penalty is called the Boltzmann factor.

The air thins with height for the same reason, since climbing against gravity costs energy and stays less likely. And a silicon chip carries more current when warmed, since more charges win the kick needed to cross its gap.

Who else was taught this wrong?

caption:
How can adding noise make a digital measurement more accurate?

A converter can only report whole steps. Everything between them is thrown away. Feed it a steady voltage and it returns the same step, again and again. Averaging a thousand identical readings hands you that same step back.

The error is stuck, and no amount of patience will shift it. Now add a little random wobble, slightly bigger than one step. The reading flickers between steps, and how often it picks each one carries the truth. A voltage just under the next step is pushed over it more often. The count tells you where it sits.

Average 256 of them and an 8-bit error of 9.8 millivolts falls to 0.35.

So noise does not only hide a signal. Aimed properly it carries one, and that trick is called dithering.

Newspaper halftone printing does this with dots, using only black ink to convey a whole range of greys. And audio engineers add faint hiss before trimming a track to sixteen bits, because it removes gritty quantisation distortion.

caption:
When do extra zeros on a voltmeter stop being a safety margin?

Your meter reads 3.300 volts. The chip you are feeding is rated to 3.30. Three decimal places look like a promise of thousandth-of-a-volt truth. They are not. The display shows steps, and the datasheet shows the error.

A typical handheld claims half a percent of reading, plus three counts. A count is one step of the last digit, here one millivolt, so three counts is three millivolts. On a 3.300 volt reading that is about twenty millivolts, not half a millivolt. So the true voltage lives anywhere between 3.280 and 3.320 volts.

The top of that range is above the chip's limit, so the margin was never real.

So extra zeros are digits, not accuracy. The honest answer is an interval, and its width is called measurement uncertainty.

A bathroom scale showing 70.0 kilograms may be two kilograms out, because its display steps are finer than its accuracy. And a satnav dot drawn to the metre can still be ten metres wrong. The drawing is finer than the fix.

What did you think the reason was?

caption:
Why would two one-coulomb charges, a metre apart, shove with nine billion newtons?

A coulomb sounds ordinary. A hairdryer pulls about ten of them every second. But that is a flow. The charge streaming past never piles up. Static charge is different. Here you hold a whole coulomb still, in one ball.

Like charges repel, and the push grows fast as the gap between them shrinks. Move them out to two metres and the push falls to a quarter. The strength constant for charge in empty space is enormous. Rub a balloon on your hair and you collect about a millionth of a coulomb.

So one coulomb is a monstrous pile of static charge. Real spheres spark first.

So the coulomb is sized for currents, not for charge sitting still. That rule, force falling with the square of the gap, is called Coulomb's law.

A lightning bolt carries only about fifteen coulombs, yet the same law makes it tear a path through the air. And gravity follows the same square-of-the-distance rule, which is why the Moon's pull weakens so quickly with distance.

Which part of this surprised you?

caption:
How can four totally different experiments share the same correlation?

Four data sets. Same mean in x, same mean in y, same best-fit line. Same correlation number too, 0.816 in every single case. Correlation only asks how tightly the points hug one straight line on average, nothing more. Now plot them. The first is an honest scattered straight trend.

The second is a clean curve, and a straight line is simply wrong for it. The third is a perfect line with one outlier dragging the fit sideways. The fourth is one column of points plus a distant dot doing all the work.

The summary numbers are identical, and the stories could not differ more.

So a correlation number squeezes an experiment until its shape vanishes. This set of four is called Anscombe's quartet.

An average salary can hide a company where almost everyone earns little and one founder earns an enormous amount. And a drug trial mean can hide two groups, one helped and one harmed, since the average erases the shape.

Did anyone explain it to you this way at school?

caption:
Why does one radioactive atom have no age, but a billion of them make a clock?

Take a single carbon-14 atom. Ask it when it will decay. There is no answer. It carries no memory of how long it has waited. An atom that has sat for ten thousand years is as fresh as a new one.

Each atom only carries a fixed chance of decaying in the next second. The same fraction goes each year, so whatever is left always takes the same time to cut in half. Take a billion atoms and those chances average out beautifully. After 5730 years half of them are gone. After another 5730, a quarter remain.

The crowd is predictable to a fraction of a percent, though no member is.

So a radioactive atom has no age, but a crowd keeps a schedule. That fixed halving time is called the half-life.

Insurance works the same way, since nobody knows your day but a million policies give a steady yearly rate. And gas pressure holds steady for the same reason, because countless random particle hits average into one smooth push.

Guess before you scroll, then check.
