caption:
At room temperature, what is the least heat from erasing one bit?

Erasing means forcing a switch to one known state, whatever it held before. Before erasing it could have been either way. Afterwards, only one way. That lost choice is disorder, and disorder cannot simply vanish.

So the same disorder has to be pushed out into the surroundings, as heat. The size of that debt is set by the temperature of the room. A warm room is already jumbled, so it takes more heat there to carry the same extra disorder away. About three zeptojoules at room temperature. A colder room charges less.

At three hundred kelvin the bill is roughly three zeptojoules for each bit.

So erasing one bit must dump a little heat, near three zeptojoules. That floor is called the Landauer limit.

A laptop chip burns tens of thousands of times this per switch, so real machines waste heat elsewhere. And a shuffled deck cannot be sorted for free either, because removing disorder always costs work somewhere.

Who else was taught this wrong?

caption:
Why does energy flow into a resistor from the sides?

A wire carrying current gets hot, and that heat comes from somewhere. The obvious story is energy running along the copper, like water in a hose. The charges in the copper crawl far too slowly to be delivering that power along the wire. But look just outside the wire's surface instead.

There is an electric field along it, pushing the current forward. And a magnetic field wrapped around it, made by that very current. Where an electric and a magnetic field cross, energy flows at right angles to both. Here aims straight at the wire. One watt of heat made. One watt arriving through the sides.

Those two fields together carry energy, and the flow points straight inward.

So the resistor is fed by the field around it, not by the metal core. That inward field flow is called the Poynting vector.

A transmission line carries its power in the space between its wires, which is why spacing matters. And a transformer moves energy through the field in its iron, with no charge crossing between the coils.

caption:
Why do two identical double pendulums stop matching each other?

Release the two of them from angles differing by a millionth of a degree. For the first few seconds they swing as one, shape for shape. Then they part, and within a second they are clearly doing different things.

A tiny gap does not stay tiny here. It grows by multiplying itself. Each swing the arms fling each other about, so whatever difference exists gets amplified again and again. A thousand times closer at the start buys about one extra second. The gap grows roughly tenfold every half second, again and again.

So a thousand-fold better start buys under one and a half seconds more.

So identical twins here are not predictable twins. The growth rate of that gap is called the Lyapunov exponent.

Weather forecasts fade after about two weeks, because tiny errors in today's data keep doubling. And the solar system's exact orbits are unpredictable beyond a few tens of millions of years.

A thousand times closer at the start buys about one extra second. The gap grows roughly tenfold every half second, again and again.

caption:
Why does adding a third filter let light through two blacked-out ones?

Cross two polarizing sheets and the pair goes almost perfectly dark. Each sheet passes only the part of the light lined up with its axis. The first sheet leaves light waving vertically. The second accepts only horizontal.

Vertical waving has no horizontal part, so nothing survives the pair. One sheet at forty-five degrees changes the whole stack. Slide a sheet at forty-five degrees between them and it turns the survivors. Light that gets through a sheet leaves waving along that sheet's axis, not its old one.

Half of that light now lines up with the last sheet, so it passes.

So the third filter does not only block. It turns light partway, and that projection rule is called Malus's law.

Photographers rotate a polarizing filter to kill glare, because reflected light already waves mostly one way. And a liquid crystal screen twists light between crossed sheets, so each pixel can darken on command.

caption:
Can trapping pure light make a sealed mirror box heavier?

Light itself has no mass. A beam on its own weighs nothing. But weight belongs to the whole sealed system, not to its parts. Energy locked inside a closed box adds to what that box resists with.

Trapped light pushes on the mirrors from every side as it bounces. Shove the box and the light bouncing inside pushes back harder from behind, so the box resists more. A gigajoule of trapped light weighs about a fifth of a salt grain. Divide that energy by the speed of light squared to get the extra mass.

A gigajoule of light adds eleven micrograms, which a fine balance could read.

So the box gets heavier while its contents stay massless. That bookkeeping is called mass-energy equivalence.

A hot cup of coffee is very slightly heavier than a cold one, by its stored heat. And a helium nucleus weighs less than its parts, because binding energy left when it formed.

Go and test it, then report back.

caption:
Why can no oil drop ever carry half of one electron's charge?

Millikan sprayed fine oil between two charged plates and watched single drops. He tuned the voltage until one drop hung still in the air. That balance gives the drop's charge, to a few parts in a thousand. A hanging drop means the electric pull exactly matches its weight, and its weight comes from its size.

Thousands of drops gave thousands of answers, scattered all over. A two-charge drop read three point two. A three-charge drop, four point eight. But the answers were not spread evenly. They landed on a ladder.

Every rung sat one fixed step from the next, and nothing in between.

So charge comes in whole steps of one electron, never two halves. That step is called the elementary charge.

Money behaves the same way, because no till in the world ever holds half a penny. And atoms always carry whole numbers of charges, which is why chemistry works in tidy ratios.

Who else was taught this wrong?

caption:
Why can a wave's phase race past light without breaking relativity?

Cross two long rulers at a shallow angle and slide them together. The crossing point can sweep along faster than either ruler moves. Nothing material travels with it. It is a pattern, not an object.

Waves guided down a metal pipe do the same. Their crests are crossing points. Inside the pipe the wave zig-zags off the walls, so a crest is where two slanted waves cross. The crests outrun light while the energy crawls behind. So the crests sweep the walls faster than light, carrying no signal.

Any message rides the packet's envelope, and that always crawls slower than light.

So the phase pattern may outrun light, while every signal stays below it. That cap is called the signal velocity.

A searchlight spot on a distant cloud can sweep faster than light, since no material crosses. And a stadium crowd can send a wave around the bowl faster than any person moves.

caption:
Why does dim violet light kick out tiny charges called electrons, when bright red light cannot?

Turn the red lamp up as bright as you like. Still nothing. Switch to a dim violet lamp and the charges leave at once. Light does not arrive as a smooth stream. It comes in packets.

One packet must pay the whole escape cost by itself. A violet packet carries three point one electron volts. A red one, one point eight. So a violet packet carries nearly twice the energy of a red one. The metal's escape cost sits between the two, so violet clears it and red never can.

Brighter red means more packets, but each one is still too weak.

So brightness counts packets, while colour sets each packet's punch. Those packets of light are called photons.

Sunburn comes from ultraviolet packets, because visible light packets cannot break the bonds in skin. And a solar panel only uses packets above its threshold, so infrared warmth passes straight through.

What did you think the reason was?

caption:
Why must a very short laser flash contain many colours?

A single pure colour is an endless train of identical waves. That train never starts and never stops, so on its own it cannot make a flash. Add waves of slightly different colours and they drift out of step.

They reinforce each other in one narrow window, and cancel almost everywhere else. Colours further apart drift out of step sooner, so the window where they all agree is shorter. Shorter flash, wider spread of colours. The trade is strict. The shorter you want that window, the more colours you must add in.

A ten-femtosecond flash needs about ninety nanometres of colour spread.

So a short flash is not one colour hurried along. It is many colours added, and that trade is called the time-bandwidth limit.

A sharp drum thump carries many pitches, because a brief sound cannot be one steady tone. And a radio station needs bandwidth, since faster data demands a wider band of carrier colours.

Check it at home and tell me what you saw.

caption:
How can counting one laser fringe measure a move of 316 nanometres?

A beam splitter sends the light down two arms to two mirrors. Both two halves travel back and land on the same screen together. With equal arms the crests line up and the screen goes bright. Shift by half a wave and a crest meets a trough, so the two cancel and the screen goes dark.

Move one mirror and that arm's round trip grows by twice the shift. Three hundred sixteen nanometres of mirror travel makes one full fringe. A shift of 316 nanometres adds one full wave to the round trip.

So the whole pattern cycles once, from bright to dark and back.

So the fringe count is a ruler with red light for tick marks. Reading them off is called interferometry.

LIGO counts the same way, because a passing gravitational wave stretches one arm more than the other. And chip-making stages hold position to nanometres, using the laser's own waves as tick marks.

caption:
Why did RANDU's random points stack into just fifteen invisible sheets?

RANDU multiplied each number by sixty-five thousand and kept the remainder. Now plot every three numbers in a row as one point inside a cube. From almost every angle it looks like a formless fog of random dust.

Rotate the cube slowly and the fog snaps into flat parallel slabs. Fifteen slabs, where a good generator of this size allows two thousand. Each new number is a simple whole-number recipe of the last two. The recipe ties the three numbers by one fixed sum. Every whole-number value of that sum is one flat sheet.

That fixed recipe forces every triple onto one of fifteen flat planes.

So RANDU's dust was never random in three dimensions. Those hidden sheets are called a lattice structure.

A Monte Carlo integral can land on a badly wrong answer, because its samples secretly avoid regions. And shuffling cards with too few riffles leaves order behind, which sharp players can exploit.

caption:
How can one random bump show up after a million searches?

A detector plots its counts against energy, bin by narrow bin. Each bin wobbles up and down a little, purely by chance. A three-sigma high bin turns up about once in seven hundred and forty tries. Three sigma just means a bin sticks up three times further than its usual random wobble.

That sounds rare, until you remember that you scanned a million bins. A million bins hand you about thirteen hundred three-sigma bumps for free. So chance alone hands you roughly thirteen hundred striking looking bins.

Demand five sigma instead and the expected haul of fakes drops below one.

So a striking bump means little until you count your searches. That correction is called the look-elsewhere effect.

A lottery winner is unremarkable, because millions of tickets make somebody's improbable win a certainty. And testing a hundred drugs at once will hand you false successes, unless you raise the bar.

Who else was taught this wrong?

caption:
Why does curved data straighten when the axes count by ratios?

Plot planet period against orbit size and you get a sweeping curve. Now space the marks so each step multiplies by ten instead of adding ten. The curve becomes a straight line, and nothing about the data changed.

A power law says one quantity is the other raised to some power. The slope is the power. Planets sit at one point five. Ten times the input multiplies the output by ten raised to the power, so that power is the slope. Multiply the input by ten and the output changes by a fixed factor.

Equal ratios become equal steps, so a fixed factor becomes a constant slope.

So counting by ratios straightens the curve, and the line's slope is the power. That picture is called a log-log plot.

Earthquake magnitudes count by ratios, so each whole step means about thirty times the energy. And animal metabolism plotted against body mass gives a clean straight line, of slope three quarters.

caption:
How can a five-year trip take only three years on the ship?

Earth's clocks say five years out to the star. The ship says three. Both clocks are right. They are not measuring the same thing. Time is measured along a path through space and time, like distance along a road.

A straight road and a bent road between two towns differ in length. Unlike a road, moving through space subtracts from the time a clock counts, so the bent route reads less. Earth's route reads five years. The ship's route reads three. The ship takes a different route between the very same two events.

Travelling at eighty percent of light speed shrinks its reading to three years. The faster you move, the more of your journey is spent covering space instead of ageing.

So no clock is wrong. The trip is three years long for the ship, and that reading is called proper time.

Muons made high in the air reach the ground, because their own clocks run through less time. And GPS satellites correct their clocks daily, since motion and height change the time they record.

What did you think the reason was?

caption:
Why is a metre stick four times harder to spin from its end?

Balance it at the middle and it whips around with a flick. Hold one end and the very same stick fights you. How hard a thing is to spin depends on where its mass sits.

Each gram counts by the square of its distance from the axis. A part twice as far must move twice as fast and sits on twice the leverage. It counts four times over. Same stick, two axes. The end axis costs four times more. Spinning about the middle, no part sits more than half a metre away.

Shift the axis to the end and the far parts double their distance.

So doubling the distance quadruples the cost. Spinning from the end is four times harder, and that shift is called the parallel axis theorem.

A tightrope walker's long pole resists tipping, because its mass sits far from his body. And a hammer is easy to wave near its head, but heavy to swing from the handle.

caption:
Why does clear glass turn into a perfect mirror at forty-two degrees?

Look up from under water and the surface goes silver past a certain tilt. Light bends when it leaves glass for air, because it speeds up outside. One side of the beam crosses first and speeds up first, which swings the ray away from straight on. The steeper your angle inside, the more the escaping ray flattens toward the surface.

Past forty-two degrees inside glass, no escaping ray is left. There is no direction left outside for the light to leave through. So every bit of it turns around and travels back inside the glass.

Nothing was coated. The boundary itself sent the light home.

So the glass becomes a mirror with no silver at all. That tipping angle is called the critical angle.

An optical fibre carries light for miles this way, because every bounce inside the glass is total. And a cut diamond traps light through many internal bounces before letting it out, so it flashes.

Why can you cut a hologram in half and still see the whole scene?

Tear a photograph in half and half the picture is simply gone. A photograph records where each ray landed, one grain per point of the scene. A hologram instead records the ripple pattern the whole scene makes across the plate.

Light from every point of the object reaches every part of that plate. Half the plate is half the window, not half the scene. Shine the original beam back onto the plate and the pattern rebuilds the very light the object sent. So a small piece still replays those ripples and rebuilds the same view.

You lose viewing width and some sharpness, not the objects themselves.

So each half of a hologram is a smaller window onto the same scene. That spreading is called distributed information.

A radio telescope array works this way, because each dish samples the same arriving wave front. And your two eyes each catch the full scene through a small window, differing only in viewpoint.

caption:
Why doesn't a precise stopwatch rescue a sloppy distance measurement?

You time a cart along ten metres of track to find its speed. The stopwatch is good to one part in two hundred, easily. The tape reading is good to only one part in twenty.

Speed is distance over time, so both errors carry across as percentages. Distance contributes five percent. The stopwatch contributes half of one. Errors combine as squares, so the small one nearly vanishes beside the big one. Two independent errors sometimes cancel each other, so you add their squares rather than the errors.

A perfect clock would cut the total from 5.025 percent to 5.000.

So the stopwatch was never the weak link. Fix the widest bar first, and that rule is called the dominant uncertainty.

A telescope on a shaky mount gains nothing from a sharper lens, because the wobble dominates. And a queue moves no faster when you speed up any step except the slowest one.

Who else was taught this wrong?

caption:
Why does adding one crossing to a trapped wave cost energy?

Trap a quantum particle between two walls and it behaves like a wave on a string. The lowest note is one smooth arch that never touches zero in between. The next one up has to cross zero once, right in the middle.

Crossing means bending, and bending the wave more sharply costs energy. A sharper bend means a shorter wave, and a shorter wave means a faster particle. The sharper the bend, the more motion energy the particle is carrying. One smooth arch, or one crossing. The price is not a small one.

So each extra crossing forces tighter bends, and the energy climbs again.

So one extra crossing tightens every bend and the energy jumps fourfold. That rule is called the node theorem.

A guitar string touched at its middle jumps an octave, because you force it to cross zero at that point. And an antibonding state sits higher in energy, because its wave is forced to cross zero between two atoms.

caption:
Why does touching a circuit with a voltmeter change its voltage?

Two equal resistors across a ten volt battery split it evenly, five each. Put the probes across the lower resistor and you read four point seven six. A voltmeter is not a bystander. It is another path for current.

Its own ten megohm resistance now sits alongside the one megohm resistor. True five volts. Measured four point seven six volts. Together the two act like nine hundred kilohms, so the split shifts down.

The meter is honest. It reports the circuit that it created by arriving there.

So the voltmeter reads a circuit its own arrival changed. That is called the loading effect.

A tyre gauge lets a little air out, so the pressure it reports is slightly low. And a cold thermometer cools the drop it touches, which is why small samples read wrong.

What did you think the reason was?

caption:
Why are there five gravitational parking spots between two bodies?

Spin your view so the Sun and Earth stand still, and you turn along with them. Two pulls act on a small probe, plus the outward push of going in a circle. The outward push is there only because the probe circles along with your turning view. Add those three together and you get one landscape of hills and dips.

Some places in that landscape are perfectly flat, and a probe there simply stays. A flat place is a place where nothing drags the probe off in any direction. Counting the flat places carefully, they come to exactly five. On the line the pulls can balance in three places, and off the line in two more.

Three sit on the line through the two bodies, and two sit off to the sides.

So a parking spot is just a flat place in that combined landscape. Those five places are called Lagrange points.

The James Webb telescope sits at one of these spots, 1.5 million kilometres out. So it keeps the Sun permanently behind it. And thousands of Trojan asteroids sit in Jupiter's two side spots, herded there by the same landscape.

Which part of this surprised you?

caption:
Why does glowing hot metal need quantum rules to avoid infinite energy?

Treat the light inside a hot oven as waves rattling between the walls. Count the ways a wave can fit, and short waves have far more ways. Old physics handed every one of those ways exactly the same share of energy.

Short waves are unlimited in number, so the total energy runs away to infinity. The old curve soars. The real furnace does nothing of the kind. Planck's fix was to let each wave take energy only in whole lumps. The shorter the wave, the bigger the one lump it has to swallow.

A short wave needs a big lump, and the oven rarely has one to spare. The oven's heat only offers energy up to a certain size, so the biggest lumps almost never get paid.

So quantum lumps starve the short waves and the total stays finite. Those lumps are called quanta.

The cosmic background fits this curve better than any laboratory source, pinning the early universe at 2.7 kelvin. And a furnace's colour tells you its temperature, which is how steelworkers judge heat without a thermometer.

Did anyone explain it to you this way at school?

caption:
How can sunlight push a mirror when no charges cross it?

Light carries a push of its own, stored in its travelling fields. When that light strikes a mirror, it turns around and heads straight back. Turning around means its push reverses, and that change has to go somewhere. Push is never lost, so whatever the light gives up the mirror must take on.

It goes into the mirror, exactly as a bouncing ball kicks the wall it hits. A black sheet absorbs the push once. A mirror gets it twice over. In full sunlight this works out to about nine millionths of a pascal.

Air presses on you ten billion times harder, which is why you never feel it.

So sunlight pushes because light carries its own store of push that must go somewhere. That store is called field momentum.

A solar sail the size of a tennis court gains speed continuously, and after months that tiny push adds up. And a comet's dust tail points away from the Sun, because sunlight keeps shoving the grains outward.

Guess before you scroll, then check.

caption:
Why can a flood of red light free no charge from zinc, when one ultraviolet packet can?

Charge a clean zinc plate and shine a bright red lamp on it. The leaf of the meter stays put, no matter how long you wait. Now a weak ultraviolet lamp, and the charge drains in seconds.

Each packet of light deals with one bound charge, on its own. Zinc demands four point three electron volts. Red brings one point eight. Zinc holds its charges behind a fixed toll of four point three electron volts.

A red packet brings one point eight, so no number of them adds up. A charge loses the energy again almost at once, so a second packet always arrives too late.

So light is not a pooled fund. Each packet pays alone, and zinc's toll is called its work function.

A photomultiplier tube counts single packets, because one packet frees one charge from its coated plate. And night-vision sensors use materials with a low toll, so faint infrared packets still free charges.

Who else was taught this wrong?

caption:
Why does light bouncing off one electron change colour, not speed?

Light always travels at the same speed, so bouncing can never slow it down. But light carries a push of its own, and a push can be handed over. Hit a free electron and it recoils, carrying away part of that energy.

Light with less energy is redder, with a longer stretch between its crests. Off a mirror, nothing. Off one electron, a real and measurable shift. A mirror is different, because the whole heavy mirror recoils instead. A heavy object takes the same push but barely moves, so it steals almost no energy.

Billions of atoms share that kick, so the loss is far too small to see.

So the light changes colour because one lightweight electron takes a real kick. That is called Compton scattering.

Gamma rays in a lead shield lose energy step by step this way, each bounce reddening them a little further. And hot gas in a galaxy cluster blue-shifts the cosmic microwave background, the very same exchange running backwards.

caption:
Why does a one-atom wire carry current in fixed jumps?

Squeeze a metal contact until only a handful of atoms bridge the gap. That neck is now narrower than the electron wave that has to cross it. Only a whole number of wave patterns can fit sideways across such a neck.

Each pattern that fits carries the same share of current, no more and no less. Electrons in a faster pattern are spread thinner, so every pattern ends up carrying the same current. One pattern, then two. The total climbs in equal treads. That share works out at seventy seven and a half millionths of a siemens.

So pulling the contact apart drops one pattern at a time, in clean steps.

So a one-atom neck carries current in equal steps, because whole wave patterns come and go. That step is called the conductance quantum.

A gold break junction shows a staircase as it snaps, each tread one pattern wide, visible on an ordinary meter. And the quantum Hall effect fixes resistance to a similar universal value, now used to define the ohm.

What did you think the reason was?

caption:
Why is swapping two particles in a flat world a braid, not a trade?

Swap two identical particles and nothing you can measure has changed. Do it twice and you are back exactly where you started. A swap can leave the wave turned by some angle, and two swaps must cancel that turn. In three dimensions you can lift one path over the other and untangle any swap.

So every double swap looks the same, and only two kinds of particle survive. If the turn must undo itself it can only be a half turn or none, which is the two kinds. In a flat two-dimensional world there is simply no room to lift. One particle must go round the left or round the right, and those paths differ.

Draw the paths through time and they weave, like strands in a plait.

So in a flat world a swap remembers its own path. Particles that keep that memory are called anyons.

In a fractional Hall state, quasiparticles pick up a sixty degree twist per swap, a third of an electron's. And a quantum computer could store information in how these strands are plaited, since knots resist small disturbances.

Which part of this surprised you?

caption:
How can an untouched wave already have an uncertain amount of motion, called momentum?

The usual story blames the measurement, as if looking must bump things. But the spread is already there before anyone looks. A wave squeezed into a short stretch cannot be one pure ripple spacing. One pure ripple runs on forever, so other spacings must be added to cancel it outside the bundle.

Building that short bundle takes a range of ripple spacings added together. Squeeze the bundle to one nanometre and its speed spread jumps tenfold. Each ripple spacing in the mix stands for a different amount of motion.

So the bundle carries that spread on its own, untouched by anybody.

So the wave owns its spread. The narrower it is, the wider its momentum range, and that is called the uncertainty principle.

A very short musical note has no exact pitch, because too few cycles fit inside it. And a radar pulse trades sharpness in range against sharpness in speed, for the same reason.

Did anyone explain it to you this way at school?

caption:
How can a hilltop in space still trap an asteroid that rolls off it?

The two sideways parking spots sit at the highest point of that gravity landscape. Turn your view with the two bodies, and their pulls plus the outward push make a landscape. A marble on a hilltop should roll away, and at first it really does. But in a turning view, anything that moves gets shoved off to one side.

That shove points at right angles to the motion, so it bends the path. Bend the escape enough and it becomes a loop that comes back. The marble rolls out, the sideways shove curls it, and it swings back around.

This only works when one body is far heavier, above about twenty five times. The sideways shove only wins if the hill is gentle, which needs one body far heavier.

So the hilltop holds on because a sideways turning shove curls escapes into loops. That shove is called the Coriolis force.

Jupiter is about a thousand times lighter than the Sun, so its two side spots hold thousands of asteroids. And a hurricane's winds curl for the same reason, bent sideways by the turning Earth instead of falling straight inward.

Guess before you scroll, then check.

caption:
Why does cutting just over half a grid's links kill it?

Take an endless square grid where every crossing is joined to its neighbours. Now delete links at random, one coin flip at a time. Delete a few and the grid still carries you from any point to far away.

Delete more and it breaks into islands that touch nothing beyond themselves. Different grids break at different points, but each one has a sharp value. The switch is not gradual at all. It happens at one sharp fraction. A long path needs every link in a chain, so its chance collapses suddenly once links get scarce.

For a square grid that fraction sits at exactly one half.

So the grid dies once its surviving links fall past one half. That sudden switch is called a percolation threshold.

Rubber loaded with carbon black conducts only once the grains link up, which is exactly this threshold in three dimensions. And a forest fire sweeps across a whole wood only when tree density crosses its own sharp value.

Who else was taught this wrong?

caption:
Why does a planet sweep equal areas in equal times?

Watch the planet swing in close to the Sun, and it races along. Let it swing far away, and it crawls. Draw a line from the Sun to the planet, and watch the area it sweeps.

Near the Sun that line is short, but the planet covers ground fast. Far away the line is long, but the planet barely moves. Short and fast, or long and slow. The swept area comes out the same.

The Sun's pull points straight along that line. So it can never twist the planet sideways. That turning quantity is just the swept area rate, so keeping one fixed keeps the other fixed.

So the sweep rate is fixed because nothing twists the planet. That fixed turning quantity is called angular momentum.

Halley's comet races at 54 kilometres a second near the Sun, then crawls at under one out past Neptune. And a skater pulling her arms in spins faster, because nothing twists her either, so the same quantity holds.

caption:
What lopsidedness in an atom's energy well makes hot metal grow?

Two bonded atoms sit in a valley of energy, at their comfortable spacing. Push them together and the energy climbs very steeply, because the cores resist. Pull them apart and the energy climbs gently, because the bond simply weakens.

So the valley is steep on one side and shallow on the other. A symmetric valley would not move at all. A lopsided one does. Heat makes the pair rattle, and rattling explores the shallow side much further. At the same rattling energy the atoms get much further out than they get in.

So the average spacing creeps outward, even though nothing pulled the atoms apart.

So metal grows because the valley is lopsided, so rattling drifts outward. That lopsidedness is called anharmonicity.

Railway tracks are laid with gaps, because a rail in high summer grows enough to buckle without them. And a bimetallic strip bends when heated, because two metals with different lopsidedness grow by different amounts.

What did you think the reason was?

caption:
Why must a wandering walker return home on a flat grid, but not in space?

Let a walker step at random, each direction as likely as any other. On a flat grid the walker wanders, but keeps recrossing its own old tracks. The ground it can reach grows, but so does the number of visits it makes.

In three dimensions there is a whole extra direction to escape into. Flat, and it comes home for certain. In space, usually not. Space opens up faster than the walker can ever fill it. The region grows as the square of its range in the plane, but as the cube in space.

So the tracks thin out, and many paths simply never come back.

So a walker comes home for certain on a flat grid. In space it returns only about a third of the time. That is called Polya's theorem.

A protein sliding on a flat cell membrane keeps rediscovering the same targets. So reactions there run faster than in open fluid. And a smoke particle drifting in open air is very unlikely to ever return to where it began.

Which part of this surprised you?

caption:
Why does today's tiny weather error swallow the whole forecast in two weeks?

A forecast starts from measurements, and measurements are never exact. Say the starting error is one part in a thousand, a tenth of a percent. In a chaotic flow small differences do not stay small. They grow by doubling. A swirling flow pulls neighbouring parcels apart, so any difference is stretched a little wider each hour.

In the atmosphere that doubling takes roughly a day and a half. After five days the error is about one percent. That is still a good forecast. After ten doublings it has grown a thousandfold, and fills the whole signal.

Ten doublings is about fifteen days, which is where useful skill runs out.

So the weather is not unpredictable in principle. Its errors simply double. That limit is called the predictability horizon.

A billiard table loses predictability within a few bounces, because each hit magnifies the tiny aiming error. And planetary orbits scramble after millions of years, since the same doubling runs at a far slower rate.

Did anyone explain it to you this way at school?

caption:
Why won't a hundred tiny particles called molecules crowd back into one half?

Nothing forbids it. Each particle is free to be on either side. Count the possibilities. Every particle has two choices, left or right. For a hundred particles that gives two multiplied by itself a hundred times.

That is roughly a thousand billion billion billion different arrangements. Exactly one of those puts every single particle on the left. Every one of those arrangements is equally likely, so the odds just follow the counting. Almost all of the rest sit near fifty-fifty, because so many ways split evenly.

So the gas spreads out by counting alone, not by any force pushing it.

So a hundred molecules avoid one half simply because the odds are hopeless. That counting is called entropy.

A shuffled deck never returns to factory order, because one arrangement hides among an astronomical number. And cream stirred into coffee stays mixed, since the mixed arrangements outnumber the separated ones enormously.

caption:
How can a charge's far field beat the field right beside it?

A resting charge has a field that falls off as one over distance squared. Double the distance and that field drops to a quarter of its value. Now jerk the charge sideways for a moment.

News of that jerk travels outward at light speed, as a kink in the lines. That kink fades only as one over distance, and not as distance squared. Distance stretches the kink sideways as well, and that stretching keeps its strength up. So it falls a hundred times more slowly over a hundredfold range.

So far enough out, the kink is all that is left to see.

So the field near the charge fades fastest, and the kink wins far away. That kink is called radiation.

A radio mast reaches distant towns only because the kink from its shaking charges survives. And a phone signal weakens as one over distance, so doubling the range needs four times the power.

Who else was taught this wrong?

caption:
Why can the same setting leave a system in two completely different states?

Some systems have two stable states available at once, for one input. Which one you sit in depends on where you came from. A stable state is a dip, and nothing leaves a dip until the dip itself is gone. Raise the input slowly and the system holds its low state past the middle.

It only jumps up when the low state runs out and disappears. Lower the input again and it clings to the high state well past that point. So the jump up and the jump down happen at two different settings.

The loop between them is a memory of the path you took.

So the setting alone does not decide the state. Its history does too. That loop is called hysteresis.

A thermostat switches on at eighteen degrees and off at twenty, so it cannot chatter. And a magnet keeps its north pole after the coil is off, because both states survive there.

caption:
How can a bridge have a mode that a perfect rhythm cannot excite?

A bridge has favourite shapes it likes to move in, each with its own rate. Push at exactly that rate and you expect a huge response. But rhythm is only half the story. Where you push matters just as much.

The second favourite shape rises on one half and falls on the other. So a push spread evenly along the deck helps one half and fights the other. What a push gives a shape is the push times the motion, added along the whole deck. The two contributions cancel, and that shape receives exactly nothing.

So you can drive at the right rate all day and see no motion.

So the bridge ignores a perfect rhythm applied in the wrong shape. That cancelling overlap is called modal orthogonality.

Pushing a swing sideways gets you nowhere, because that push has no grip on the swinging motion. And a loudspeaker placed at a room's exact centre cannot drive the modes that stay silent there.

What did you think the reason was?

caption:
Why does perfect copper near melting keep one empty site per ten thousand atoms?

Pulling an atom out of a crystal and parking it on the surface costs energy. For copper that cost is about one electron volt, which is a great deal. So at room temperature the crystal is essentially perfect throughout.

But an empty site can sit in any one of a huge number of places. Having many arrangements is itself worth something, and heat cashes it in. A thing that can happen in many more ways is far more likely to happen at all. Cold, and there are none worth counting. Hot, and they appear.

Near melting the heat available is a tenth of that cost, and the balance tips. With heat a tenth of the cost, about one site in ten thousand ends up empty by chance.

So the crystal keeps empty sites because disorder pays for their cost. Those gaps are called vacancies.

Atoms diffuse through a solid by hopping into these gaps, which is how steel is case hardened with carbon. And a battery's solid electrolyte carries charge only because vacancies let ions hop from site to site.

Which part of this surprised you?

caption:
Why do a cube's three standing waves all ring at the same pitch?

Trap sound in a cube. It can only hold whole numbers of half-waves. Put one half-wave along the width, and two along the depth. Now swap those two numbers over. The wave is a different shape entirely.

But a cube has equal sides, so both shapes fit exactly the same way. The pitch depends only on the three numbers, not on which edge got which. The same pair of numbers can also sit along the height, which makes three shapes in all. So three different shapes all ring at four hundred and twenty hertz.

Stretch one side by a tenth and that agreement breaks into three separate pitches.

So the cube's symmetry forces three different shapes onto one pitch. That coincidence is called degeneracy.

A hydrogen atom has three matching orbitals at one energy, because the atom looks the same in every direction. And a square drum gives matching pairs of notes, since swapping its two edges changes nothing.

caption:
How can a particle with no force on it still double its size?

Pin an electron down to the width of a single atom, then let go. Nothing pulls on it. Empty space, no fields, no pushes at all. But pinning it that tightly forces a wide spread of possible speeds.

That is the trade the uncertainty rule demands, tight in place means loose in speed. Some of those possible speeds run left quickly, and some run right quickly. So the region where it might be found simply grows.

The cloud swells outward, with nothing pushing on it at all.

So no force is needed. Squeeze an electron to an atom's width and it doubles in about one femtosecond. That is called wavepacket spreading.

A cold atom cloud released from its trap balloons outward, and the shape it reaches reveals its original speed spread. And a beam in an electron microscope must be kept short, because a tightly focused packet spreads as it flies.

Guess before you scroll, then check.

caption:
How can two steady rhythms draw a line that never closes on a doughnut?

Picture a bead running around a small ring, while that whole ring slowly turns. Two independent turns, so the bead's home is the doughnut surface itself. Each turn keeps its own steady rate, and neither one pushes the other.

If the two rates form a simple fraction, the path soon bites its own tail. Three laps one way, two laps the other, and the bead is exactly home. But pick a ratio that no fraction can hit, and that return never happens.

So the line keeps missing itself, and slowly it covers the whole surface. Each loop lands slightly beside the last, and those small shifts never repeat, so they eventually pass everywhere.

So the path never closes because the two rates share no common beat. That is called quasi-periodic motion.

A satellite's orbit and the planet's spin rarely share a common beat. So its ground track drifts and never quite repeats. And two tuning forks with an unfittable ratio never repeat their combined sound, so the pattern wanders forever.

Who else was taught this wrong?

caption:
Why does pulling a needle back one atom's width collapse the current?

A particle facing a wall it cannot climb does not stop dead at the face. Its wave leaks into the wall, fading away smoothly as it goes deeper. The leak shrinks by a fixed factor for every fixed step into the wall.

Double the wall's thickness and you square that shrinking, rather than halving it. A tenth of a nanometre wider, and almost nothing gets through. The current is simply how much of the leaking wave survives to the far side. For a typical metal, each extra tenth of a nanometre cuts the current eightfold.

So the current reports the size of the gap with atomic sharpness.

So the current collapses because the leaking wave shrinks step after step. That leak is called quantum tunnelling.

A scanning tunnelling microscope maps single atoms, because a bump a tenth of a nanometre high changes the current eightfold. And flash memory holds data for years behind a barrier just thick enough to make that leak absurdly slow.

caption:
With steam at a hundred degrees, why is seventy-nine percent still wasted?

An engine takes heat from something hot and dumps the rest somewhere cold. Only the difference between those two can be turned into useful work. Heat only does work while it falls from hot to cold, so with no gap nothing comes out. And the sums only work in kelvin, counted from absolute zero. The gap is measured against the whole drop to absolute zero, so only kelvin gives the honest fraction.

Steam at a hundred degrees is three hundred and seventy-three kelvin. The cold air at twenty degrees is two hundred and ninety-three kelvin. The fraction you can keep is the gap divided by the hot number.

Eighty divided by three hundred and seventy-three is about twenty-one percent.

So the steam engine is not badly built. The two temperatures set the ceiling. That limit is called Carnot efficiency.

A power station uses steam near six hundred degrees, purely to lift that ceiling higher. And a fridge runs the same sums backwards, costing more work as the inside gets colder.

caption:
Why does a speeding cube look rotated rather than contracted?

Measuring a moving object and seeing it are two quite different jobs. Measuring means catching every part of it at the very same instant. Seeing means catching the light that happens to arrive at your eye together.

Light from the far side left earlier, so it shows you an older position. Squashing predicts one thing. What reaches your eye is quite another. That delay reveals the cube's back face, which a still cube would hide. The back face shows where the cube was, offset by exactly the amount a turn would give.

The squashing is still there, but it cancels against that revealed face.

So the cube looks rotated because delayed light swings its back face into view. That is called the Terrell rotation.

A sphere rushing past still shows a perfectly round outline, because the same delay refills the squashed edge. And a galaxy jet can look faster than light for the same reason, since its own light keeps catching up.

Which part of this surprised you?

caption:
Why do two identical photons leave a mirror by separate doors zero percent of the time?

Send one photon into each side of a half-silvered mirror. Each can pass straight through, or bounce off. That is four combinations. Two of those combinations send the pair out of separate doors.

Those two routes carry equal weight, but a reflection flips the sign of one. Routes ending in the same outcome are added together first, so opposite signs wipe each other out. So when the photons are truly identical, those two routes cancel exactly. The only survivors send both photons out of the same door, together.

Make them slightly different in colour or timing, and the cancelling fails. If the photons differ you could tell the two routes apart, so they never add and nothing cancels.

So two identical photons refuse to separate at a mirror. That cancelling is called Hong-Ou-Mandel interference.

Electrons do the opposite at a splitter and leave separately, because their two routes cancel the other way. And a quantum computer built from light uses this silence to check that its photons match.

Those two routes carry equal weight, but a reflection flips the sign of one. Routes ending in the same outcome are added together first, so opposite signs wipe each other out. So when the photons are truly identical, those two routes cancel exactly. The only survivors send both photons out of the same door, together.

Make them slightly different in colour or timing, and the cancelling fails. If the photons differ you could tell the two routes apart, so they never add and nothing cancels.

So two identical photons refuse to separate at a mirror. That cancelling is called Hong-Ou-Mandel interference.

Electrons do the opposite at a splitter and leave separately, because their two routes cancel the other way. And a quantum computer built from light uses this silence to check that its photons match.

caption:
Why does one millivolt make a superconductor hum at four hundred and eighty-three gigahertz?

Two superconductors with a thin gap between them still behave as one. Paired charge carriers can tunnel across that gap with no push at all. Now put a small steady voltage across the barrier.

The voltage makes the quantum clocks on the two sides tick at different rates. A quantum clock ticks faster when it has more energy, and the voltage gives one side more. The current across the gap depends on how far out of step the two clocks are. The current then sloshes back and forth at the difference between those rates. That rate is set by the voltage, and by two constants of nature.

One millivolt gives four hundred and eighty-three gigahertz, a microwave tone.

So a superconductor turns a steady voltage straight into a pure rate. That conversion is called the AC Josephson effect.

The volt itself is now defined this way, because the conversion depends only on constants of nature. And a SQUID sensor uses the same junctions to sense fields a billion times weaker than Earth's.

caption:
How can a curved hill look flat to a quantum wave?

A quantum particle climbing a hill is really a ripple with a definite length. That length depends on how much energy the particle has left above the hill. On a gentle slope the ripple barely notices any change across one wave.

So locally it looks exactly like a wave running over flat ground. Gentle or steep, the question is always how much changes in one wave. Make the hill steeper and the ripple's length shifts a lot in a single step.

Then the flat-ground picture breaks, especially where the particle runs out of energy. Where the energy runs out the ripple stretches without limit, so it changes fast on any hill.

So a curved hill looks flat when the ripple's length barely shifts across one wave. That trick is called the WKB approximation.

The rate of alpha decay is worked out this way, since the barrier changes slowly compared with the particle's ripple. And light in a graded fibre follows the same rule, bending smoothly because the glass changes little across one wave.

Who else was taught this wrong?

caption:
How can two shapes share one string and yet overlap by exactly zero?

A guitar string can hum in a single arch, or in two opposite humps. Take those two shapes and multiply them together, point by point. Where both are positive the product is positive. Where one flips, it turns negative.

Add it all along the string and the positive half cancels the negative half. The total comes out exactly zero, and not merely close to zero. Multiplying and adding like this is how you measure how much of one shape hides inside another. That zero is forced by the string's fixed ends and its even tension.

So each shape is independent. No amount of one is hiding inside the other.

So two shapes can live on one string and stay completely separate. That property is called orthogonality.

A tuning app pulls one pitch out of a messy recording, because the other shapes contribute nothing. And breaking any signal into pure waves works for the same reason, since every pair multiplies to zero.

caption:
Why does a Mexican hat shape have a direction that costs no energy?

Picture the energy of a field drawn as a surface. The middle is a bump. Around that bump runs a circular trough, the lowest ground there is. No direction round the hat is special, so every point in the trough sits at the same height. A ball settles somewhere in the trough, and that choice breaks the symmetry.

Push it outward, up the wall, and you must pay energy to climb. Push it sideways round the trough and the ground never rises at all. So one direction is stiff, and the other is perfectly flat.

A flat direction means a ripple that can be as slow and gentle as you like.

So the hat hides two different wobbles. One costs energy, one costs none. The free one is called a Goldstone mode.

A magnet picks one direction to point, and turning every atom together afterwards costs almost nothing. And sound in a crystal is the same idea, because sliding the whole crystal sideways costs nothing.

What did you think the reason was?

caption:
Why can some defects never be smoothed away, no matter how you try?

Take a field of little arrows, each pointing some direction in the plane. Walk a closed loop and watch the arrow turn as you go. You end on the same arrow you started with, so the turning must come to whole turns. By the time you return, the arrow has turned a whole number of times.

Round a smooth patch that count is zero. Round a vortex it is one. You cannot slide from one whole number to another by nudging arrows gently. Any smooth change keeps the count fixed, since a whole number cannot drift.

So the defect is locked in by counting, not by its strength.

So the defect cannot be smoothed away, because a whole number cannot change slowly. That count is called the winding number.

You cannot comb a hairy ball flat, so any such field must have at least one bald spot. And a vortex in a superfluid keeps spinning for the same reason, since its count cannot slip.

Which part of this surprised you?

caption:
Why is the power in a cable not travelling inside the wire?

Picture a coax cut open: a copper core, a plastic gap, a woven copper sleeve. Push one volt across a fifty ohm line and twenty milliwatts reach the far end. Between core and sleeve sits an electric pull and a circling magnetic field.

Those two fields cross, and where they cross, energy slides along the gap. An electric push and a magnetic field together hold energy, which travels at right angles to both. Almost all twenty milliwatts ride that gap. Only a whisper soaks into the copper. The source pours its energy straight into the gap, so it never enters the metal at all. The copper's job is to steer the fields, not to ferry the energy.

So charges in the metal barely crawl, while the energy runs near light speed.

So the cable carries its power in the empty gap beside the wire. That energy flow is called the Poynting vector.

A transformer moves power with no wire between its coils, because the field in the iron carries it across. And a microwave oven feeds its energy down a hollow pipe with no centre wire at all.

Try it tonight and tell me what happened.

caption:
Why does a near light-speed electron throw all its light into a narrow cone?

A slowly moving charge is fair about it. It sprays light out sideways, fairly evenly. Ride alongside a fast one and you would see that same even spray. But you are not riding alongside. You watch from the laboratory floor.

And angles do not survive a change of viewpoint at these speeds. The whole source is rushing forward past you, and that sweeps every emitted direction toward the front. Light sent sideways in its own frame arrives pointing almost straight ahead in yours. The faster it goes, the tighter that forward cone closes.

The half width is one over gamma, the factor by which energy beats rest energy.

So the electron still radiates every way. Your viewpoint folds it into a cone one over gamma wide. That is called relativistic beaming.

A synchrotron beamline gets its pencil thin X-ray beam this way, because each stored electron sweeps a searchlight past you. And a quasar jet looks far brighter when it points at us, since the same folding concentrates its glow.

Guess before you scroll, then check.

caption:
Why does an attosecond flash arrive two thirds of a cycle late?

A strong laser field can bend an atom's grip enough to let a charge slip out. That tiny charge, called an electron, is now loose in the laser field. The field drives it away, then reverses half a cycle later and hauls it back. The electron starts from rest, so the journey back takes longer than the journey out.

It comes flying home and slams into the atom it left. All the energy it gathered is dumped out as one burst of extreme ultraviolet. The charge drops back into the empty place it left, and the energy it gained leaves as light. For eight hundred nanometre light the round trip takes about one thousand seven hundred attoseconds.

That is close to two thirds of the laser's two point seven femtosecond cycle.

So the attosecond flash is late because the charge must leave, turn, and return. That three step path is called high harmonic generation.

A boomerang returns with the energy you gave it, because the same push that sends it out brings it back. And a ball thrown upward lands back in your hand after a delay set by gravity.

Who else was taught this wrong?

caption:
Dark means not glowing. So why does your body shine brightest at nine micrometres?

Point a thermal camera into a pitch black room and people light up like lamps. Everything above absolute zero radiates, and the colour depends only on temperature. A stove ring at eight hundred degrees glows dull red, just inside our range.

Your skin sits near thirty three degrees, far cooler, so its glow sits far past red. Divide one fixed constant by the temperature in kelvin and you get the peak. For skin that lands at nine and a half micrometres, deep in the infrared.

Our eyes simply stop near zero point seven, so we call the room dark.

So your body is not dark at all. It shines at nine micrometres, where eyes cannot follow. That rule is called Wien's law.

A rescue drone finds people at night by this glow, because warm skin outshines the cold ground. And an astronomer studies cold dust clouds in the infrared, since their peak sits far beyond red.

caption:
Can a probability map dip below zero and still predict real lab counts?

Physicists draw a quantum state as a landscape over position and speed. For ordinary states that landscape is a simple hill, positive everywhere. For a single-photon state the middle of that landscape dips below zero.

No detector ever reports a negative count, so nothing here is broken. The rule is that you never measure the landscape itself. You always measure a squashed version of it, a shadow along one direction.

Every one of those shadows comes out positive, so the predictions stay sane. The dip is always shallow enough that adding along any direction still leaves a positive total.

So the probability map is a bookkeeping tool, not a list of odds. That map is called a quasiprobability.

A cat state of light shows the same negative fringes, which is how labs prove it is non-classical. And a medical scanner rebuilds a body from shadows, using exactly the same projections in reverse.

What did you think the reason was?

caption:
How can a stable state vanish while the knob moves perfectly smoothly?

Picture a ball resting in a shallow valley, with a hill just next to it. The valley floor is a stable state. The hilltop is an unstable one. Turning the knob raises the valley and lowers the hill together. The same tilt that lifts the valley floor also drops the hilltop, so they close in together.

So the two move toward each other, and the gap between them shrinks. The gap shrinks like a square root, so it closes faster near the end. At one exact setting the valley and the hill meet and flatten out.

One nudge past that and both are gone. The ball simply rolls away.

So a stable state can disappear with no warning in the knob. That collision is called a saddle-node bifurcation.

A buckling ruler holds fine until one extra gram, then it bows sideways with no warning. And an ice sheet can pass a setting where its stable size simply stops existing at all.

Which part of this surprised you?

caption:
What does one extra step of earthquake magnitude really cost you?

Magnitude is a logarithmic scale, so each step is a fixed multiplier. One step up multiplies the shaking recorded on the instrument by ten. But the energy released climbs faster still, by about thirty-two times per step. A bigger quake shakes harder and breaks a longer fault for longer, so energy outruns the shaking.

So a magnitude seven releases thirty-two times the energy of a magnitude six. Counting quakes shows the other half of the pattern. For every magnitude seven, the world sees about ten magnitude sixes.

So each step costs thirty-two times more, and arrives ten times less often.

So one earthquake step is not small. It is thirty-two times the energy. That counting rule is called the Gutenberg-Richter law.

Solar flares follow the same shape, with the big ones rarer by a steady factor per size step. And city sizes follow a similar rule, since a few giants sit above very many smaller ones.

Did anyone explain it to you this way at school?

caption:
Why can you never pull a single quark out of a proton?

Pull two of them apart and the force between them does not fade. The pull stays roughly constant, like a rubber band that never weakens. That band is a narrow tube of colour field, and stretching it stores energy. Colour field lines pull on each other, so they bunch into a tube instead of spreading out.

Its tension is about sixteen tonnes of pull, on one pair of particles. So the stored energy climbs the further you pull, with no end in sight. Long before it runs out, that energy is enough to make a fresh quark pair. Enough energy can simply turn into matter, and a quark pair is what this energy buys.

So the tube snaps, and each new quark caps one loose end.

So you never get a lone quark. You get two new particles instead. That trapping is called colour confinement.

A magnet cut in half does something similar, since each piece grows a fresh north and south pole. And smashing protons harder makes sprays of new particles, because the extra energy keeps snapping fresh tubes.

Guess before you scroll, then check.

caption:
How can a gas push outward at absolute zero?

Normally a gas pushes because its particles are hot and hammer the walls. Cool it toward absolute zero and that hammering should die away completely. But tiny charges called electrons obey a strict seating rule.

No two of them may sit in the same state, so they must stack upward. Each higher seat in the stack means faster motion, so the ones on top race even when cold. Even with all heat removed, the ones near the top are moving extremely fast. In a white dwarf core that crowding beats hot gas pressure roughly eighty fold.

So the hammering never stops, and it is what holds the dead star up.

So a cold gas still pushes, because crowding forces motion even at absolute zero. That push is called degeneracy pressure.

A neutron star holds itself up in the same way, with neutrons crowded instead of charges. And ordinary metal resists being squeezed largely because its electrons refuse to share states.

Who else was taught this wrong?

caption:
Why do the charges in room temperature copper sit at an eighty thousand kelvin scale?

Copper carries current because tiny charges called electrons roam freely inside it. You would expect them to be as sluggish as the warm metal around them. But no two may occupy the same state, so they cannot all settle low.

Room warmth only nudges the thin skin of charges right at the top.

So copper hides an eighty thousand kelvin energy scale in a cool wire. That top level is called the Fermi energy.

A metal's heat capacity is far smaller than expected, since only the topmost charges can take up energy. And a white dwarf holds itself against gravity by the same rule, at far higher density.

caption:
If air particles called molecules average five hundred metres per second, why does the graph peak lower?

At room temperature nitrogen particles share one pot of energy through constant collisions. Some end up slow, some end up fast, and a steady spread settles in. The spread is lopsided. There is a floor at zero, but no ceiling above.

So the peak of the curve sits at four hundred and twenty-two metres per second. The long fast tail drags every average upward, away from that peak. The plain average speed is four hundred and seventy-six metres per second.

And the five hundred figure is a squared-then-rooted average, five hundred and seventeen. Squaring counts the fastest molecules extra heavily, so that average lands highest of all.

So molecules do not share one speed. Three different averages describe one lopsided curve. That curve is called the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution.

Water evaporates at room temperature because the fast tail of that curve escapes the surface. And a star burns hydrogen thanks to the same tail, since only its fastest particles clear the barrier.

caption:
Why does liquid carbon dioxide lose its surface at thirty one degrees?

In a sealed tube, liquid carbon dioxide sits under its own gas, with a clear line between. At twenty degrees the liquid below is four times denser than the gas above. Warm the tube. The liquid thins out and the gas above it packs tighter. Heat swells the liquid and drives more of it into the sealed gas, so both densities move together.

The liquid gets lighter, the gas gets heavier, and the gap between them closes. At thirty one degrees the two densities meet, so there is nothing left to separate. The line goes milky, shimmers for a moment, and then is simply not there.

Above that point there is one single fluid, neither liquid nor gas.

So the surface vanishes because carbon dioxide runs out of two densities to keep apart. That temperature is called the critical point.

Decaffeinated coffee is made with this fluid, which soaks into beans like a gas and dissolves like a liquid. And a power station boiler above two hundred and twenty bar shows no water line at all.

caption:
At a black hole horizon, what actually blows up?

Write down the standard black hole solution and something does go infinite at the horizon. But that is a warning about your map, not about the place itself. Stand at the North Pole and ask for your longitude. The answer is meaningless.

The ice under your boots is perfectly ordinary. Only the grid drawn on it failed. So ask something the grid cannot spoil: how hard does the tide stretch you? At a giant hole's horizon that stretch is gentle. At a small one it is lethal. A bigger hole's horizon sits further out, where gravity changes gently across your body.

Either way it is a finite number, so nothing physical blows up there.

So at the horizon only the coordinates blow up. That harmless failure is called a coordinate singularity.

A flat map of the world smears each pole into a whole stretched edge, though the ice is unremarkable. And a compass spins uselessly near the magnetic pole, because the labels fail where the ground does not.

Did anyone explain it to you this way at school?

caption:
Why does turning infrared light into green need both colours to travel alike?

Send a strong infrared beam into a crystal and it stirs the charges inside. Those charges shake at twice the beam's rhythm, so they radiate green light. The crystal pushes back unevenly, so the charges' wiggle picks up a beat at double the rate. Every thin slice of the crystal makes a little green, all along the path.

Those small contributions only build up if they stay in step with each other. But the crystal slows green more than infrared, so the green slips behind. Left alone they fall out of step after fourteen micrometres, then start cancelling.

Cut the crystal at the right angle and the two speeds match for ten millimetres.

So green grows only while the two colours travel alike. Keeping infrared and green in step is called phase matching.

A radio antenna array beams strongly only when every element is fed in step, because otherwise the signals cancel. And a green laser pointer hides exactly this cut crystal, turning invisible infrared into the beam you see.

Guess before you scroll, then check.

caption:
How can cooling a gas make millions of atoms act like one wave?

Every atom is also a ripple, and a slow atom is a wide ripple. The slower an atom moves, the more spread out its ripple has to be. Cooling slows the atoms down, so each ripple grows wider. At a hundred nanokelvin a rubidium ripple is about six hundred nanometres wide.

The atoms themselves sit only about two hundred nanometres apart. So the ripples now overlap, and you cannot say which atom is which. Identical atoms that overlap prefer to pile into the very same state. For atoms of this kind, a state already occupied is the more likely one to join, not the less.

Once that starts it runs away, and almost all of them join.

So cooling does not squeeze the atoms together. It stretches each wave until they merge. That is called a Bose-Einstein condensate.

An atom laser pours out a steady coherent beam, because every atom in the cloud shares one wave. And superfluid helium creeps up its container walls, its atoms locked into a single shared state.

Who else was taught this wrong?

caption:
How can light hitting lead turn into matter above one megaelectronvolt?

In a cloud chamber, an invisible ray sometimes ends in a sudden V of two tracks. The two tracks curve opposite ways in a magnet, so they carry opposite charge. Nothing was there before. Light went in, and a pair of particles came out.

Underneath, light and matter are both ripples in fields that fill all space. A ripple in the light field can hand its energy across to the matter field. Charge cannot appear from nothing, so the particles must arrive as a plus-and-minus pair. But the bill is fixed: two particle masses, one point zero two two megaelectronvolts.

A heavy lead nucleus has to stand nearby to soak up the leftover push.

So light becomes matter the moment it can pay for two masses. That conversion is called pair production.

A PET scanner runs this backwards, where an antiparticle meets a charge and two gamma rays fly out. And a thundercloud makes the very same pairs, because its gamma rays clear the same threshold.

caption:
How can a silent black hole crash release three Suns of energy?

Two black holes circle each other, faster and faster, closer and closer. Each orbit shakes spacetime itself, and the shaking runs away as ripples. Carrying ripples away costs the pair energy, so they spiral in tighter.

In the final moments they whirl round hundreds of times a second and merge. Add the masses: sixty five Suns went in. The hole left behind weighs sixty two. Mass is a form of energy, so mass that goes missing has left as energy. Three solar masses are simply missing, turned into ripples in under a second.

No light, no fireball. The energy left as a stretching and squeezing of space. There is no matter out there to heat, so nothing is left that could shine.

So the crash is silent because three Suns of energy depart as ripples in spacetime. Those are called gravitational waves.

A hydrogen bomb works the same way, since the pieces left over weigh slightly less than what went in. And the Sun shines by losing four million tonnes of its own mass every second.

What did you think the reason was?

caption:
Can gravity fake a star's speed by eighty kilometres a second?

Starlight carries dark lines at colours that atoms always absorb. If the whole set shifts red, the textbook answer is that the star is receding. Sirius B is a white dwarf: a Sun's worth of mass squeezed into an Earth sized ball. Squeezed that small, the surface sits far closer to all that mass, so its pull is enormous.

Light leaving that surface has to climb out of a very deep gravity well. Climbing costs it energy, so it arrives redder than it set out. Light cannot slow down, so it pays the toll in colour: less energy means redder. For Sirius B that mimics eighty kilometres a second. For our Sun, well under one.

Astronomers measure the star's real motion separately, and the leftover shift matches gravity.

So a red shift need not mean speed. Gravity buys the same shift for free, and that is called gravitational redshift.

GPS satellites run fast by thirty eight microseconds a day, because their clocks sit higher in the well. And X-ray lines from gas near a black hole arrive far redder through the very same climb.

Which part of this surprised you?

caption:
Inside a black hole, why is outward no longer a possible future?

From any event, the paths you could take fan out inside a cone set by light. Gravity tips that cone over, and near a black hole the tipping gets severe. Space itself falls inward here, and past the horizon it falls faster than light can swim back. At the horizon the whole cone leans inward. Every allowed path now heads in.

So inward stops behaving like a direction and starts behaving like later. Falling toward the centre becomes as unavoidable as next Tuesday. Firing your rocket outward does not help. It only shortens the time you have. A rocket bends your path through time sideways, which spends your remaining time faster.

For a ten solar mass hole that remaining time is well under a millisecond.

So outward is not blocked inside. It has simply stopped being a future you can pick. That tipping is called the horizon.

A river past the lip of a waterfall carries you down whatever you paddle, since the water outruns your stroke. And tomorrow arrives however you move, which is exactly what the tipped cone is saying.

caption:
Why do rod shaped particles line up when you simply add more of them?

A thin soup of tiny rods points every which way, and happily stays that way. Lining them up looks like added order, which disorder ought to resist. Now crowd them. Each rod needs room to turn without striking a neighbour.

A tumbling rod claims a whole sphere of space. An aligned one claims a thin sliver. So aligning costs the rods freedom to point, but buys them freedom to move. Past a crowding threshold the second gain wins, and longer rods need far less crowding. A longer rod sweeps a far bigger sphere when it tumbles, so it runs out of room sooner.

So the soup snaps into an aligned state all by itself.

So rod shaped particles align because packing more in creates freedom rather than destroying it. That threshold is called the Onsager transition.

A liquid crystal display twists these aligned rods to block or pass light at every pixel. And logs floating down a narrow river end up pointing along the flow, for the same reason.

Guess before you scroll, then check.

caption:
Which loop test tells an ordinary field apart from confinement?

Drag a quark and an antiquark apart, hold them a while, then bring them back. Their path traces a rectangle in space and time. Call that rectangle a loop. The theory assigns the loop a number, and the number shrinks as the loop grows. That number falls off with the energy it takes to hold the pair apart for that long.

The question is what governs the shrinking: the loop's edge, or the area inside it. An ordinary electric field gives edge scaling, so pulling the pair apart stays cheap. Double the loop and the edge only doubles, while the area goes up fourfold. The area is the separation times the waiting time, so area cost means energy that grows with distance.

Area scaling means the cost climbs without limit, so the quarks never get free.

So one loop settles it. Area scaling is the signature of confinement, and the test is called the Wilson loop.

A rubber band stores more energy the further you pull, so its two ends never come apart. And a magnet cut in half just gives two smaller magnets, never a single loose pole.

caption:
How can a wave inside a metal pipe move faster than light?

A microwave in a hollow pipe does not run straight down the middle. It bounces off the walls, crossing the pipe at a slant as it travels. Two of those slanted waves overlap, and their crests meet in a moving pattern.

Where the crests meet, that meeting point slides along the pipe very fast. Two crests meeting at a shallow angle sweep their crossing point far along the pipe for a tiny step sideways. In a standard pipe the crossing point runs at one hundred and thirty percent of light speed. But a meeting point carries nothing. It is a pattern, not a messenger.

The energy follows the slant, so it lags behind at three quarters of light speed. The energy zigzags wall to wall, so it covers less ground along the pipe than it travels.

So nothing outruns light. Only the crossing pattern of the wave does, and that number is called the phase velocity.

A searchlight spot swept across distant clouds can cross them faster than light, because no single ray makes that trip. And ocean waves meeting a beach at a slant send a foam line racing along the sand.

The energy follows the slant, so it lags behind at three quarters of light speed. The energy zigzags wall to wall, so it covers less ground along the pipe than it travels.

So nothing outruns light. Only the crossing pattern of the wave does, and that number is called the phase velocity.

caption:
How can a crystal make a single charge behave hundreds of times heavier?

In empty space a tiny charge called an electron has one fixed mass. Inside a crystal it is never alone. It sits in a dense sea of other charges. As it moves it shoves neighbours aside, dragging a cloud of disturbance along.

Accelerate the charge and you must accelerate that whole cloud with it. So it answers a push sluggishly, exactly as a far heavier particle would. Sluggish carriers sit on more tightly packed levels, so far more of them can soak up heat. Heat capacity reveals this: uranium platinum three beats copper six hundred fold.

It is still one charge. Only its response to a push has changed.

So the crystal never makes the charge truly heavier. It dresses it, and the dressed object is called a quasiparticle.

A balloon held under water accelerates slowly, because it must shove surrounding water along with it. And heavy fermion crystals turn superconducting at low temperature, driven by these very sluggish carriers.

caption:
Why does freezing water warm itself back up to exactly zero degrees?

A still bottle of clean water can be chilled to minus eight and stay liquid. Ice needs a seed to build on, and very clean still water offers none. Tap the bottle and a seed appears. A slush front races through the water.

Water molecules locking into ice give up stored energy, so the bottle heats itself. That released energy is large: enough to warm the same water by eighty degrees. But it cannot climb past zero, because ice and water only sit together there. Above zero ice cannot survive, so the moment the mixture reaches zero the freezing halts.

So the slushing stops once about a tenth has frozen, and the rest stays liquid. Eight degrees of chill is a tenth of eighty, so only a tenth can freeze before it stalls.

So freezing heats the bottle until it reaches zero degrees and stalls there. That stored energy is called the latent heat of fusion.

A hand warmer snaps a metal disc to seed crystals, releasing exactly this stored heat on demand. And orange growers spray their trees with water, since freezing it releases heat and protects the fruit.

caption:
Why does one passing photon make an atom twice as likely to emit?

An excited atom will drop down on its own, at some steady average rate. The light it can drop into is not blank space. It is a set of possible modes. Each mode can hold none, one, two, or many more particles of light.

Light particles like company. A mode already holding some pulls harder on the atom. Photons are perfectly identical, and identical particles of this kind are more likely to join a crowd. The rate into a mode goes as the number already sitting there, plus one. That plus one is the lone atom's own rate; the rest is the pull of photons already there. An empty mode gives one unit of rate. One photon already there gives two.

And the new light joins that same mode, matching it exactly.

So one photon doubles the chance the atom will emit into its mode. That doubling is called stimulated emission.

A laser is built on this, since every added photon makes the next one likelier still. And a maser cloud in space amplifies radio light the same way across light years of gas.

Guess before you scroll, then check.
