caption:
Why does erasing one bit of memory have to release heat?

Before erasing, a bit can be in two states. You do not know which. After erasing, it is in one known state, whatever it held before. So the number of ways the memory can be arranged has been cut in half.

But the whole world's count of arrangements is not allowed to shrink. So the missing count has to reappear somewhere else, as disorder in the warmth around. The only way to give the surroundings more arrangements is to hand them energy as heat. Two point nine zeptojoules at room temperature. Far less when it is cold.

The bill is small, but it is a floor no clever design can dodge.

So erasing is the step that costs, not computing. That minimum heat is called the Landauer limit.

Maxwell's demon fails for this reason, because the demon must erase its notes and pay the bill. And reversible computers dodge the cost by never throwing information away, keeping every step undoable.

What did you think the reason was?

caption:
Why does slowing a neutron make uranium far easier to split?

A neutron born in fission flies out fast, at about two million electron volts. You would think a faster hit breaks the nucleus more easily. The opposite happens. Slow it down, and splitting gets far more likely.

A slow neutron spends far longer near the nucleus, so it has more chance to be caught. A barn just measures how big a target the nucleus looks to the neutron. Fast neutron, about one barn. Slowed neutron, five hundred and eighty five. Once caught, the extra binding energy alone is enough to wobble the nucleus apart.

So reactors deliberately bounce neutrons off light atoms like water until they slow down.

So a slow neutron is a better splitter than a fast one, because it lingers. That lingering is called resonance capture.

The first reactor used graphite blocks, because carbon slows neutrons without swallowing too many of them. And neutron imaging uses slow neutrons, because they interact strongly enough to reveal plastic inside metal.

Which part of this surprised you?

caption:
Why is there one spot on a bat where a hit does not sting your hands?

Hit the ball near the handle and your palms take a hard jolt. A struck bat does two things at once. It recoils backwards, and it rotates. The recoil pushes the handle back into your hands.

The rotation about the bat's balance point swings the handle forward. The handle is on the far side of the balance point, so the spin swings it opposite to the hit. Balance point sits at forty three centimetres. The quiet spot sits further out. At one impact point those two motions of the handle exactly cancel.

So the handle stays still, and your hands feel almost nothing.

So the bat has a spot where the recoil and the rotation of the handle undo each other. That is called the centre of percussion.

A hammer has one too, which is why a well made handle barely twists in your grip. And a swinging door has a point where a push moves it without straining the hinges.

caption:
Why does a disturbed electron in a metal survive long enough to be useful?

A metal is packed with charges, all shoving each other constantly. You would expect any single disturbance to be smeared out instantly. But at low temperature the low energy seats are all taken. No two electrons may share a seat, so a full seat is simply closed to it.

To scatter, it must find an empty seat, and hand its energy to someone who can move up. Both conditions get harder as you approach the filled level, and each costs a factor. A tenth of a volt above, hundreds of femtoseconds. A full volt, a few.

So the decay rate falls as the square of how far above the filled level it sits.

So a gently disturbed electron has almost nowhere to go, so it lives a long time. We call that long lived thing a quasiparticle.

A sound quantum in a crystal is the same idea, a shared wobble treated as one travelling object. And a missing charge in silicon behaves like a real positive particle, which is how transistors are designed.

Guess before you scroll, then check.

caption:
Why do physicists need a density matrix when state vectors already work?

A single isolated system can be written as one clean wave description. But make two particles share a state, and neither one has a state of its own. The pair only has an answer together, so each one alone has nothing fixed to report. Look at just one of them, and your answers come out random.

Fifty fifty, exactly like a tossed coin you have not looked at. Alone, fully known. Half of a pair, only half known. So you need a way to book both real randomness and hidden partners.

A small table of numbers does that, carrying every prediction the particle can support. The table lists the chance of every answer plus how those chances lean, which one wave cannot hold.

So one particle out of a pair has no clean state of its own, only a table of chances. That is called a density matrix.

An unpolarised light beam needs one too, because it is a blend of orientations rather than a single one. And every real qubit needs one, because it slowly picks up randomness from its warm surroundings.

Who else was taught this wrong?

caption:
How can a particle try every wild route and still arrive as if one mattered?

Quantum rules say a particle takes every possible path from start to finish. Each path carries a little clock hand, and the hand turns as the path runs. To get the answer you add all those hands, tip to tail.

Wild detours have hands pointing every way, so their sum curls up and cancels. That special path is the one with the least total turning, and near any least, small changes do almost nothing. Near one special path, small changes barely turn the hand at all. So those neighbouring hands point the same way and stack up.

For a thrown ball that stack is thirty four digits long.

So the particle really does try every route. Only the stationary one survives the adding up, and we call it the classical path.

A lens works this way, because every ray path through it takes the same time and adds up. And a grating mirror reflects at odd angles, because its grooves remove the paths that would have cancelled.

caption:
Why did a new footbridge start swaying the moment a crowd walked on?

London's Millennium Bridge opened in 2000 and closed two days later. Its deck swung sideways, not up and down. Every step you take pushes a little sideways as well as down.

In a scattered crowd those sideways pushes point every way and mostly cancel. A crowd never cancels perfectly, so a tiny sway always starts, and then the loop takes over. But if the deck moves, people widen their stance and step in time with it. Stepping in time makes the pushes add up, which moves the deck more.

A quiet deck moves millimetres. That day it moved seventy.

So the crowd did not simply load the footbridge. It joined the swaying and fed it. That is called a synchronisation instability.

A grandstand can do this too, when a crowd bounces in time with the stand's own sway. And two pendulum clocks on one shelf fall into step, because each nudges the shelf the other feels.

What did you think the reason was?

caption:
How can empty space press two neutral plates together with thirteen pascals?

Empty space is not still. Electric and magnetic fields jitter in it constantly. Those jitters come in every possible wave size, like notes on a string. Slide two mirrors close together, and only waves that fit between them survive.

So the gap holds fewer jitters than the wide space outside it. Every one of those waves presses on the plate it bounces off, so fewer waves means less push. More jitter pushing inward than outward means a steady squeeze. Seventy five nanometres apart, thirteen pascals. Double the gap, sixteen times less.

The push climbs as the fourth power of closeness, so it matters only when very close.

So the plates feel a push from empty space itself, because the gap is quieter than outside. That is called the Casimir effect.

Tiny machined switches stick shut because of it, since their parts sit only nanometres apart. And two ships side by side in a swell get pushed together, because the gap holds fewer waves.

Which part of this surprised you?

caption:
How can a light pulse peak leave a gas cell before it has finished entering?

A pulse is not a single thing. It is many colours added together. Their crests line up in one place, and that pile up is the peak. The gas handles each colour a little differently. The gas nudges each colour's crests by a different amount, so the place they all line up moves forward.

So the gas quietly reshapes the pile, boosting the front and trimming the back. The new pile peaks earlier, so the peak seems to run ahead. Sixty two nanoseconds early, on a pulse four thousand nanoseconds long.

But the very front edge of the pulse still arrives at the usual light speed.

So no signal beat light. The gas rebuilt the pulse from information that had already arrived. That is called pulse reshaping.

A water wave group can travel slower than its own crests, which is the same trick run backwards. And a telephone cable stretches a pulse, because each colour of the signal moves at its own pace.

caption:
Why does a perfectly excited atom fall apart in a completely empty room?

Lift an electron to a higher rung and leave the atom entirely alone. By the atom's own rules, that state should sit there forever. But the room is not empty. Empty space still carries a restless electric jitter.

That jitter tickles the atom, exactly the way a passing light wave would. A wave of the right colour pushes an electron either way, and an atom already up can only come down. So the electron gets nudged down, and a single flash of light leaves. Hydrogen lets go in nanoseconds. Sodium takes ten times longer.

How fast that happens depends on how hard the atom couples to that jitter.

So the excited atom is not really alone. Empty space is a partner that pulls it down. That is called spontaneous emission.

A neon sign glows because its excited atoms drop back down within nanoseconds, over and over again. And a mirrored box can slow that drop, because it removes the jitter at the atom's own colour.

Guess before you scroll, then check.

caption:
Why does magnetic flux through a superconducting ring come in fixed lumps?

Cool the metal enough and its charge carriers pair up and move as one. The whole ring is then described by a single wave, like one long ripple. Walk that wave once around the ring and you must come back to the same crest.

So the wave has to fit a whole number of crests around the loop. A magnetic field threading the ring shifts that count. The field through the hole adds a twist to the wave all the way round, changing how many crests fit. One lump is about two femtoweber. Two lumps is twice that.

So only certain amounts of field can thread the ring, in even steps.

So the ring only accepts flux in fixed helpings, set by the ring's single wave. That is called flux quantisation.

A SQUID sensor counts those steps, so it measures fields a billion times weaker than Earth's. And an electron in an atom sits at fixed energies for the same reason, its wave must close up.

caption:
Why does flowing water drag light along at only 44 percent of its own speed?

Light crosses water more slowly than it crosses air. So you might guess that moving water simply carries the light along with it. Fizeau split a beam, sent the two halves upstream and downstream, and recombined them.

The two halves came back slightly out of step, so he could measure the drag. Full carry would be one hundred percent. The real drag is forty four. Light is a wave in the water's own atoms, not a marble in a stream. Only the part of the journey spent inside the atoms gets carried, and that part is what slows the light.

Moving the atoms shifts the wave only partly. How much water slows light fixes the rest.

caption:
Why must a steadier little machine waste more heat than a sloppy one?

A molecular motor takes uneven steps. Mostly forward, but sometimes backward. That jitter is not bad engineering. It is the random kicking of a warm world. Run the motor longer and the wobble averages out, so the output looks steady.

But every step it takes also dumps a little heat into its surroundings. Only the heat it burns each step makes forward more likely than back, so more one-way means more burning. The two are tied together. Steadiness is bought with wasted heat, and nothing buys it cheaper. The bias you buy grows only as the square root of the heat. Half the wobble needs four times as much. Ten percent wobble costs two hundred units of waste. Five percent costs eight hundred.

So halving the wobble costs four times the heat, whatever the machine is made of.

So a steadier machine has to waste more. That floor is called the thermodynamic uncertainty relation.

A kinesin motor hauling cargo through your cells burns several fuel units per step to keep its pace regular. And a precise clock must shed heat too, which is why the most stable oscillators draw real power.

caption:
Why must a vortex be trapped before a magnet can hang stably in place?

A superconductor normally pushes magnetic field out of itself entirely. Pure pushing gives a slippery float. Nudge the magnet and it slides away. In the useful materials, field pokes through in thin threads instead.

Each thread is a tiny tube where superconductivity has been switched off. Those tubes settle into flaws in the crystal, where switching off costs least. Pinned threads also stop the current wandering, which is why this material carries so much. A house wire carries six amps per square millimetre. This carries ten thousand. Each thread is the magnet's own field poking through, so moving the magnet has to drag the threads with it.

Moving the magnet would drag the threads out of those flaws, which the material resists.

So the magnet hangs because each vortex thread is gripped by a flaw. That grip is called flux pinning.

A pinned maglev track holds a car upside down, because the threads resist moving in any direction. And an MRI magnet stays strong for years, because pinned threads stop the current from decaying.

caption:
Why does one particular electron wave get stopped dead inside a crystal?

A crystal is rows of atoms, evenly spaced about three tenths of a nanometre apart. An electron moves through it as a wave, with its own crest spacing. Most crest spacings slip past the rows with barely a reflection.

Crest spacing twice the atom spacing. That is the one that gets caught. At that spacing each row's reflection comes back one whole wave behind the last, so they all add. But when the crest spacing is exactly twice the row spacing, every row reflects in step. Forward and backward waves then add into a standing pattern that goes nowhere.

Two standing patterns are possible, one sitting on the atoms and one between them, at different energies.

So that one electron wave cannot travel, and a band of forbidden energies opens. That is called a band gap.

An LED shines at one colour because its gap fixes exactly how much energy each electron gives up. And an opal flashes colour because its stacked spheres reflect one light colour the same way.

caption:
Why does a flat band make the pushing between charges rule everything?

Normally a charge in a solid gains a lot of energy by moving. That motion energy is much larger than the push between neighbours, so motion wins. Now stack two graphene sheets with a tiny twist of about one degree.

The two patterns beat together into a huge repeating moire cell. The repeat is so wide that a charge can barely hop to the next one. Moving buys it almost nothing. Charges get caught in that pattern, so moving gains them almost nothing. The band is five millielectron volts wide. The push is twenty five.

With motion energy flattened, the push between charges becomes the biggest thing left.

So a flat band does not add anything. It removes the competition, and pushing decides. That is called a correlated phase.

Magic angle graphene superconducts near one degree, because the flattened band lets charges organise themselves. And a strong magnetic field flattens bands the same way, which is why quantum Hall states appear.

caption:
Why should you stop adding terms in a calculation at the smallest one?

Hard problems get solved by adding a correction, then a correction to that. At first each new term is much smaller, so the answer gets sharper. But the terms are also multiplied by a fast growing count of ways things can happen.

So after a while, each new term is bigger than the last. Smaller x, more useful terms before the turn. The sizes go down, bottom out, and come back up. Whatever you add next moves the answer by at least that smallest term, so it is your error.

That smallest term is the honest floor on how well the method can do.

So adding more terms past the smallest one makes the calculation worse. Stopping there is called optimal truncation.

The electron's magnet strength is computed this way, and its series would only turn around near the hundredth term. And Stirling's formula for factorials does the same, giving its best value after a handful of terms.

Who else was taught this wrong?

caption:
Why is the edge of a razor's shadow never perfectly sharp?

A blade edge is sharp to within a few millionths of a metre. So you would expect its shadow to end in a clean line. But light is a wave, and the gap between its crests is about half a micrometre. Every point of a wave spreads sideways, and blocking half leaves that spreading with nothing to cancel it.

At the blade edge the wave gets cut in half, and the cut sends light sideways. That sideways light mixes with the light that went straight past. Move the card back and the ripples get wider.

Where crest meets crest it is brighter, and where crest meets trough it is dim.

So the razor's shadow edge carries fine bright and dark ripples. That spreading at an edge is called diffraction.

A CD throws rainbows because its tiny tracks bend each colour of light through a different angle. And a telescope blurs a star into a tiny disc, because its rim bends light the same way.

caption:
Why does a jiggling pollen grain prove that atoms are real?

Under a microscope, tiny grains in water dance about endlessly. No current pushes them, and the dance never stops, even after days. Einstein said they are being hit by unseen water particles, from every side.

At any instant slightly more hit one side, and the grain lurches. He worked out how far a grain should wander in a given time. That distance depends only on temperature, the water's thickness, and the grain's size. The wander also depends on how many molecules share out the warmth, so measuring it counts them.

Perrin used it to count atoms, and landed within ten percent of today's value.

So the wandering of a pollen grain lets you count atoms. That dance is called Brownian motion.

A smoke particle in still air jitters the same way, which is how air filters are designed. And a protein inside a cell travels mostly by this jitter, which sets how fast biology works.

What did you think the reason was?

caption:
Why does an excited atom slosh when one exit exists, but drain when many do?

Put an excited atom next to exactly one matching partner state. The excitation goes across, then comes straight back, over and over. With one exit, the return trip is always in step with the outward trip.

Now open a whole band of slightly different exits instead. Each exit sends its piece back at a slightly different pace. These returning pieces are waves, so ones out of step wipe each other out. Their returns soon fall out of step and cancel, so nothing comes back.

Hydrogen's 2p level has many exits and goes in nanoseconds. The 2s level crawls.

So the number of exits decides whether an excited atom sloshes or drains. That rate is called Fermi's golden rule.

A solar cell works because a kicked charge has a huge band of exits, so it never returns. And putting an atom in a tiny mirrored box cuts it to one exit, so it sloshes again.

Which part of this surprised you?

caption:
Why does heating an empty curved space suddenly flip it into a black hole?

Picture a box of space whose walls curve inward and hold everything in. Fill it with warm radiation. At low temperature, that is the cheapest state. A black hole is also allowed inside that box, sitting in balance with the heat.

Which one wins depends on which has more disorder at that temperature. A small hole is hotter than the box, so it radiates away faster than it can feed. A hole's disorder grows with its surface, far faster than radiation's, so once it is big enough it wins. Below a certain temperature no black hole can even sit there steadily. Black holes can exist above 0.450. They take over above 0.477.

Cross the higher mark and the black hole becomes the preferred state, abruptly.

So the curved space boils into a black hole at a sharp temperature. That is called the Hawking-Page transition.

Ice melting is the same kind of switch, because one arrangement suddenly becomes the cheaper one. And nuclear matter unglues into free quarks above a sharp temperature, which this picture was built to describe.

caption:
Why does a Foucault pendulum turn by a strange angle rather than a full circle?

A long pendulum keeps its swinging plane fixed while the Earth turns beneath. At the north pole that is simple. The floor makes one full turn daily. At the equator, the plane does not turn at all.

In between, the pendulum is carried around a circle of latitude, tilted to the spin. Its plane is carried along as straight as the curved surface allows. Roll that cone flat and it is a disc with a wedge cut out. The missing wedge is exactly the turn. Going once around a cone of that surface leaves you turned by the missing slice.

At Paris the swing turns 271 degrees a day. At thirty degrees, 180.

So the pendulum angle just measures the patch of sphere it circled. That leftover turn is called a geometric phase.

Twisting an optical fibre rotates the light's tilt the same way, purely from the path's shape. And a falling cat rights itself with no net spin, by moving through a closed loop of shapes.

caption:
Why can a particle living in a flat world be neither of the usual two kinds?

In three dimensions every particle is one of two kinds. Swap two identical ones and the description either stays the same, or flips sign. Swap them twice and you must be back where you started.

In three dimensions you can always lift one path over the other and untangle it. On a flat sheet there is no over. The paths stay braided. So going around twice is a real, different journey, and any turn is allowed. Flipping sign is just turning the description half way round. The two kinds are no turn and half a turn.

A fermion swap turns it by one hundred eighty degrees. This one, sixty.

So a flat world lets particles keep a memory of how they went around. We call them anyons.

The fractional quantum Hall state hosts them, and its lumps carry one third of an electron's charge. And a topological quantum computer would store data in the braiding itself, where local noise cannot reach.

Who else was taught this wrong?

caption:
How can a solid that never repeats make sharp fivefold diffraction spots?

For a century, sharp spots meant a pattern that repeats like tiles. A sharp spot appears only where the waves bouncing off millions of atoms all arrive in step. And five sided tiles cannot cover a floor without leaving gaps. Then in 1982 an aluminium manganese alloy gave a clean tenfold pattern of spots.

Its atoms sit on a Penrose style tiling that never repeats itself. It never repeats, yet every tile placement follows a strict rule. The strict rule makes the same spacings recur at steady rates, and that is all the waves need. Ordinary crystals space their spots by whole numbers. This one uses 1.618.

So the spot spacings step by the golden ratio instead of whole numbers.

So sharp spots need order, not repetition. A solid that is ordered without ever repeating is called a quasicrystal.

A quasicrystal coating makes frying pans slippery, because a non repeating surface gives grease nothing to grip. And medieval Islamic tilework used the same non repeating patterns centuries before anyone wrote the mathematics.

caption:
How can a black hole grow ten million cubic kilometres of inside every second?

From outside, a solar mass hole keeps the same three kilometre width forever. Inside the horizon, though, the roles of space and time swap over. The direction you think of as inward is really a direction in time.

So asking for the volume inside means choosing which moment you mean. Inside, later moments sit further along in time, and each one has more room behind it than the last. Slice the inside at one moment and that slice is the volume you are measuring. Take the biggest surface that fits inside, and it keeps getting bigger. About eleven million cubic kilometres a second. In an hour, thousands of times more.

The outside stays the same size while the inside quietly grows without limit.

So a black hole has a small outside and an endlessly growing inside. That growth is called the interior volume.

A wormhole in these equations grows the same way, getting longer while its mouths stay put. And that growth is read as rising complexity, one leading guess for what the inside really counts.

caption:
Why can an ordinary laptop simulate some quantum circuits instantly?

Tracking a hundred quantum bits normally needs more numbers than atoms in a galaxy. Each bit doubles the list of possibilities you must carry along. A check is a yes-or-no question about the qubits whose answer the circuit carries along unchanged. But one family of operations only ever maps simple checks to other simple checks. Those few checks pin down every measurement you could make, so nothing else needs storing.

So instead of the whole list, you track a few hundred of those checks. Thirty one digits of numbers, or five. That is the whole difference. These circuits still make entanglement, and still beat anything a classical bit can do alone.

What they lack is one extra kind of rotation, the ingredient that makes simulation hard.

So entanglement alone does not make a quantum circuit hard. That easy family is called the stabiliser circuits.

Error correction leans on them, since the checks that spot errors are exactly this easy family. And they let engineers test a hundred qubit machine, by predicting what it should have produced.

Tracking a hundred quantum bits normally needs more numbers than atoms in a galaxy. Each bit doubles the list of possibilities you must carry along. caption:
Why is the electron's magnet strength 2.00231930436 instead of exactly two?

Dirac's equation predicted exactly two, and that was already a triumph. Careful measurement found a small excess in the fourth decimal place. An electron is never bare. It sits in a haze of borrowed light and pairs.

It can throw out a light quantum and catch it back a moment later. While the light is away the electron sits slightly spread out, so a magnet grips it a little harder. During that moment it is slightly off its usual footing, which shifts its magnetism. The first layer of borrowing adds a thousand parts per million. The second, two.

Adding up every such borrowing gives a number matching experiment to twelve digits.

So the electron's magnet is dressed by the empty space around it. That excess is called the anomalous magnetic moment.

The muon gets a bigger version of the same dressing, which is why it is watched so closely. And two hydrogen levels that should match are split slightly apart, by the same borrowed light.

caption:
Why do flat swirls merge into one giant storm instead of shredding?

In ordinary air, a big eddy breaks into smaller ones until friction eats them. But a thin sheet of fluid cannot swirl in the third direction. Losing that direction removes the trick that feeds the small eddies, called vortex stretching. With no stretching to wind swirls tighter, the total spin has no way to grow.

Now two quantities must both hold: the energy, and the total spin squared. Small swirls hold far more spin than energy, so the spin drains down to them and the energy must climb. Holding both forces the energy to move towards bigger swirls, not smaller. Energy in air falls off gently. In a sheet it falls off steeply.

So neighbouring swirls wrap around one another and merge into fewer, larger ones.

So a flat flow runs the cascade backwards, pooling energy into one giant swirl. That is called an inverse energy cascade.

Jupiter's Great Red Spot survives because its thin atmosphere pools energy into one storm sixteen thousand kilometres wide. And ocean eddies grow to hundreds of kilometres across, because a shallow ocean behaves like a sheet.

caption:
How can a sealed quantum gas look hot while staying perfectly pure?

Seal a small cloud of atoms away from everything and give it a sudden kick. Its full description never gets muddied. Sealed systems stay exactly as definite as they began. Yet measure the atoms in one small region and they look plainly thermal.

The trick is that the rest of the cloud acts as the bath. The kick spreads information across the whole cloud, out of any local reach. Nothing is lost. It is just hidden in links no small probe can see. Once a patch is tangled with everything else, its own readings come out exactly as if warmed.

Sixteen spins together carry no disorder. Half of them carry five.

So the quantum gas never really heats. Each small piece is warmed by the rest, and we call that eigenstate thermalisation.

A stirred coffee cup does this too, since its stirring is not lost, only spread beyond reach. And the universe as a whole may be pure, while every region inside it looks warm.

caption:
How can a frozen field become a gas of cold dark matter?

Suppose the early universe held a field sitting away from the bottom of its valley. Normally it would roll down and swing about the bottom. But rapid expansion acts like thick treacle, and it holds the field still. Stretching space drains a field of its motion, just as it stretches away the energy of light.

So the field stays stuck partway up the slope, doing nothing at all. Expansion slows as the universe cools, and the treacle thins out. Frozen while the universe is hotter than a few giga electron volts. Rolling below that.

Then the field rolls and swings, and those slow swings behave exactly like cold particles. A field swinging in place holds energy but goes nowhere, which is just what slow heavy particles do.

So the frozen field thaws into a sea of very cold, very light particles. That is called the misalignment mechanism.

A haloscope hunts them by tuning a cold cavity until those swings nudge it into ringing. And inflation itself is a stuck field, held partway up its slope by the same friction.

caption:
How did pure consistency predict a critical exponent better than any experiment?

Near a critical point, many different materials share the same few numbers. Those numbers were long computed by summing approximate series, then fitted to data. The bootstrap asks something else: what numbers are even allowed?

Quantum theory demands that probabilities stay positive and that answers agree both ways. Those demands carve the space of possible theories, leaving only thin islands. Feed in a wrong number and the demands force a negative probability, so it is excluded. The three dimensional Ising theory sits inside an island a few millionths wide. The exponent says how fast the order fades as you creep up on the critical point.

Experiment pins the exponent to two parts in a thousand. This pins it far tighter.

So consistency alone fixed the number, with no model to fit. That method is called the conformal bootstrap.

Liquid helium flown on a space shuttle gave the best measured value, and the bootstrap still beat it. And the same logic bounded how particles can collide, ruling out theories nobody had written down.

What did you think the reason was?

caption:
Why does a smooth faucet stream always break into drops further down?

Near the tap the stream looks like a perfect glass rod. Water's surface behaves like a stretched skin that wants the smallest area. A long cylinder has more surface than the same water as beads.

So any tiny wobble in the stream's width is rewarded, and it grows. Slow wobbles grow slowly, and very fine ones cost surface, so one size wins. A wobble shorter than the stream is wide adds surface instead of saving it. A three millimetre stream picks a spacing of about thirteen millimetres.

That winning wobble pinches through, and the stream becomes evenly spaced drops.

So the smooth faucet stream is already unstable when it leaves the tap. That break up is called the Rayleigh-Plateau instability.

An inkjet printer uses it deliberately, driving the jet at the favoured wobble to make identical drops. And a spider's web beads into droplets after rain, for exactly the same surface reason.

Check it at home and tell me what you saw.

caption:
How can a black hole store ten to the seventy seven bits on a surface?

For ordinary things, capacity grows with volume. Twice the box, twice the storage. A black hole's capacity instead grows with the area of its horizon. Drop anything in and the horizon grows just enough to cover what was hidden. Whatever you drop in adds mass, and the horizon widens in step with that mass.

Count the horizon in Planck sized patches and take one bit per four patches. A Planck patch is the smallest piece of area physics can tell apart at all. A Sun sized hole is three kilometres across, which is a huge number of patches. Seventy seven digits for the hole. Twenty three for every hard drive on Earth.

Nothing else that size can hold more. That is the ceiling on information.

So a black hole writes everything on its surface, not inside. That surface limit is called the Bekenstein bound.

The holographic principle grew from this, proposing that any region's contents are written on its boundary. And it limits any computer, because packing more memory into a box eventually collapses it.

Did anyone explain it to you this way at school?

caption:
How can light shift an atom's levels when the atom will not absorb it?

Tune a laser to an atom's own colour and the atom absorbs it eagerly. Tune far away from that colour and almost nothing is absorbed. But the light's electric field still tugs on the atom's charges as it passes.

The atom stretches slightly in time with the field, and that costs energy. That extra energy adds on to the level own energy, so the level itself moves. The cost differs for each level, so the levels get pushed apart. A level is always pushed away from whichever level the light nearly connects it to. Two levels the light nearly joins always shove each other apart, never together.

The push is millions per second. Absorbed light is about one per second.

So far tuned light shifts an atom without heating it, which is how traps hold atoms. That is called the AC Stark shift.

An optical lattice builds an egg box of shifted energy, holding thousands of atoms in place. And an atomic clock must undo this shift carefully, or its trap would change the tick.

caption:
What holds the Hall resistance perfectly still while the magnetic field keeps changing?

In an ordinary metal, sideways resistance climbs steadily with the field. Cool a clean flat sample hard, add a huge field, and it goes into steps. The field forces the charges onto a set of sharply spaced energy rungs.

Every real sample has dirt, which bends those rungs up and down locally. Charges sitting in the dips are trapped and cannot carry current anywhere. Only channels running along the sample edge stay free to carry it. The resistance depends only on how many edge channels are running, and trapped charges run in none.

Classically it would drift thousands of ohms. Measured drift is microscopic.

So changing the field only fills or empties the trapped states, and the Hall resistance stays put. That is called a quantum Hall plateau.

The ohm is now checked against this effect, because it depends on no material detail at all. And graphene shows the same flat steps at room temperature, which makes portable standards possible.

Who else was taught this wrong?

caption:
Why does the Page curve tell you when a black hole starts giving information back?

A black hole slowly leaks light, and shrinks as it does. Early on, that light looks completely random, carrying nothing you could read. Each escaping piece is paired with a partner that fell inside.

So the outside light gets more tangled with the hole as time goes on. But the hole is shrinking, and its capacity to hold partners shrinks too. Tangle cannot exceed what the hole can hold, so the curve must turn over. Once the tangle has to fall, each new photon must match ones already outside, and that match is the message.

The turn comes about two thirds of the way through the hole's life.

So the Page curve turns when the leaking light must start carrying information out. That turning point is called the Page time.

A burning book does the same, since the smoke is scrambled at first and only later reveals the text. And a shuffled deck of cards is the same idea, because a few cards say little until you see most.

caption:
How can a black hole weigh 800 million Suns only 690 million years after the start?

A quasar found at that distance holds a hole of exactly that mass. Black holes grow by swallowing gas, but the gas fights back with its own light. That light pushes outward, and it caps how fast the hole can feed. Growing by e just means getting about two and a half times heavier.

At that cap a hole takes about forty five million years to grow by e. Starting from a hundred solar mass seed needs roughly sixteen of those steps. Growth at the cap needs 715 million years. Only 510 were available.

So either the seeds were far heavier, or the feeding briefly broke past the cap.

So an early black hole is a timing problem, not a mass problem. That feeding cap is called the Eddington limit.

A massive star obeys the same cap, which is why stars above roughly a hundred suns shed mass. And a feeding neutron star brightens to this limit, then holds there however much gas arrives.

caption:
Why can a lone energy level never sit alone at certain points in a crystal?

An electron carries a built in spin, which can point two ways. Physics without magnets looks the same if you run the film backwards. Running it backwards flips the spin and also flips the direction of travel. In a crystal, motions that differ by one row spacing are the same. At those points forward and back match.

At certain points in a crystal, reversing the travel direction brings you back to the same point. There the reversed state is a genuine partner, with the same energy and opposite spin. Reverse a half spin twice and it returns with a minus sign, so it cannot be its own partner. For half spin particles, that partner can never be the original state itself.

Whole spin allows one state there. Half spin insists on two.

So the energy level at those points always arrives in pairs. That forced pairing is called Kramers degeneracy.

A topological insulator conducts along its edges, because these forced pairs cannot be gapped away. And a magnetic field breaks the pairing, which is how spin measurements read out the split.

Which part of this surprised you?

caption:
Why did the nuclear shell model fail until spin-orbit coupling was added?

Nuclei with 2, 8, 20, 28, 50, 82 or 126 particles are unusually stable. That smells like filled shells, exactly as it does for atoms. The first attempt used a simple well, and it got the first three right.

After 20 it predicted 40, but nature clearly picks 28. Mayer and Jensen added a strong tie between a particle's spin and its orbit. That tie splits each shell hard, pushing one half far down in energy. The lowered half drops in with the shell below, and its eight extra places close that shell at 28.

A plain well says the next magic number is 40. Nature says 28.

So the shell model needed the spin to feel the orbit, and then every magic number fell out. That tie is called spin-orbit coupling.

Sodium's yellow light is really two close lines, because the same tie splits its outer level. And that tie drives topological insulators, where it flips the order of two bands entirely.

Did anyone explain it to you this way at school?

caption:
Why does the vacuum we live in look only temporarily safe?

Empty space is filled by the Higgs field, sitting in a valley. The valley is energy: empty space settles wherever that energy is lowest. How steep that valley is depends on the energy you probe it at. The top quark is heavy, and it drags the steepness downward as energy rises.

Around ten to the eleventh electron volts, the steepness crosses zero. Once the sides tip downward, the energy keeps falling, so a deeper valley lies beyond. Beyond that, a deeper valley opens, lower than the one we sit in. A slightly lighter top quark would keep us safe. Ours is heavier.

Getting there needs a rare quantum tunnelling, so the wait is astronomically long.

So our vacuum sits in a valley that is low, but not the lowest. We call that metastable.

Supercooled water is the everyday version, staying liquid below zero until something gives it a start. And diamond is metastable too, since graphite is lower, but the rearrangement takes effectively forever.

Around ten to the eleventh electron volts, the steepness crosses zero. Once the sides tip downward, the energy keeps falling, so a deeper valley lies beyond. Beyond that, a deeper valley opens, lower than the one we sit in. A slightly lighter top quark would keep us safe. Ours is heavier.

Getting there needs a rare quantum tunnelling, so the wait is astronomically long.

So our vacuum sits in a valley that is low, but not the lowest. We call that metastable.

caption:
Why does a fluid turn milky just as its liquid and gas become the same?

Below the critical point you see a clear liquid with a clear surface above it. Raise the temperature and pressure together, and that surface fades away. At the critical point it costs almost nothing to be denser here and thinner there.

So the fluid breaks into clumps of thick and thin, constantly reforming. As you close in on the point, those clumps grow from atom sized to huge. Ordinary liquid clumps are a nanometre. Here they reach five hundred. Light bends wherever the density changes, and it bends most off a patch about its own size.

When clumps reach the size of a light wave, they bounce light strongly.

So the fluid goes milky because its clumps have swollen to the size of light itself. That is called critical opalescence.

The sky is blue for a related reason, since air's own density lumps bounce blue light best. And milk is white because its fat droplets happen to match the size of light waves.

caption:
How can swimming bacteria make a fluid easier to stir, not harder?

Add solid particles to water and stirring always gets harder. Each rigid grain resists the flow around it, so it adds to the thickness. But a bacterium is not passive. It drives fluid backwards with a spinning tail.

That pushes fluid out along its body and pulls it in from the sides. When you stir, the flow tips the swimmers into a preferred angle. A stirred flow turns long thin swimmers and leaves them lingering along the stretch. Tipped that way, their own pushing points along the stirring, helping it along.

Water reads one. A dense swimming culture reads essentially zero.

So swimming bacteria pay the stirring cost themselves, out of their own food. That behaviour is called active matter.

A living cell stirs its own insides the same way, using motors instead of outside forces. And a flock of starlings turns together with no leader, since each bird supplies its own push.

caption:
Why do tiny magnets line up opposite when their charges only push each other apart?

In some crystals, each copper atom holds exactly one loose charge. Repulsion is so strong that two charges will not share a site, so nothing moves. But quantum rules let a charge borrow a moment on its neighbour's site. Two electrons may share one site only if their spins point opposite ways.

That borrowed hop is only allowed if the two spins point opposite ways. In quantum physics, letting a particle spread over more room always lowers its energy. Being allowed to hop lowers the energy, so opposite spins are cheaper. Same direction buys nothing. Opposite directions saves one hundred and sixty millielectron volts.

So neighbour after neighbour alternates, up down up down, right across the crystal.

So repulsion itself builds the magnets that point opposite. That borrowed hop is called superexchange.

High temperature superconductors start from this state, so their magnetism and their pairing share one origin. And an ordinary rust coloured oxide is antiferromagnetic for the same reason, through its oxygen bridges.

What did you think the reason was?

caption:
Why does a spin liquid answer a neutron with a smear instead of a sharp line?

In an ordinary magnet, all the little spins line up and stay put. Flip one spin and the flip travels as a clean wave with a fixed energy. A neutron bouncing off it loses exactly that energy, giving a sharp peak.

Now put the spins on triangles, where no arrangement can satisfy every neighbour. Neighbouring spins want to point opposite, and on a triangle the third can never please both. They keep fluctuating down to the lowest temperatures, never settling into a pattern. A flipped spin there splits into two loose two halves that wander apart. With no fixed pattern holding it together, a flip costs nothing to break in two.

An ordered magnet gives a line a fraction wide. This gives a smear.

So the neutron's energy is shared between two halves, in any split. A spin liquid therefore answers with what is called a continuum.

The fractional quantum Hall state splits charge the same way, into lumps worth one third. And a struck quark never comes out alone, since pulling on it makes new particles instead.

Which part of this surprised you?

caption:
Why does the drag on a sphere suddenly drop when it speeds up?

You would expect pushing through air faster to always cost more. A thin sheet of slowed air clings to the ball's surface as it flies. Past the widest point the air must climb against rising pressure, and the slowed sheet gives up. That sheet peels away early, leaving a wide low pressure wake behind.

The wide wake sucks backwards, and that suction is most of the drag. Speed up enough and that clinging sheet becomes churning instead of smooth. Churning air carries more punch, so it hugs the surface further around.

A smooth sphere sits near 0.50. Past the crisis it falls to 0.10.

So the drag on the sphere falls because a rougher flow clings longer and narrows the wake. That fall is called the drag crisis.

Golf ball dimples trigger it early, so a driven ball flies far further than a smooth one would. And a cyclist's rough textured suit does the same, tripping the air to narrow the wake behind.

Did anyone explain it to you this way at school?

caption:
Did the muon really disagree with theory, or did the error bar move?

A muon is a heavy cousin of the electron, and it spins like a tiny magnet. Put it in a ring and its spin wobbles at a rate set by its magnetism. Fermilab measured that wobble to a few parts per billion.

Theory must add up every way empty space can dress the muon. A cloud of short lived particles surrounds the muon, and each one nudges its magnetism. The messiest part involves quarks briefly appearing, and that piece is hard to pin down. One method reads it from old collision data. Another computes it on supercomputers.

Against the old data the gap is 249. Against the computers, 105.

So the muon may be fine, and the argument is really about the theory's own uncertainty. That piece is called the hadronic contribution.

The electron's version is a thousand times cleaner, because it is far less sensitive to quarks. And lattice computing is now the referee, since it needs no experimental input at all.

Guess before you scroll, then check.

caption:
Why does an atomic clock need one magic colour of trapping light?

To keep atoms still, you hold them in a standing pattern of laser light. But light pushes an atom's energy levels around, just by being there. The tick is set by the gap between those two levels, and nothing else. If it pushes the two clock levels by different amounts, the tick changes.

How much each level shifts depends on the colour of the trapping light. Plot both shifts against colour and the two curves cross somewhere. For strontium that crossing sits at 813.4 nanometres, deep in the infrared.

An ordinary trap colour moves the tick by kilohertz. The magic one, not at all.

So the clock is trapped hard and still ticks true, because both levels move together. That colour is called the magic wavelength.

An ion clock does the same trick with its trap fields, cancelling shifts instead of avoiding them. And optical tweezers for quantum computing use magic colours, so holding a qubit does not disturb it.

Who else was taught this wrong?

caption:
How did listening to current noise weigh a charge of one third?

Current is not smooth. It is grainy, because charge arrives in lumps. Listen to the hiss and its loudness tells you how big each lump is. Fewer, bigger lumps arrive more unevenly, so the same current hisses louder. Heavy raindrops on a roof sound different from fine drizzle, at the same downpour.

In a strong field, a cold flat chip enters a strange state at one third filling. Squeeze the current through a narrow gate so lumps pass one at a time. The hiss came out three times quieter than single electrons would give.

An electron carries one. These lumps carried one third.

So the current noise weighed the lumps directly, and they were thirds of an electron. Those lumps are called quasiparticles.

Shot noise in a photodiode does the same, telling you light arrives in countable lumps. And counting coins by the rattle of a tin works on exactly the same idea.

caption:
Why is there an energy ceiling for cosmic rays arriving from far away?

Space is filled everywhere by faint leftover microwave light from the early universe. That light is icy cold, barely a thousandth of an electron volt per piece. But a proton moving near light speed sees that light hugely blue shifted.

Above about fifty billion billion electron volts, that light looks like a gamma ray. The collision has to pay for a whole new particle mass, so below that energy nothing happens. The proton then absorbs it, makes a short lived heavy state, and sheds energy. It happens again and again, bleeding the proton back below the ceiling.

At ten to the nineteenth it crosses a thousand megaparsecs. Ten times higher, fifty.

So the highest energy cosmic rays we see must come from nearby galaxies. That cutoff is called the GZK limit.

The Pierre Auger Observatory sees the spectrum bend right where this predicts, using thousands of detectors. And high energy gamma rays are blocked the same way, by starlight filling intergalactic space.

Go and test it, then report back.

caption:
Why does gravity have a tiny quantum correction to Newton's law?

Newton's law says the pull falls off as one over distance squared. Einstein adds a small correction, growing as the masses get closer. Quantum theory adds another, from the jitter of space itself between the two masses. The two masses swap faint ripples of space, and those ripples add a pull of their own.

This piece is calculable, because it comes only from the long range, gentle wobbles. Unknown short range physics acts only at a point, so it cannot make a slow fall off with distance. The hard, unknown short range part of gravity does not touch this piece. So we get a genuine quantum gravity prediction, without knowing the full theory.

For two protons a femtometre apart, both corrections are absurdly small.

So a quantum correction to Newton is fully computable, even without a finished theory. That approach is called effective field theory.

Pion physics is handled the same way, describing low energy nuclear forces without solving the strong force. And water waves obey simple rules at long scales, whatever the molecules are doing underneath.

Which part of this surprised you?

caption:
How can light bounce off light when torch beams pass straight through?

Two torch beams crossing a dark room show no sign of hitting each other. Light carries no charge, so one beam has nothing for the other to push. Quantum rules let energy be borrowed for an instant, long enough to make a pair. But light can briefly turn into a pair of charged particles and back again.

While that pair exists, the second beam can push on it. The nudged pair turns back into light heading a new way, so the beams have bounced. The pair lives for almost no time, so the effect is fantastically weak. Lead nuclei flying near light speed carry enormous fields, giving a strong enough source.

Twelve events expected from background. Fifty nine actually seen.

So two beams of light do push each other, through a borrowed pair. That is called light-by-light scattering.

A magnetar's field is so strong that empty space near it bends light like glass. And a gamma ray can bend around a heavy nucleus's field, with no matter needed at all.

caption:
Why did the 1919 eclipse shift star positions by 1.75 arcseconds?

Newton's gravity, with light treated as tiny bullets, already predicts a small bend. That guess gives 0.87 arcseconds for a ray grazing the Sun's edge. Einstein said mass does two things: it slows clocks, and it curves space itself.

Slowed clocks alone give Newton's answer. Curved space adds an equal second helping. Light runs slower on the side nearer the Sun, so the beam swings that way, like a wheel in sand. Newton's bending is 0.87. Einstein's is 1.75. Eddington measured the larger. Only during totality can you photograph stars right beside the Sun. Your eye traces the bent ray straight back, so the star looks shifted away from the Sun.

Eddington's plates showed the stars pushed outward by the larger amount.

So the eclipse doubled Newton's number, and curved space was the missing half. That is called gravitational light bending.

A distant galaxy can appear as a ring, because a nearer mass bends its light around every side. And a radio signal grazing the Sun arrives late, from the same slowing of clocks nearby.

caption:
Why is it strange that the whole microwave sky has one temperature?

The oldest light we can see fills the sky, from every direction. Its temperature matches everywhere to one part in a hundred thousand. Two things match in temperature after they have touched and traded heat.

But that light left when the universe was only 380 thousand years old. Nothing travels faster than light, so nothing could have carried heat any further than that. In that time, light could only have crossed a patch about two degrees wide. A patch in contact spans two degrees. The sky spans one hundred eighty.

So opposite sides of the sky had no chance to trade anything at all.

So the matching microwave sky demands that those patches once touched, before being flung apart. That is called the horizon problem.

Inflation answers it, by starting the sky as one tiny touching patch then stretching it enormously. And the same stretch explains why space looks flat, since any curve gets ironed out.

Check it at home and tell me what you saw.

caption:
How can a Kibble balance use a coil strength it never actually measures?

The kilogram is now fixed by a number, so a balance must realise it. In force mode, current in a coil inside a magnet holds the mass up. The lift is the coil strength times the current, the same strength that sets the voltage. That balance needs the coil strength, and it is hard to measure well.

So the same coil is then moved slowly through the same magnet, with no mass. Moving it makes a voltage, set by the same coil strength and the speed. Divide one measurement by the other and the coil strength cancels out.

Guessing the coil leaves you with milligrams. Cancelling it gives micrograms.

So the Kibble balance compares weight against electrical power, and the coil drops out. That cancelling trick is called virtual work.

A Wheatstone bridge works the same way, by finding a balance rather than measuring anything absolutely. And a beam balance compares two masses directly, without ever needing to know gravity's local strength.

caption:
Why does empty space only spark at 1.3 billion billion volts per metre?

Dry air breaks down and sparks at about three million volts per metre. There, the field rips charges off air atoms and they avalanche through. In a perfect vacuum there is nothing to rip, so nothing should happen.

But empty space constantly borrows pairs of charges for an instant, then pays them back. A strong field can pull such a pair apart and settle the debt with its own energy. Dragging two opposite charges apart, the field does work, and that work is the payment. To do that it must supply the pair's rest energy across their own tiny size.

Air sparks at seven digits of volts per metre. Vacuum needs nineteen.

So empty space does spark, but only when the field can pay for a whole pair. That threshold is called the Schwinger limit.

The strongest lasers are still a thousand times too weak, so this has never been seen directly. And a magnetar's surface field comes within reach, which may be why they flare so violently.

Which part of this surprised you?

caption:
Why does a proton weigh 938 mega electron volts when its quarks add to only nine?

A proton holds three quarks, two up and one down. Weighed on their own, those three come to about nine million electron volts. That leaves ninety nine percent of the proton's weight unaccounted for.

The quarks are tied together by a field that pulls harder as they separate. Holding them in a tiny box costs enormous energy, and energy weighs. Squeezed into a tiny space, the quarks must move violently fast, and that motion is energy. Nine from the quarks. Nine hundred and thirty eight in total.

So most of a proton is churning field, not stuff.

So the proton is mostly bound up energy wearing the disguise of mass. That is called mass from binding.

A helium nucleus weighs less than its parts, and that missing weight is what the Sun burns. And a wound spring is very slightly heavier than a slack one, for exactly the same reason.

caption:
Why can a dirty chip settle at exactly 25812.807 ohms?

No two chips are alike. Their dirt and thickness differ everywhere. Yet cooled hard in a strong field, they all report the same number. The field bends the charges into tight circles, locking their energies into rungs.

Dirt traps every charge in the middle of the chip, so the bulk carries nothing. At the rim a circle cannot close, so charges skip along the edge instead of being trapped. Only the rim conducts, in channels that cannot turn around or double back. Each channel carries exactly the same current for a given push. With no way back, no dirt can scatter them, so nothing about the chip can change the number.

One channel gives 25812.807 ohms. Two give exactly half.

So the dirty chip reports only Planck's constant divided by the charge squared. We call that the von Klitzing constant.

The ohm is now defined through this, so any good lab can rebuild the standard for itself. And it gives the fine structure constant directly, checking a completely different branch of physics.

caption:
How can a taller barrier become easier for an electron to cross?

In ordinary matter, a wall you cannot climb leaks only a faint trickle through. Make the wall taller and that trickle drops away fast. In graphene, a single sheet of carbon, charges behave like massless particles.

Such a charge also carries a label saying which band it rides in. That label is locked to the direction of travel, so head on it cannot flip. Inside a tall barrier, the only states available belong to the other band. Raise the barrier past the gap and the electron energy now lands inside the band below. Its label lines up perfectly with those states, so it just carries straight on.

Head on, an ordinary electron gets nowhere. This one goes clean through.

So a taller barrier hands the electron a better match, not a bigger wall. That is called Klein tunnelling.

Very strong fields near a heavy nucleus let pairs appear the same way, straight out of the barrier. And it makes graphene hard to switch off, which is why simple graphene transistors leak.

Who else was taught this wrong?

caption:
Why does magnetism die 37 nanometres inside superconducting lead?

Cool lead below seven kelvin and it pushes magnetic field out of itself. It does that by running a current in a thin skin, which cancels the field inside. In the normal metal, that current would fade away against resistance.

Below the transition, charges bind into pairs that all share one wave. The pairs all move together to oppose any field, and that pushback is what weighs it down. That shared wave gives the magnetic field an effective weight inside the metal. A heavy field cannot travel far before it runs out, so it fades within a set depth. A field with weight cannot spread. It dies away over a fixed distance.

Thirty seven nanometres when superconducting. Thousands when it is not.

So the field stops just inside the lead because the paired charges give it weight. That is called the Meissner effect.

The W particle is heavy for the very same reason, weighed down by the Higgs field filling space. And a superconducting shield keeps stray fields out of a delicate quantum chip entirely.

caption:
Why does helium refuse to freeze however cold you make it?

Cool almost anything enough and its atoms should settle into a rigid pattern. Helium stays liquid right down to absolute zero, at ordinary pressure. Quantum rules forbid an atom from being both exactly placed and exactly still. A light atom pinned in place must move fast, and fast means it wanders further.

Helium atoms are very light, so that leftover jiggle is unusually large. And helium atoms attract each other only very feebly, far weaker than most. So the well that should trap each atom is shallower than its own jiggle.

Water freezes under one atmosphere of pressure. Helium needs twenty five.

So helium stays liquid because its own restlessness outweighs its feeble pull. That leftover motion is called zero point energy.

Superfluid helium flows with no friction below two kelvin, straight out of this same restlessness. And solid hydrogen melts strangely low for the same reason, because it is light too.

What did you think the reason was?

caption:
Why does an area law make one dimensional systems easy for a computer?

Describing a hundred quantum spins normally needs a list thirty one digits long. That is because every spin doubles the number of possibilities you must carry. But real ground states of a chain are not random. They are unusually tame.

Cut the chain in two and measure how tangled the two halves are. In a line, the cut is a single point, so the tangle comes from the border only. A tame chain of a hundred spins scores about one and a half. A random one, sixty nine.

Tame tangle means the state compresses into a short chain of small tables.

So an area law caps how tangled a one dimensional chain can be, so a laptop can hold it. That is called matrix product states.

Density matrix renormalisation uses exactly this, and it solves chains to near perfect accuracy. And in two dimensions the cut is a whole line, so the tangle grows and the trick struggles.

Which part of this surprised you?

caption:
Why can a few gentle DNA pulls outweigh hundreds of rough ones?

Grab a single DNA strand with laser tweezers and pull it slowly open. Repeat it and the work you spend differs every single time. Every pull costs at least the true energy difference, and usually more. Pull fast and some work is lost as heat, so only the gentlest pulls come near the true cost.

Averaging the work the ordinary way gives you too large an answer. Instead you average the exponential of the work, which weights small values heavily. A pull five units above the minimum counts a hundred and fifty times less.

So a handful of unusually gentle pulls carries almost the whole average.

So the rare gentle pulls hold the real answer, and an exact relation extracts it. That is called the Jarzynski equality.

The same trick measures how much energy it really costs to unfold a single protein molecule. And computer simulations use it to get true free energies out of short, violent runs.

Did anyone explain it to you this way at school?

caption:
Why does a Weyl semimetal grow surface states shaped like open arcs?

On any ordinary metal surface, the allowed states trace closed loops. Here they trace arcs that simply stop, with loose ends in the middle. In the bulk, two bands touch at isolated points instead of along a surface.

Each touching point acts like a magnetic source, but in the space of states. It means the states wrap around that point the way a field wraps around a magnetic pole. They come in pairs with opposite sign, and every crystal's charges must cancel. One touching point carries plus one. The whole crystal carries zero. The surface has to carry the wrapping the bulk points leave over, and only an arc can.

The arc on the surface has to start at one point and end at its partner.

So the Weyl semimetal arcs are the visible ends of bulk sources. That link is called the bulk boundary correspondence.

A topological insulator shows it too, since its insulating inside forces a conducting skin. And the quantum Hall edge channels are the same story, forced by what the bulk holds.

Guess before you scroll, then check.

caption:
Why do particle physicists draw little pictures instead of doing integrals?

A collision's answer comes as a long sum of ever smaller corrections. Each extra junction costs a small factor, so the busier pictures matter less. Each correction is a huge integral, and writing them out by hand is brutal. Feynman noticed each term matches one simple cartoon of what could happen.

A line means a particle travelling, and a junction means two of them meeting. So you draw every cartoon allowed, then read the integral straight off it. The pictures are bookkeeping, not photographs of any real particle journey.

At three loops there are seventy two pictures. At five, over twelve thousand.

So the little pictures are a filing system for terms, not photographs of events. They are called Feynman diagrams.

Chemists draw curly reaction arrows the same way, as bookkeeping for how electrons shift about. And a circuit diagram is the same idea, since it stands for equations rather than actual wires.

caption:
How can deeper inward mean lower energy in a holographic picture?

One idea says a theory on a surface can describe a whole volume inside. The volume has one extra direction the surface does not have. So something on the surface must play the role of that extra direction.

On the surface, the free choice is what size of detail you look at. Looking at finer detail means using shorter waves, and shorter waves carry more energy. The theory itself lives on the surface, so its finest detail sits right at the edge. Fine detail, high energy, sits near the boundary. Coarse detail sits deep in. Look at a trillion volts and you stay shallow. A billion, and you go deep.

Moving inward is the same as blurring the picture, step by step.

So deeper inward is just looking at coarser detail. That correspondence is called the energy scale dictionary.

Blurring a picture step by step is the everyday version, where the finest detail is dropped first. And a confining theory ends the extra direction at a wall, which is why its particles have a lowest mass.

caption:
Why does a changing neutrino flavour prove that neutrinos have mass?

Neutrinos come in three flavours, tied to the electron, muon and tau. A beam made of one flavour arrives partly as another. Each flavour is a blend of three states with definite masses.

Each of those travels as a wave, and its wave ticks at a rate set by its mass. A heavier state carries more energy, and more energy means a faster tick. Different masses tick at different rates, so the blend slowly slides out of step. A sliding blend is a different flavour, so the beam appears to have changed.

The two gaps are tiny: seventy five millionths, and two and a half thousandths.

So a changing neutrino flavour means the states tick differently, which needs different masses. That change is called oscillation.

The Sun's missing neutrinos were the first clue, since two thirds arrived as other flavours. And two slightly mistuned tuning forks beat the same way, because their ticks drift apart.

caption:
How rare is a movie where entropy runs backward for a moment?

In everyday life you never see a smashed glass reassemble itself. But squeeze a single molecule with tweezers and it sometimes gives energy back. These backward moments are not forbidden. They are just heavily outvoted.

There is an exact rule for how heavily: each unit of disorder costs a factor. One unit of disorder means roughly three times more ways forward than back. The forward version is more likely by the exponential of the disorder made. Five units of disorder, a hundred and fifty times rarer. Twenty units, far worse.

For a real smashed glass, that count runs to billions of billions of units.

So backward entropy is allowed but crushed by sheer counting. That exact rule is called the fluctuation theorem.

A molecular motor in your cells slips backward sometimes, and this rule fixes exactly how often. And a tiny heat engine can briefly run in reverse, which now limits nanoscale machine design.

Which part of this surprised you?

A muon has the same charge and the same spin as an electron. It differs in one way only. It is about two hundred times heavier. Mass is stored energy, so a heavier particle is simply carrying more of it. Extra mass means extra energy, and nature likes to shed energy when it can.

A weak interaction lets the muon turn into an electron plus two ghostly partners. The electron cannot do the same, because there is nothing lighter for it to become. The weak interaction is feeble, so the whole business takes microseconds rather than instants.

Half a million electron volts for one, against a hundred and six million.

So the muon decays only because it outweighs the electron, with somewhere to fall. That slow route is called the weak interaction.

Cosmic ray muons still reach the ground, because their fast motion stretches that lifetime many times over. And the tau is heavier again, so it has even more ways down and lives far shorter.

Did anyone explain it to you this way at school?

caption:
How might a robin see the Earth's magnetic field with a chemical pair?

Earth's field is feeble, millions of times weaker than the jostling of body heat. So a simple magnetic sensor inside a warm bird should be drowned out. In the bird's eye, blue light splits a molecule into two linked fragments.

Each fragment holds one unpaired spin, and the two spins start matched. Earth's field turns one spin slightly faster than the other, so they drift apart. The two fragments sit in different surroundings, so the same field turns one a little faster. Matched and unmatched pairs react along different chemical routes.

Earth's field turns a spin in under a microsecond. The pair lives about that long. Heat cannot hurry the turning, so a feeble field still wins if the pair waits long enough.

So the robin does not fight the heat. It reads a pair of spins before they react. That is called the radical pair mechanism.

Cryptochrome is the suspected molecule, and disrupting it with weak radio waves confuses migrating birds. And chemists watch magnetic fields change reaction yields the same way, in ordinary test tubes.

Guess before you scroll, then check.

caption:
If black holes scramble fastest, why does the butterfly front crawl at 0.816c?

A black hole spreads a small disturbance through itself as fast as anything can. Poke it in one spot and the mess spreads outward as a front. You might expect that front to travel at the speed of light.

It does not. In the simplest case it moves at about four fifths of that. Scrambling is not one signal racing out. It is chaos spreading through stuff. Chaos passes from one piece to the next, and every handover takes time light would not need. A dropped disturbance falls toward the horizon and drags along it as it spreads. Part of the disturbance motion goes into falling, so less of it is left for spreading sideways.

Light travels at one. The chaos front travels at nought point eight two.

So a butterfly front is a spreading of chaos, not a signal, and we call its pace the butterfly velocity.

A hot fluid spreads disorder at a similar pace, which links chaos to how heat travels. And a cold atom simulator measures the same front directly, by poking one atom and watching.

Who else was taught this wrong?

#astrophysics #astronomy #signalprocessing #waves #jeeadvanced #apphysics #class12physics #howthingswork #sciencefacts #learnphysics #fermi
